#7821. Tool Trials: Putting Ridgid’s Cordless Crown Stapler To the Test

Is a cordless stapler a real upgrade, or just a nice-to-have? I put one to the test to find out.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Last spring, I was sitting at home with my family watching football on a Sunday when my wife caught me doing what I often do: scrolling Zillow. “What don’t you like about the house we’re in?” she asked. I told her that ever since I finished the basement, I’d missed having a shop space to work on projects.

Her answer: “Then build that garage you always wanted.”

Fast forward eight months, and my new garage is up. I’m insulating the main level and sheathing it with OSB before adding cabinets and shelving and moving on to the upstairs. It’s a big garage; we’re talking 30-plus rolls of insulation on the main level, so on a run to pick up the next half-dozen rolls, I wandered down the tool aisle and saw the Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler staring back at me.

Beyond getting the garage insulation up faster, it looked like a tool I’d keep using on future wiring and upholstery projects, and the same goes for anyone re-screening a porch, recovering a chair seat, or tacking down low-voltage wire.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The Ridgid 18V Cordless 3/8-in. Crown Stapler is a 3-lb. battery-powered stapler that runs on Ridgid’s 18V battery platform. It features an integrated LED light, an onboard wire and screen attachment, a depth adjustment knob, and a belt hook.

It drives 3/8-in. crown (T50) staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long. Ridgid claims it can drive 105 staples per minute and up to 6,800 staples on a single charge of a 4.0 Ah battery.

One last note, and in full transparency, I’m a regular user of Ridgid tools myself: Ridgid offers a lifetime service agreement on its tools as long as you register them within 90 days of purchase.

My goal was to install a half-dozen rolls of insulation, then run wire to an outlet to try out the wire attachment. I wanted to see how easy the tool was to use, whether it jammed, and what I liked and didn’t like about it.

The short version: this tool is awesome. No jams, nothing wonky. It’s as simple as load, point, and pull the trigger. It took a little playing with the depth knob to get the staples seating at the right depth, but I had it figured out within a handful of staples.

I really like the wire attachment. I try to keep my wiring clean and neat, usually with zip ties and tie mounts. With this attachment, running the wire was simple, and the stapler did it much more neatly than I expected.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the onboard LED light. It has its own trigger, separate from the firing trigger, so I could turn it on only when I needed it.

It’s also easy on the battery. I put up six rolls of insulation during the test and a couple more off camera, and the indicator on the 2.0 Ah battery didn’t budge.

There were a couple of things I didn’t like, though they’re minor. First, Ridgid advertises dry-fire lockout on this stapler, which I took to mean it wouldn’t fire once the staples ran out. On mine, it still did. To be fair, it never marred the work surface, which Ridgid lists as one of the lockout’s benefits, so it may be doing part of its job. But it was annoying to pull the trigger and have nothing come out, and it made it easy to miss that I was out of staples.

Second, the depth drifted. After every 20 or 30 staples, I’d notice they were no longer seating at the depth I’d set and were starting to sit proud. I don’t know if that was due to denser 2x4s or inconsistencies between strips of staples, but it was something to keep an eye on. When I noticed it, I’d add a few clicks on the depth knob.

I really like this tool. If you’re only insulating a garage, it’s really nice to have, but not essential. You could get by with a standard stapler. That said, the LED light, the wire attachment, and the price, especially with the battery and charger included, make this a tool I know I’ll use more than I expected on future projects.

A cordless 3/8-in. crown stapler kit with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger, depth adjustment, an onboard wire and screen attachment, and a built-in LED light.

The tool alone retails at The Home Depot for $119, but for the last few months, there’s been a special buy that includes the tool, a charger, and a 2.0 Ah Ridgid battery for $104.

Ridgid is owned by Emerson Electric Co., which makes the red Ridgid plumbing and pipe tools directly. The orange Ridgid cordless power tools, including this stapler, are made by Techtronic Industries (TTI), the company behind Milwaukee and Ryobi, under a licensing agreement with Emerson.

No. Staple guns need staples that match the tool’s crown width, leg length, and wire gauge. The Ridgid 18V crown stapler takes 3/8-in. crown staples from 1/4 to 9/16 in. long, including standard T50 staples. Other staplers may use different types, like narrow-crown or other heavy-duty series, so check the tool or the manual before you buy.

#7820. 14 Types of Blinds Every Homeowner Should Know

Updated Nov 5, 2026 3:38 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

If you’ve weighed the benefits of curtains, shutters, and blinds in your search for the right window coverings for your home and you’ve settled on blinds, you’re in good company. According to a study by research firm Market Research Future, the size of the window blind market was an estimated $75.48 billion in 2025, and it’s expected to grow to $136.35 billion by 2035. Another research firm, Global Market Insights, found that blinds and shades dominated the window treatment industry in 2025.

With so many different types of blinds on the market, how do you decide which will suit your home best? Whether you’re looking for something sleek and modern or traditional and classic, this guide will help you figure out which ones might be the right pick for your windows.

Blinds are a type of window covering composed of numerous slats, vertical or horizontal, that can be tilted or rotated to adjust the amount of light entering a space. Blinds made of aluminum or vinyl are typically the most cost-efficient types, but there also are blinds crafted of fabric and wood.

They can be installed inside the window frame or above it. Window blinds are typically mounted with specially designed brackets that are sold with the blinds.

Blinds consist of many parts. The headrail, for example, is the top part of the blind that contains the operating mechanisms such as the cords, pulleys, or tilt wands. The headrail provides structural support for the blind. The valance is the decorative cover that hides the headrail and its workings.

Depending on the style of the blinds, there may be a cord that draws the slats up and down. A wand adjusts the tilt of the louvers, which are the collection of narrow horizontal slats that tilt to adjust the amount of light that passes into the space.

The slats are suspended from a track that runs along the top of a window frame. This style of blinds collects less dust than other types of blinds and is easy to clean. The slats just need to be wiped down with a damp cloth.

Best For: Affordability and minimal maintenance

Blinds.com’s vertical blinds are textured, available in a variety of colors, and are guaranteed to fit.

The Home Decorators faux wood Venetian blinds are cordless, making them safe for households with pets or young children.

Mini blinds are like Venetian blinds, with some minor differences. Like Venetian blinds, they are typically made from aluminum or vinyl instead of wood or bamboo. Mini blinds have smaller slats than Venetian blinds, though: Mini-blind slats are usually an inch wide or smaller. While these two types of blinds perform the same way, mini blinds have a sleeker design and thus tend to look more modern and contemporary.

With a minimalist design and cordless operation, the Achim mini blinds are safe and stylish.

Wood blinds are a popular choice for those looking to add an element of luxury to their window treatments since wood blinds offer a natural, timeless look that never goes out of style. Not only do they exude sophistication, but they are also incredibly durable and can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. They can be painted or stained to match any color palette, and different slat sizes are available to accommodate shoppers’ specific needs. Wooden blinds tend to be horizontal—or Venetian—style, though vertical wooden blinds are also available.

Best For: Homeowners who are in it for the long haul—these are built to last

Levolor’s 2-inch wood blinds have cordless lift and wand tilt and come in a variety of wood stains.

Aluminum blinds are one of the most popular types of window blinds because of their affordable price and lightweight yet durable design. A sleek, modern look that can complement many decor styles, they are easy to install and incredibly long-lasting. Aluminum blinds also come in a variety of colors, sizes, and textures, allowing homeowners to customize the look of their windows to suit many different aesthetics. In terms of energy efficiency, aluminum blinds help keep a home’s interior cooler by reflecting the sun’s rays away from the window. This helps reduce air conditioning costs since less energy is required to maintain steady temperatures inside the house.

Best For: Easy installation and durability

Sleek and affordable, Blinds.com’s 8-gauge aluminum blinds are available in a variety of neutral colors.

If you’re looking for blinds to cover sliding doors or large windows, consider panel blinds. These window treatments are composed of several panels affixed to a headrail at the top of the window. Each panel is attached to a carrier that slides along a track in order to open or close the blinds. They offer a unique look that differs from standard vertical blinds, making them a great choice for design-forward shoppers.

Roller blinds are technically a type of window shade, making them different from many of the other types of blinds on our list. An alternative to curtains, these shades are made up of a single piece of fabric material that rolls up and down to control the amount of sunlight that enters the space. Roller shades can be made from a variety of fabrics, ranging from sheer materials to opaque options. While roller blinds might have a reputation for being low quality and not performing well, their design has actually come a long way in recent years.

Chicology’s blackout roller shade has a cordless design and is made from hypoallergenic polyester that won’t attract dust.

UNISHASDES bamboo blinds  partially filter sunlight and come in a variety of sizes and finishes.

Motorized blinds are a modern window covering solution that allows users to open and close their blinds using a remote control, phone app, or voice command. Some models come with sun sensors that automate the opening and closing of your blinds at certain times of the day. Unlike traditional blinds that must be adjusted manually, motorized blinds use either electric or battery-powered motors to raise and lower them. This makes it easier to control the lighting in a room without ever having to leave your seat. Today, many window blind types can be motorized.

Our Recommendation: Custom Home Collection Designer 2-Inch Wood Blinds at The Home Depot, priced from $105.70.Featuring a traditional Venetian aesthetic, these motorized blinds offer both familiarity and convenience.

Our Recommendation: Coolaroo Exterior Roller Shade at Amazon, priced from $35.25.This exterior window treatment is affordable, cordless, protects against UV rays, and comes in a wide range of finishes.

Sometimes called layered or dual shades, zebra blinds consist of two layers of fabric, each with alternating horizontal bands of sheer and opaque fabric. You can adjust, or roll, the fabric to line up the stripes on the two layers of fabric, meaning opaque is lined up with opaque, and sheer with sheer; this allows light to enter. If you roll the shade such that the opaque stripes on one layer are lined up with the sheer strips on the other layer, the effect is that of an opaque shade, and no light comes through.

Our Recommendation: Chicology Zebra Blinds at Amazon starting at $36.58. These cordless, pull-down zebra blinds are available in four colors and numerous sizes.

Also called cellular blinds or cellular shades, honeycomb blinds are constructed of two sheets of fabric that are seamed together horizontally at regular intervals. When looking at these blinds from the side, the resulting pattern somewhat resembles that of a honeycomb. Highly insulating, the design is considered one of the most energy-efficient, and the cellular construction is also good at noise cancellation

Best For: Energy-efficiency; they also offer a modern vibe

Our Recommendation: BlindsAvenue Cellular Honeycomb Cordless Shade at Amazon starting at $32.85.Made of polyester, these cordless, pull-down blinds are available in 10 colors and a wide variety of sizes.

Pleated blinds are made from a single length of woven fabric that is pressed into sharp, horizontal pleats at regular intervals, yielding a zig-zag appearance. The blind is raised or lowered to adjust the amount of light entering the room. While they’re often compared to honeycomb blinds, pleated blinds don’t offer the same insulating properties as cellular blinds. Pleated blinds offer a clean, modern look.

Best For: Decorators in search of an elegant, minimalist  look.

Our Recommendation: Calyx Interiors Pleated Fabric Window Shade at Amazon, priced from $30.97.Semi-sheer and cordless, these pull-down blinds are available in four colors and several sizes.

“Blackout” is a descriptor applied to a number of types of blinds and shades that are designed to block out all light. Not only do they work to block light from entering a room, but they’re also typically made of thick, dark-colored materials that absorb light. Blackout window coverings might be cellular blinds or roller shades.

Best For: Rooms in which someone needs to sleep during the day.

Our Recommendation: Persilux Custom, Cordless Blackout Cellular Blinds at Amazon starting at $63.99. These cordless, pull-down blinds are available in five colors and numerous sizes.

The prices listed here are accurate as of March 31, 2025.

#7819. "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I thought I'd pass along this smart and readable analysis from Bill Otis (Ringside at the Reckoning); as I've mentioned before, he and his coauthor Paul Mirengoff are my go-to people for hardheaded, pragmatic, but principled conservative views. They are probably on balance more conservative than I am, but I always much enjoy their legal and political commentary. An excerpt:

In an election where overwhelmingly the preeminent issue was affordability — in other and more candid words, the increasingly obvious decline in the standard of living huge numbers of people are feeling — what has Trump been occupying himself with? Here's a partial list: Building the White House ballroom (from which, in a tone deaf rendition that defies description) he gave his election post-mortem; re-doing the East Potomac Golf Course to make it a "premium" experience; building a Triumphal Arch no one asked for or thought about when they elected him; demanding prosecutions for imaginary vandalism at the Reflecting Pool; invading Greenland; making Canada the 51st state; re-naming Lake Ontario; re-naming the Gulf of Mexico; and perhaps most prominently, making sure his name gets put on the Kennedy Center even though he had nothing to do with its creation. Then there are numerous other items: Trump passports, Trump one-dollar gold coins, and "commemorative" $100 bills, to name three.

Exactly what does this Adventure in Narcissism seem like to the voter — actually, the millions of voters — who feel like they're being stretched thin? You don't need a florid imagination to answer that one. They gave their answer last night.

It's not like Trump has had no successes. He's made three excellent Supreme Court appointments. He has tackled corrosive and unjust racial preferences like no one else had the guts to. He declines to bow to transgender bullying. Objective economic data show that, whatever "feelings" may be, the economy grew at a healthy clip just this last quarter. He used force with Iran when, for nearly 50 years before him, Presidents were content to kick the can down the road as the mullahs got closer and closer to getting the atomic bomb.

These are considerable and important achievements, not less so because Trump often acts like an oaf. But his character flaws throw a wrench into nearly everything he does. It's less that he's an oaf than that he's a child, far too often content to do what's quick and easy while leaving to adults what's messy and hard. The catch is: He's supposed to be the adult. The main thing behind the failures that got Trump his butt-kicking last night is not his classlessness, his carefree attitude [toward] the truth or his gargantuan self-absorption.

The whole thing, as usual, is much worth reading.

There’s always something new and exciting on the horizon in the world of gardening. Around this time every year, various organizations release their favorite gardening and landscaping trends for the coming year. From the color of the year to new plants and outdoor décor, the list below represents our favorite 2027 gardening trends for you to consider as you plan or update your outdoor space in the coming months.

Garden Media Group has identified ancient blue as the garden color of the year for 2027. As the first manufactured color in history, blue was created by the Egyptians 5,000 years ago to imitate precious lapis lazuli. While blue is consistently the favorite color around the world, it is the rarest color in the garden, showing up in fewer than 10 percent of flowers. “This makes growing it in the garden feel like victory,” says Katie Dubow, president of Garden Media Group.

Here are some planting and décor tips to seamlessly incorporate this calming color into your garden:

Gardeners prefer more from their edible plants than just fruits and vegetables to harvest, according to Monrovia’s 2027 Garden Design Trends Study. “We’re seeing shoppers be more discerning in their edible choices,” says Katie Tamony, chief marketing officer and trend spotter at Monrovia. “They’re looking for plants that add a design element or feel more exotic than the common choices their neighbors grow. People are also interested in edible plants that look good all season long.”

Adding an edible garden ranks among the highest-interest projects in Monrovia’s survey, with more than 45 percent of respondents saying they are looking for more unique selections. Enhance your edible garden with specialty herbs; berries with year-round interest; and conversation-starting selections like pomegranate, figs, kiwi, and olives.

After years of beige minimalism and tidy rows of shrubs, the “Let’s Go Rococo” theme is all about exuberance over restraint, says Dubow. Emerging in early 18th century France, rococo design was a deliberate rebellion by artists and craftsmen against the stiff grandeur of Baroque and societal wealth inequality. Think flowers, shells, gilded flourishes, ruffles, jewel-tone palettes, and asymmetry. “It’s ornamental, romantic, a little over the top, and joyful,” notes Dubow.

Here are some ways to infuse rococo style into your garden:

Garden Media Group’s OutdooRx trend positions the garden as medicine, says Dubow. “In the United Kingdom, doctors now “socially prescribe” gardening programs to patients, and research continues to show that gardening lowers stress hormones like cortisol while boosting mood-lifting dopamine and serotonin,” she explains. Approaches like the Sunday Garden Trend can provide relaxation.

Fortunately, you don’t need a prescription to benefit. You can create a therapeutic garden in your own backyard with these helpful tips:

This long-handle digging tool allows gardeners to work the soil more comfortably (and for longer periods of time) from a standing position.

National Garden Bureau also tracks garden trends, especially when it comes to which specific plants are the most popular in a given year. “Coming up in 2027, we see an enormous interest in hellebores, and that is our Year of the Crop for Perennials,” says Diane Blazek, executive director for All-America Selections at National Garden Bureau.

Often called the Christmas rose or Lenten rose, the hellebore is a hardy perennial that does well in full shade and brings beauty to winter and early spring gardens when most other flowers have faded. It produces elegant 2- to 3-inch blossoms in a cup shape that resemble roses. Hellebore flowers grow in a variety of colors, so you have plenty of options. It grows in USDA Hardiness Zones 5 to 8, and does best in cottage gardens, winter gardens, or woodland gardens. Take note that this plant is toxic and should be handled with caution.

As another season of the popular show The Gilded Age is released this month, romance and beauty are alive and well in gardens, too. This look maximizes the popularity of European-inspired garden design with an elevated, modern twist, shining a spotlight on classic plants like roses, peonies, hydrangeas, and boxwood. In addition to these timeless plants, this trend showcases artful hedges, chartreuse foliage, and collector statement plants.

“This trend appeals to established gardeners,” says Tamony. “Homeowners who have invested in their interior design are taking that high-end look to the garden.” Their interest in rare, collector plants is increasing, and Monrovia’s research shows their willingness to pay for premium plants and exquisite blooms is up between 5 and 9 percent since 2025.

Another style that is expected to be popular is the Palm Springs outdoor space. This works well for gardeners looking to create an attractive desert oasis through containers as well as the landscape. “The Palm Springs Style trend is all about creating a calming, wellness-focused outdoor space that feels more upscale,” says Tamony. With this aesthetic, gardeners can transform their landscape by choosing structured succulents and lush, tropical colors found with species from Agave, Bougainvillea, Mandevilla, and tropical hibiscus.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.

#7817. Your Level Might Be the Wrong Size, and It Could Be Throwing Off Your Work

A short level works for some projects, but longer surfaces need a wider check. Learn how to pick the right size and use it accurately.

Levels come in many different shapes and sizes, and figuring out how long a level should be for a certain project isn’t always straightforward. Choosing the right size matters because a level that’s too short can miss uneven spots, while one that’s too long can be difficult to use in tight spaces.

Here’s how much of a surface a level should cover, which sizes work best, and when overhang is okay.

It depends on the project, but a longer level is usually better for checking bigger surfaces. A shorter one might show that the middle of a board is level without catching a problem closer to either end.

The level doesn’t have to stretch across the entire surface, though. A 24-inch level can work on a four-foot shelf, for example, as long as the installer checks several spots along its length. For longer surfaces, a smaller level can sit on a long, straight board to check a wider area. A laser level is another option, especially when lining up things across a room.

The way the level sits on the material matters, too. A little sawdust or dirt underneath can affect the reading, so both surfaces should be clean. The tool also needs to sit firmly without rocking.

There’s no set rule for how much of a surface a level needs to cover, but it should fit comfortably and have enough contact to stay steady.

Different sizes work better for different jobs:

“Use a 4-foot carpenter’s level for framing whenever you have room for its length,” according to The Home Depot. “Warps or waves in the boards can throw off a shorter carpenter’s level.”

Another common concern is whether the level can hang over the edge of whatever is being checked. Some overhang is fine, provided the tool has enough support to stay steady.

If it starts tipping or rocking, a shorter level will likely work better. The bubble doesn’t need to be directly above the material, either. It can still give an accurate reading even when that part of the tool hangs past the edge.

#7813. Judge advances McDonald’s McRib lawsuit that alleges deceptive marketing

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients. (Photo from Getty Images)

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients.

The plaintiffs allege that the McRib, which costs $7, is shaped to look like ribs and misleads customers in ads to think that it contains rib meat instead of cheaper pork cuts.

In Chicago, U.S. District Judge April Perry of the Northern District of Illinois dismissed some claims, but she did not accept the McDonald’s argument that a reasonable customer could expect the McRib to contain rib meat. Perry said ads of the rib-shaped patties could possibly be an attempt to defraud, but more proof was needed, according to coverage by Reuters.

“Plaintiffs’ proffered understanding of ‘McRib’ is not unreasonable or fanciful,” Perry wrote.

McDonald’s contends that it does not use hearts, tripe or stomach as McRib ingredients, which the suit alleges. The fast-food giant, which has sold the sandwich since 1981, said distinctive product names do not fool reasonable consumers.

“This lawsuit distorts the facts, and ⁠the claims are meritless,” McDonald’s said in a statement.

#7811. ‘Judge Stone’ by Viola Davis and James Patterson wins inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Legal Fiction

Viola Davis (left) and James Patterson appeared in New York City in March for a discussion of their book, “Judge Stone,” which was chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction. (Photo by Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

Judge Stone, by acclaimed actor Viola Davis and prolific author James Patterson, has been chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction.

The prize, which is being awarded by the ABA Journal, the University of Miami School of Law and the University of Miami College of Arts & Sciences, was determined by a panel of judges that featured former ABA Presidents Deborah Enix-Ross and Carolyn Lamm, California Court of Appeal Justice Lee Smalley Edmon and Turow himself.

A public poll hosted by the ABA Journal also chose Judge Stone as the favorite for the prize from among the field of three finalists, which also included A Pair of Aces by Marie Benedict and Victoria Christopher Murray, and Grave Danger by James Grippando.

The Turow Prize aims to honor the work that best illuminates the role of lawyers in society and their power to effect meaningful change. It is a successor to the prestigious Harper Lee Prize, which the Journal and the University of Alabama previously awarded to outstanding works of legal fiction, including novels by John Grisham, Michael Connelly and Grippando.

Judge Stone is a legal thriller about a Black woman judge from a small town in Alabama who presides over a controversial case. It is the first collaboration between Davis and Patterson.

Davis is one of a select group of celebrities who are “EGOT” winners for taking home Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards. In 2025, she was honored by the Golden Globes with the Cecil B. DeMille Award for “outstanding contributions to the world of entertainment.”

She won an Emmy for TV’s How to Get Away with Murder and has appeared in numerous films, including Academy Award–nominated Doubt, The Help and Fences (for which she received the Oscar). She won two Tonys (for Fences and King Hedley II) and a Grammy for best audiobook, narration and storytelling recording for her memoir, Finding Me. She also took home a Screen Actors Guild Award for her role in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom.

In his long career, Patterson has created notable characters and series including Alex Cross, the Women’s Murder Club, Jane Smith and Maximum Ride. He’s written true stories about the Kennedys, John Lennon and Tiger Woods, and has coauthored No. 1 bestselling novels with Bill Clinton, Dolly Parton and Michael Crichton. He’s received an Edgar Award, ten Emmy Awards, the Literarian Award from the National Book Foundation and the National Humanities Medal, according to jamespatterson.com.

Named in honor of pioneering attorney and international bestselling author Scott Turow—the “father of the modern legal thriller”—the Turow Prize seeks to unearth compelling works of fiction that illuminate the dynamics of law, the justice system and the human experience.

Turow’s 13 fiction and two nonfiction books, including Presumed Innocent and the current Presumed Guilty, have sold over 30 million copies worldwide and been adapted for film and television.

Davis and Patterson will receive a cash prize and a signed copy of Presumed Innocent at the award ceremony and reception on Nov. 19 hosted by the University of Miami, along with the exclusive right to feature the prestigious Turow Prize logo on their winning book’s cover.

#7810. Manhattan’s Lost Its Screen Presence

The other weekend, I pulled up Woody Allen’s Manhattan (1979) on YouTube because I’ve been starved for the highbrow and the funny, a rare marriage that movies used to achieve with some regularity, but now hardly ever bother to attempt. 

Let’s disregard the plot, here, and the characters, for there is a great deal about both that resists easy or simple discussion in the present American climate, and focus instead on the surface: the look of the film, the feel of it, the particular New York it conjures and holds up to the light like a jeweler with a loupe.

My feeling for New York City has always come in a peculiar Southern blend of love and affliction. I don’t care for the rudeness, or the flat, clipped music of the accent, the way a sentence up there lands like a screen door.

But some years ago—high school, through college, on into my early twenties—my family made a yearly trip north around Christmas, either before the holiday or just after it. Mother, father, sister, brother, and myself. We took rooms near Times Square. We saw the shows. We ate at the restaurants with the heavy menus and the heavier check.

My mother and sister went shopping. The first year, my father, brother, and I made the mistake of going along, and we stood there in Macy’s—the famous one—waiting among the racks like the accused waiting outside a courtroom, until finally we drifted, defeated, to the section where they sell the beds.

And there, without much discussion, the three of us climbed up onto the display mattresses and took our naps in full view of the shoppers, three Southern males asleep in a snowdrift of goose-down pillows while New Yorkers and tourists alike rushed past us toward their purchases. We never went shopping with the women again.

Manhattan opens with a voice reciting its own first sentence, over and over, dissatisfied, revising itself in real time: “Chapter One. He adored New York City. He idolized it all out of proportion…” What we are watching, before a single frame of story unspools, is the composition of New York, its narration into existence by a man who admits, within the first 30 seconds, that his version of it is a romance rather than a record.

Isaac Davis, played by Allen, drafts Manhattan, discards the draft, drafts it again, each revision a further layer of gloss over a city that by the film’s own admission was never quite there to begin with. Gershwin swells. The skyline assembles itself in black-and-white, denuded of the actual chromatic clutter of a real metropolis: no exhaust-brown, no bodega-awning red, no garbage-day green.

The result is not less than New York, but more: a hyperreal locus, a city more New York than New York, purified into its own advertisement. By the time the narration settles on its final version of the sentence, we have watched a myth being built in front of us, brick by adoring brick, and we have watched it happen with the confidence of a myth that knows it will outlast its subject.

Consider, in this light, why the film insists on monochrome: color would have been the honest choice, but the lesser one. The black-and-white suggests a setting already understood as the past. Allen may have shot it that way because that’s how he remembered the city from boyhood. The image does not become nostalgia, but arrives already nostalgic, already a simulation of an image of a city, twice removed from the referent before the referent has even appeared.

The formal choices reward the kind of patient gazing that asks not what a shot means, but what it does: how it organizes the eye, how it withholds and releases. Willis’s camera holds wide and still. And it is Allen—small, voluble, anxious—who is made to cross the frame, dwarfed by the buildings on either side. The city is never made to accommodate the man. The compositions insist on this dynamic with a kind of moral clarity: architecture as fixed, permanent, indifferent; the human figure as transient, comic, and a little absurd against so much stone. There’s no accident in the fact that the funniest lines are often delivered in the widest shots: the humor is small; the buildings aren’t.

The bench scene deserves a word of correction before anything else, since even devoted admirers of the film misremember it: the silhouette behind Isaac and Mary at dawn is not the Brooklyn Bridge, but the Queensboro—the 59th Street Bridge, the one Simon and Garfunkel made feel groovy—shot from a little park at Sutton Place, the bench itself (according to my Internet searches) trucked in by the crew for that single image and trucked out again after.

Which is, in its own way, the whole method of the film in miniature: even the most iconic, most seemingly eternal image of New York on offer here was a temporary prop set down in front of a bridge for one morning’s shoot. The permanence is manufactured.

>>> Mamdani’s $22 Billion Housing Lunacy Proposal Will Socialize the Skyline

The film’s two registers—the melancholy of the story and the euphoria of the imagery—do not cancel each other out so much as run on parallel tracks, and the gap between those tracks is where the picture does its real work. Consider the function of the montage sequences against that of the dialogue scenes. The montages are non-diegetic in feeling even when diegetically grounded: they exist to establish a rhythm of civic wonder, asking nothing of the viewer but admiration.

The dialogue scenes, by contrast, are shot with almost no cutting at all: long, static two-shots, characters talking past each other in real time, the visual monotony forcing attention onto the halting, self-undermining texture of what is actually being said. The film is, formally speaking, telling us two different things simultaneously and daring us to notice the seam: the city as sublime, continuous, orchestral; the people within it as fragmented, hesitant, unable to complete a sentence about their own feelings without doubling back on it, exactly as the opening narration doubled back on itself.

The visual grandeur is never undercut by irony—Allen does not mock the skyline—but it is placed in a kind of formal tension with human smallness that neither element resolves. That unresolved tension, held shot after shot without comment, is the melancholy, and it’s built into the cutting pattern before it is ever spoken aloud.

Now, alas, to the present city—the real one—as it stands to be reorganized, and to the politics of the mayor presently promising to reorganize it.

New York has been bleeding people for years. The arithmetic of it is no longer a matter of dispute: the city and state have shed net domestic migrants every year for over a decade, hundreds of thousands of taxpayers relocating to Florida, Texas, and the Carolinas, taking with them not just households, but the tax base itself, since a disproportionate share of those leaving sit at the top of the income ledger.

Economists have written this story many times over. They generally tell it thus: rent regulation suppressing housing supply, tax rates chasing away the earners who fund the very programs meant to help everyone else, business formation slowing as regulatory and labor costs climb, the tax burden left to redistribute itself across a shrinking and less mobile base.

It is, by now, a familiar and well-documented indictment, and further democratic-socialist experimentation of the kind Zohran Mamdani proposes (price controls, municipal enterprises, steeper taxation of capital) is likely only to accelerate a trend already well underway. What economists rarely pause to mention, in this careful accounting of bad economics, is the bad aesthetics: the fact that a shrinking, flattened, price-controlled city is not only a poorer city, but a less legible one, a city that stops producing the aspirational, ambitious textures that an environment needs to be worth writing a Manhattan about in the first place.

Rent freezes, city-owned grocery stores, free buses, government-run childcare, union-built housing pinned beneath the same frozen rents, higher taxation on the wealthy who have historically financed the city’s theater of distinction: this is a program that wants New York to stop signifying, to stop chasing visual excess, to level unnecessary beauty, and to disappear the glorified aesthetics that defined Manhattan (the film).

The free market is a machine for producing urban variety and diversity. It sorts neighborhoods into strata, forces competition among restaurants and shops and doormen and galleries to distinguish themselves, and out of that sorting comes precisely the texture Isaac Davis fell in love with: the specific bookstore, the specific delicatessen, the specific bench.

Price signals are semiotic: a rent freeze not only caps a number, but also removes the mechanism by which neighborhoods differentiate themselves through investment, turnover, and risk. A city-owned grocery store cannot, by definition, be a particular grocery store as Zabar’s is particular because its entire justification is that it’s the same everywhere, fungible, a public utility rather than a character.

>>> Mamdani’s “Tax First, Think Later” Budget Plan

Today’s Manhattan looks different from Allen’s black-and-white mise-en-scène partly because of the regulations governing its buildings: facade inspection mandates have wrapped whole blocks in sidewalk sheds for years at a time, and emissions caps are pushing owners to retrofit prewar towers with electric heat pumps, through-wall units, and rooftop equipment.

Universal childcare and free buses, worthy as they may sound to the ear of compassion, are administered goods, which, besides being economically harmful to the very communities they purport to help, do not accumulate the patina of specificity, tenacity, drive: the worn brass rail, the eccentric owner, the 40 years of small adjustments to changing taste. These details turn a mere service into a grand milieu that a person can photograph in black-and-white and mean something by it. You can’t rent-control your way to a Rizzoli’s.

The specific aesthetic New York that this film so lovingly constructs was the product of an economy that permitted radical unevenness, permitted some blocks to become Sutton Place and others to remain what they were. The old New York could be ugly in reality and beautiful in art because it left room for artists to look upward, to take its disorder and inequality and noise and transfigure them into myth. The danger of Mamdani’s New York is not merely that it becomes poorer or more regulated, but that it becomes aesthetically downward-looking, a city preoccupied with administering what is wrong with it rather than generating the beauty that makes people want to imagine it as something more.

A politics organized entirely around flattening unevenness in the name of universal provision will tend to produce a city whose surfaces mean less. Mamdani’s New York, should it fully arrive, promises a setting that is more equal and more affordable and, quite possibly, less quotable, a city no future Woody Allen would find himself compelled to open his picture with “Chapter one. Dissatisfied. Starting over.”Top of Form

Bottom of Form

Which brings me back to that Christmas Macy’s, my father asleep on a showroom mattress, three Southerners playing hooky from the shopping. I think that’s what I’m partially mourning when I mourn the New York of Manhattan: not the wealth, not even the skyline, but the specificity, the sense that the city was a collection of unique rooms rather than a portfolio of interchangeable services.

The people I know who have left for Texas, for Florida, for the redder counties of this reddening country, will tell you they left the taxes, the crime, the cost. But listen long enough, and what they are really grieving, underneath the ledger, is that the New York which could still surprise you is going, has been going for a while now, and no rent freeze, however kindly meant, will bring it back, because you cannot legislate a city into being irreplaceable. You can only leave it alone long enough, and love it hard enough, to let it become so on its own, the way, once, at dawn, on a borrowed bench under a borrowed bridge, it did.

#7809. Why MAHA Must Keep Conservative Roots

For over two years now, the MAHA movement led by Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has attracted some unlikely bedfellows. Everyone—from religious homeschool moms to more hippy food-as-medicine advocates—has filled rooms to try to find solutions to America’s chronic disease epidemic. But sometimes the tent grows so big that it invites people whose ideas are completely at odds with the movement’s original priorities.

The goal of healthier Americans should be fairly bipartisan, but the means to achieve it, and the underlying philosophies that drive it, can differ. Technocrats and transhumanists offer interesting solutions to the mechanisms of our dysfunctional healthcare system, such as updated systems for patient records and data collection. However, true and lasting reform requires solutions rooted in more conservative moral worldviews that maintain the natural order of God’s design.

Nowhere were the divergent approaches to making America healthy again more apparent than at last month’s MAHA Summit in Washington, D.C.

Bryan Johnson, the man doing his best to “not die,” headlined the Summit, touting his new religion, which claims the “body is God.” His followers embrace an “opening ritual” (like prayer, communion, or the sign of the cross), and a “mantra” (like the Our Father).

>>> Restoring Reproductive Health: A Policy Framework for Advancing Restorative Reproductive Medicine and Payment Reform

They even have a path to repentance. Rather than confession and forgiveness from God, there is “a part where people apologize to their body for something they’ve done that has inflicted harm upon themselves,” Johnson explains. Apparently, they absolve themselves of their own sins.

Rather than accept a view of human nature rooted in the theological principles of the Judeo-Christian tradition, Johnson wants to “reimagine human nature.” He discussed revolutionizing the way humans age and extending man beyond his “biological limit.”

His fellow panelists, Alex Colville and Max Marchione, agreed that the foundations of good health—diet, sleep, and exercise—can go only so far. Genomic medicine, including gene-editing technology, must be embraced.

One need not be a devout Christian to understand the danger of Johnson’s rhetoric. We are already seeing discussions of selective gene editing and “made-to-order” babies.

And while Johnson occupies the extreme end of the longevity movement, he does represent a concerning faction of the MAHA zeitgeist that believes humans can overcome any limitations placed on them—and will go to extraordinary lengths to do so.

This progressive narrative is in direct opposition to the more organic, grassroots uprising of those who believe that medical sovereignty, healthy soil and food, and meaningful human relationships are the fundamentals for human flourishing; those who believe that freedom is not found by removing all limitations, but through embracing struggle, pain, and even death to grow, change, and become the image bearers of Christ. Again, even if one does not embrace Christianity, a human-centered approach requires humility, a virtue often lacking in the technocrat’s vocabulary. Scientific progress can be good, but it should not be fueled by hubris or come at the expense of rejecting the natural order.

Thankfully, not all at the Summit embraced Johnson’s new, dystopian religion.

Michael Boes, the first chief MAHA officer of Steak ’n Shake, echoed the cries of those who embrace the real world, with all its obstacles, rather than one built on artificial intelligence and gene manipulation.

For Boes, the solution is much simpler. Eating real food and returning to the fast food of our grandparents’ generation—cooking fries in beef tallow and using buns without seed oil—can help restore vibrancy and order to the body.

For others, like the martial artist Michael Chandler, it’s about performing well, having a good attitude, and setting an example for his family. “My gratification is my children,” he said on a panel with MAHA-focused athletes.

>>> America’s Chronic Disease Crisis: How to Understand and Reverse It

Chandler also commented on the failures of striving for perfection, saying, “If we strive for perfect, we will never reach it … if perfection is the goal, you’re always going to be let down,” and intimated that doing so can lead to mental health disorders. He encouraged the audience to “enjoy themselves like a human being, sometimes.”

There is no such thing as moral neutrality. Any position or policy, whether it prioritizes American farmers or creates genomic medicine, has an end in mind, and ultimately a why that motivates it.

The MAHA movement has the potential to return to what is good, true, and beautiful, a harkening back to the food and medicine of our forefathers. Or it can lead to transgression, not merely progression, of the limits that God has placed upon human biology.

If conservatives fail to remember the why of MAHA, it will soon be co-opted by dystopian mad scientists who eat sandy green mush and clone themselves.

The future of the MAHA movement doesn’t have to be binary. Technological advancement and AI can drive meaningful change in how Americans reclaim medical sovereignty and access their own health data. But it must not abandon its roots in the fundamental truths of human nature.

One can and should pursue a healthy life, but death will never be optional. MAHA is about redeeming the time we’re given, not trying to outlive our expiration date.

#7808. China Dominates Global Shipbuilding and the United States Ranks 14th by Tonnage. The Case for an Allied Counterweight.

On October 13, the Navy celebrated its 251st year, a birthday that predates our Republic by almost a year. President Trump used this historic moment to announce the opening of a new Baltimore shipyard and recommit to a national maritime revival he launched early in his second term.

While the President’s commitment is vital, reviving America’s shipping and shipbuilding will take generations. Today America ranks 14th in shipbuilding by tonnage, operates 190 U.S. flagged ships representing less than 0.3 percent of total shipping engaged in U.S. trade, and graduates several hundred naval architects when thousands are needed. Thankfully, we have trusted allies who would benefit from our maritime revival and support an American maritime renaissance.

It is time to make the American revolution in shipping a global project that lets partner nations benefit together and course-correct our collective overreliance on China’s shipbuilding and shipping.

Trump’s welcome leadership comes after decades of neglect. But this isn’t an impossible task, and as a nation, we’ve overcome worse. Still, today’s threats make reviving our shipping and shipbuilding industry an urgent prerogative of national survival.

Today, American ships can move only 267,799 shipping containers in total, while nationally over two million containers move monthly, making our economy and security dependent on ships from nations many consider hostile. Mitigating this dependency will require a fleet of 1,315 various classes of ships, and building them or securing those ships can most effectively be achieved with our trusted allies.

>>> Why the U.S. Navy Needs Escort Carriers

The pace of this revival has quickened in recent months—buoyed in part by allies. On Sept. 30, Vice President Vance attended the groundbreaking of Port Alpha—a $3 billion shipbuilding project that will double today’s American commercial shipbuilding capacity. The Baltimore project, Arsenal-2, is anticipated to generate 3,100 direct and an additional 11,000 indirect jobs to support nuclear submarine production.

Importantly, this project splits the cost of capital investments between upstart firm Anduril ($3.7 billion) and the government ($ 2.9 billion). Before this there were significant investments by Canadian shipbuilder Davie ($1 billion) in Galveston, Texas to build icebreakers, and by South Korean shipbuilder Hanwha ($5 billion) in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; who is being contracted to build maritime training vessels and recently missile tracking vessels for the Navy.

This is a good beginning, but we need more than 250,000 new skilled shipbuilders and engineers, and new shipyards to be built if America’s industry is to deliver the maritime capacity it needs.

Today’s sustained bipartisan effort builds on work begun in Spring 2022 by a small group of experts called the Revolution in Shipping. It lives on in presidential executive orders and the SHIPS for America Act, which the Senate is reviewing. They all acknowledge that without our allies’ technical capacity, our maritime revival will falter. Consider the shipbuilding bridging strategy called the Finland Model, which uses initial orders for overseas construction, conditioned on parallel domestic investment to eventually build the ordered ships in the U.S.

Attracting investment capital to American shipyards has so far been a success. But ships must be built, and that requires technical competence as well as industrial capacity. It also requires sustained demand for American-made ships, which can only be assured if they become globally competitive over time. Today, initial orders for new American ships will be for the federal government, but near-term decisions must set the conditions for this to expand into more commercial orders, like Port Alpha.

Timing for America’s maritime revival is opportune; the global commercial fleet today averages just over the typical viable service life of 20 years, and new technologies are taking hold. One is civilian use of nuclear propulsion, where American industry can build on decades of naval nuclear propulsion. Here again, however, is where trusted allies familiar with and trusting of American nuclear propulsion and sharing a common security interest can set market conditions to welcome a new era of nuclear shipping.

>>> To Build Golden Fleet Frigate Fast, Two Shipyards Are Needed

Today China dominates the global shipping and shipbuilding market and our allies, like South Korea, are hungry to retake market share. More broadly, a growing group of like-minded nations is seeking to grow their own maritime industries, as India made clear at the recent third Sagarmanthan maritime conference.

As such, now is the time to form a maritime group of nations to ensure our collective efforts complement and nurture our revived maritime industry and no longer remain hostage to a single nation: China. The idea is memorialized in legislation sponsored by Rep. Young Kim (R-Calif.), the FLEETS Now Act.

Modeled on the G7, this “M9” maritime group can enable collective action in multinational maritime regulatory bodies (e.g., IMO, IAEA, UN), coherently focus investments, and act to defend against Chinese predation (see USTR sec. 301 complaint) that could kill our maritime industrial revival before it leaves the pier.

Moving out and forming a maritime group starts with a White House invitation to like-minded nations. But success will depend on energetic American ambassadors in key capitals who can communicate the agenda and ensure the right participants. The recent departure of Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle from Greece could complicate things in a critical nation for the effort. As such, her replacement, preferably someone with shipping or shipbuilding experience, should be named quickly and confirmed by Congress.

Keeping investments flowing into the U.S. maritime industry, reviving strategic shipyards, and ensuring sustained orders depends on sustaining today’s momentum, something an M9 with key allies can facilitate.

#7807. South China Sea is Key to Invigorate Positive U.S.–Malaysia Relations

Reality is coming home to roost for many in southeast Asia regarding the implications of China’s emboldened claims in the South China Sea, which would place all of the seabed resources and fish stocks within its Ten-Dash-Line. Acquiescence to this would cost Malaysia dearly. Fortunately, it’s awakening to the fact that a new approach is needed.

At the 9th South China Sea Conference hosted by Maritime Institute of Malaysia in Kuala Lumpur, the desire for quiet resolution of disputes played out against reality. That reality is China’s insistence and that its neighbors acquiesce to its claims. For the past few years, the Philippines has been at the forefront of a more vigorous pushback on those claims—even lethally like last year’s fratricide of several Chinese Coast Guard sailors killed in a collision with their own Navy destroyer while harassing Philippine vessels.

If Malaysia fails to strike a balance in relations with Beijing and secure its economic rights in the South China Sea, the political implications would be significant. For one, China has consistently ranked as Malaysia’s top trade partner since 2009, making a crisis with Beijing quickly an economic dilemma. But at the same time, Malaysia’s national oil and gas company Petronas is having to seek new petroleum reserves deeper in contested the South China Sea.

Reduced output is driving Petronas to search for new wells to restore lost output; production dropped by 2.1 percent Q1 2026, continuing a yearlong trend. On the table now are exploration of at least five deep water blocks in Malaysia exclusive economic zone that will surely agitate Beijing. The result could be a replay of when Petronas chartered the drill/survey vessel West Capella to explores these waters in 2020, resulting in a month’s long crisis with China.

>>> Two Decisive Theaters for Safeguarding America in Dangerous Times 

The ghosts of the 2018 election loom on some minds. That’s when the long dominate political party, UMNO, was ousted and its Prime Minister eventually jailed for corruption—some of it emanating from the 1MDB scandal. During that election, Beijing actively supported UMNO setting back its local interests for a time. Importantly, UMNO lost its hold of the kingmaker eastern Malaysia states of Sabah and Sarawak critical to carry for whoever wants to be prime minister. And both states are beneficiaries of the offshore petroleum industry in the South China Sea.

The inevitability of crisis with Beijing over Malaysia’s resource rights in its waters looms, with hotly contested Malaysian elections coming before the end of 2027. Despite this, the current prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim, has taken an overly conciliatory posture with Beijing. He stated in July that he rejects “inevitable conflict” over its claims in the area, and in August accepted China’s use of force to settle its dispute with Taiwan, but then walked these comments back days later.

Prior to these less than helpful statements by Ibrahim, President Trump visited Kuala Lumpur in October 2025 for a very positive trip. Given the stakes today, the need for more petroleum production and management of South China Sea crises, renewed American senior level engagement is warranted—the sooner the better given looming elections.

>>> 10 Years After the Permanent Court of Arbitration Ruling—Might Makes Right in the South China Sea 

Between now and the Malaysia elections, the goal for the U.S. should be to telegraph its regional presence as a benefit to upholding norms of behavior at-sea beneficial to Malaysia—while deterring China from a wider confrontation. This would marry America First with Malaysia First in a very tangible way over maritime rights.

However, better relations with Kuala Lumpur will require addressing at least one sticking point: managing differences over Israel that the current Anwar administration has taken. All this likely becomes moot if Saudi Arabia signs onto the Abraham Accords, likely drawing Malaysia along.

Malaysia is a strategically located nation with a moderate population. The potential for forging even closer ties based on shared interests in the South China Sea are high—and can be done without forcing unnecessary friction with China.

#7806. Lawprof's First Amendment Case Against Univ. of Kentucky, and a Case's "Journey so Circuitous it Would Make a Baggins Blush"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Benjamin Beaton Tuesday (W.D. Ky.) in Woodcock v. Capilouto (E.D. Ky.):

Ramsi Woodcock, a tenured University of Kentucky law professor, has been under investigation for more than a year for controversial comments regarding Israel and Palestine. The alleged comments varied in both content and forum: an online petition calling for the invasion of Israel, listserv blasts to the University faculty and broader legal academy accusing Israel of genocide, the interjection of far-afield remarks about colonization at an antitrust panel in Hong Kong, shouts of "Free Palestine!" while driving two law students near campus, and more.

None of the remarks came in the classroom and none appears to have disrupted school activities. Yet all related in some manner to his role as a state-employed professor—rendering all the more curious the University's July 2025 decisions to promote him to full professor one week and call him in for questioning (literally) the next. {Curiouser still, Woodcock maintains that the remarks in question dated as far back as February 2024 and were known (at least in part) to the University since March 2024.}

The following week brought a public denunciation from the University's President, the start of a formal investigation into potential harassment under Title VI, reassignment from teaching duties to "professional development," and a (since rescinded) ban from campus. {This first of two "Notice[s] of Investigation" laid out four allegations that Woodcock "may have violated" the University's code of conduct and other policies. The notice declared (without elaboration) that the "investigation … is consistent with the First Amendment" and "addresses requirements under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act." A second notice, based on reports from four students, identified four additional allegations that may have "created a hostile environment on the basis of race, color, or national origin."}

Rather than participate in the investigation, however, Woodcock filed this [federal] lawsuit …. The pleadings characterize his treatment by leaders of the University and its law school as retaliation for protected academic or personal speech, violations of the Due Process and Establishment Clauses, and racial and religious discrimination…. The issue ripe for resolution today is Woodcock's request for temporary emergency relief halting the investigation and reinstating his teaching duties.

This is Woodcock's second or third such request, depending on how one counts. And it follows a journey so circuitous it would make a Baggins blush.

The judge previously assigned to this case held a preliminary-injunction hearing in December 2025. Instead of granting or denying interim equitable relief, however, that judge decided to abstain [under Younger v. Harris] on the ground that the University investigation should precede any federal adjudication. The Sixth Circuit, in the spring and summer of 2026, declined to issue a stay, reversed on appeal, and declined to accelerate the mandate. {See Woodcock v. University of Kentucky (6th Cir. 2026) (Because the "the disciplinary proceedings against Woodcock remain[ed] in a preliminary, investigatory stage," the proceedings were not "ongoing," rendering Younger abstention inapplicable). Concurring with the denial of Woodcock's request to immediately issue the mandate, Judge Gilman wrote that "the panel's opinion" did not "in any way limi[t] the sound discretion of the district court regarding how to proceed on remand," but instead "simply h[eld] that the district court erred in declining to accept jurisdiction based on Younger" without "purport[ing] to dictate what should happen upon remand; i.e., whether the district court should immediately proceed with a ruling on Woodcock's preliminary-injunction motion, or whether it should first consider the University's motion to dismiss, or whether it should stay proceedings to allow for the University to complete its investigation."}

Woodcock, meanwhile, filed a parallel lawsuit and TRO request in state court in September 2026—relief that the Franklin (County) Circuit Judge denied without prejudice. {The Franklin Circuit Court consolidated the new case's request [for] a TRO with the First Amendment suit Woodcock originally filed in federal court seeking to prevent former-Judge Van Tatenhove from assuming his role as dean of the UK Law School. After this Court denied his requests for emergency relief, Woodcock voluntarily dismissed the federal claims and refiled in state court.} The Sixth Circuit then remanded and reassigned this federal case to a judge outside the Eastern District after one of that court's [judges] was appointed dean of the law school. Woodcock had previously filed still another lawsuit—also reassigned here, and also to eventually land in state court—seeking to block the dean's appointment on First Amendment grounds. The University investigation (led by a private law firm) resumed in September. And this Court held a TRO hearing in October. Although the investigator anticipated that this phase of the investigation would finish by November 2, that date has come and gone.

Such unusual litigation can raise unusual—and unusually tricky—legal questions. This is true here, even though the crux of Woodcock's claim is superficially simple: the University leaders (Defendants here) took adverse action (investigation and reassignment) against him because of his constitutionally protected speech (chiefly, at least on his telling, Woodcock's self-titled "Petition for Military Action Against Israel"). But resolving this question, at least in the context of preliminary equitable relief, raises several others that Supreme Court precedent leaves significantly undertheorized.

None of the answers to these questions are obvious based on the record in this Court or the precedential decisions of others. Whether an investigation into speech and related conduct amounts to unconstitutional retaliation depends on whether the First Amendment protected the underlying speech and whether the state's response would deter a person of "ordinary firmness" from speaking similarly. Protection for the speech, in turn, depends on whether Woodcock spoke in either his personal or his "academic" capacity. And even if one of those carve-outs apply, courts may still ask whether the "employee's interest in speaking on a matter of public concern outweigh[s] the employer's interest 'in promoting the efficiency of the public services it performs through its employees.'" {Courts also consider "whether the statement (a) impairs discipline by superiors or harmony among co-workers, (b) has a detrimental impact on close working relationships for which personal loyalty and confidence are necessary, (c) impedes the performance of the speaker's duties or interferes with the regular operation of the enterprise," or (d) undermines the mission of the employer."} Additionally, the appropriateness of interim equitable relief turns on similarly difficult—even incommensurable—considerations, including the burdens on Woodcock's ongoing political speech (which appears to have continued in forums outside the classroom), the Commonwealth's interest in controlling the taxpayer-subsidized education offered to its citizens and future officers of the court, and the public's interest in open dialogue, effective investigations, and the avoidance of harassment.

Each of these determinations, courts have illustrated time and again, is fact-dependent. And although a previous judge held an evidentiary hearing nearly a year ago, time and events have not stood still. Woodcock has not, at least not yet, shown that the mere fact of an investigation would chill an ordinary speaker (to say nothing of a tenured professor) in these strange circumstances from engaging in speech on public questions inside or outside the classroom. After all, a university has an interest in "determin[ing] for itself on academic grounds who may teach, what may be taught, how it shall be taught, and who may be admitted to study."

Nor has Woodcock yet shown that the idiosyncratic lawprof speech at issue—in listservs, foreign conferences, links from the UK website, carpools, and the like—is necessarily protected, heedless of forum or audience. {For instance, whether institutional IT policies that restrict a professor's use of school email resources amounts to a "prior restraint," is hardly clear given the prevalence of content-neutral time/place/manner restrictions. And whether a professor's off-topic panel remarks amount to an unprotected "shout-down" or instead protected academic speech, for example, likewise casts at least some doubt on Woodcock's argument that this amounts to pure academic or political speech.} To be sure, whether he spoke in his professorial capacity is hotly contested by the parties—and cannot be determined with confidence or specificity at this stage.

Whether reassignment from all teaching duties would deter a speaker in a retaliatory manner is a closer question. This is particularly true because the University has seemingly identified no past or future campus disruption, little risk that Woodcock's speech has or will infect classroom instruction, and any reason why responses other than prior restraint would be unavailable if Woodcock stepped outside the bounds of his role in the future. On the other hand, Woodcock hasn't convincingly identified any aspect of this investigation or reassignment that is vindictive, disproportionately burdensome, or otherwise out of the ordinary.

Such showings are neither obvious nor obviously foreclosed on the current record. Indeed, they are not susceptible to prudent resolution by a distant district judge in the middle of a semester, when interim relief measured in two- or four-week increments [the duration of typical TROs -EV] is highly unlikely to benefit Woodcock in a manner that outweighs the concomitant disruption to the University's orderly governance of academic affairs. Since Woodcock bears the burden of justifying temporary emergency relief, but has not carried it, the Court must deny his TRO request. When in doubt, the Sixth Circuit has reminded us, "[t]he administration of the university rests not with the courts, but with the administrators of the institution.

These are important questions worthy of further evidentiary presentation, however. To that end, the Court will schedule a second preliminary-injunction hearing later this month. The balance between state governance and individual speech can tilt too far in either direction, of course, and investigations cannot last forever. In hopes of limiting any federal judicial intervention to its appropriate role, and with "reluctan[ce] to trench on the prerogatives of state and local educational institutions," therefore, the Court sets a preliminary-injunction hearing for Thursday, November 19 ….

UPDATE: I originally stated that the case was from the Western District of Kentucky, and the opinion does indeed have that heading. But, as the text of the opinion explains, the case is being litigated in the Eastern District of Kentucky, though Judge Beaton is a judge of the Western District (who is, for this particular case, sitting by designation in the Eastern District).

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 5, 1917

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7805. Satanic Temple can host holiday celebration at state Capitol building, judge rules

The Satanic Temple of Iowa coloring pages. The temple will be allowed to host a family-friendly holiday celebration in the Iowa Capitol building, a federal judge has ruled. (Photo courtesy of Magick Moth Media via the American Civil Liberties Union)

Iowa state officials must allow the Satanic Temple to host a family-friendly holiday celebration in the Iowa Capitol building without conditions or restrictions, a federal judge has ruled.

Chief U.S. District Judge Stephanie Rose of the Southern District of Iowa granted a preliminary injunction Monday ordering the state to approve the Satanic Temple’s application, which has been denied for the past three years despite other religious organizations being approved, Courthouse News Service reports.

The application was denied this year because a state official said the event’s costume contest—featuring a figure from European folklore known as Krampus who carries a stick—would harm children.

Rose reasoned that whether a costume may frighten a child is not a permissible basis for excluding speech, and the entire event cannot be denied simply because someone might carry a stick.

The American Civil Liberties Union and the temple filed the lawsuit in August.

“Congregants of the Satanic Temple have every right to live their authentic religious identity in public and are entitled to the same dignity and the same access to public spaces as members of more familiar traditions,” said temple attorney Matt Kezhaya in a Nov. 2 press release.

#7804. How to Thaw the Frozen Housing Market

Today’s housing market is painful for just about everyone involved, from builders to buyers to sellers. Government failures over the last seven years froze the industry and made homeownership less affordable, but the problem could be solved if Congress would act. 

To understand the solution, though, we first must know how we got here.

Beginning in 2020, Congress increased annual spending by trillions of dollars, and the Federal Reserve simply created the money to cover the massive deficits. The Fed also pushed interest rates to near zero and bought mortgage-backed securities (MBS).

The low interest rates made it cheaper for the government to borrow, but also for everyone else to borrow, including would-be homebuyers. Lower mortgage rates allowed people to take on much larger mortgages without making monthly mortgage payments prohibitively expensive. The resulting bidding wars sent home prices to stratospheric levels.

Fed purchases of MBS were fuel on the fire. They incentivized banks to make more loans at lower interest rates, stimulating mortgage lending. That’s precisely why the Fed bought MBS for the first time in the wake of the mortgage meltdown in 2009—it was attempting to rescue the industry. This time, the Fed bought MBS from early 2020 through early 2022.

The result was even larger mortgages from even lower interest rates as home prices went to the moon. Additionally, the runaway spending, borrowing, and printing of money by the government devalued the dollar and sent inflation to 40-year highs. The weaker dollar also meant it took more of those dollars to buy the same home, further inflating prices, but it also caused the Fed to change course.

>>> Government Broke the Housing Market—Only This Will Fix It

What followed was the sharpest rise in interest rates in four decades. Suddenly, mortgage rates were three or four times their previous levels. Ordinarily, higher interest rates would put downward pressure on home prices so that monthly mortgage payments stay roughly the same, but that didn’t happen.

If you bought a home in 2020 with a 2 percent interest rate mortgage, you effectively can’t sell your home today, not without downsizing. If you sell today, your old mortgage gets paid off and your next mortgage will have an interest rate closer to 8 percent. You can’t borrow anywhere near as much on the next home, or your monthly mortgage payment will explode.

These golden handcuffs have kept many existing homes off the market and even those that are for sale have unrealistically high prices. Sellers want those high prices so they’ll have more money to put down on their next home and therefore need to borrow less. That makes the higher interest rate much less painful and keeps the monthly mortgage payment manageable.

But that’s left a massive mismatch between buyers and sellers. Would-be buyers can’t afford today’s high prices with today’s high interest rates. Homeownership affordability is near an all-time low because it takes 44% of the median household pre-tax income to afford a median-price home. The after-tax figure is well over 50 percent.

Consequently, pending sales of existing homes have fallen to the lowest level on record, a full one-third below the level from a quarter century ago.

>>> U.S. Government-Backed Homebuying Market Drives Up House Prices for Ordinary Americans  

The situation is painful for new homes too. Residential construction is trending down, and homebuilder sentiment has fallen to the lowest level in 14 years. Builders are being squeezed by costs 60% higher than before the pandemic, and buyers who can’t afford today’s prices. About two-thirds of builders are using sales incentives to clear inventory, with more than 40 percent cutting prices.

For transactions to increase and the housing market to clear, home prices ultimately need to come down relative to incomes, which will take time because sellers need to adjust their expectations. But lower interest rates would also give buyers some relief and reduce the lock-in effect on current homeowners looking to sell. 

That’s where Congress needs to act. The legislature has no direct control over interest rates, but they do control spending, which is at obscene levels. In the last fiscal year, which just ended on September 30, the federal government spent $7.4 trillion and had to borrow almost $2 trillion of it.

Everyone, including the government, competes for loans and that additional $2 trillion of competition drives up the price to borrow money, which is the interest rate. Reducing government spending would reduce the deficit and immediately put downward pressure on interest rates, including for mortgages.

Granted, other recent factors have contributed to higher interest rates—like the Iran war increasing oil prices, which increase inflation expectations, which increase interest rates. Ending that conflict would help stabilize energy markets and eventually reduce interest rates too. But it’s the spending that’s squarely within Congress’s control and which would have a faster impact.

But given the abundance of ineptitude and lack of fortitude within the halls of Congress, don’t expect those spending cuts anytime soon.
