#7789. Freedom Isn’t Automatic—Each Generation Must Fight To Keep It

President Ronald Reagan’s famous warning that “Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction; it has to be fought for and defended by each generation” is even more relevant today than when he first said it.

He correctly identified that prosperity is not a predetermined outcome. It is created and sustained by culture, institutions, and economic freedom, and it must therefore be the responsibility of every generation to protect and preserve it.

The comforting but misguided belief in economic determinism—holding that prosperity is determined by geography, natural resources, or historical circumstances—must be rejected. By this logic, the United States was destined to be a superpower simply because it occupies a resource-rich continent and is protected by two oceans.

Natural resources and geography may create opportunities, but they do not guarantee prosperity. History shows that Americans have intentionally pursued free enterprise, transparent institutions, and a limited federal government system that transformed opportunity into prosperity and allowed the nation to flourish.

The myth of economic determinism can be revealed by one of history’s most compelling natural experiments: North Korea and South Korea. The stark development trajectories between the two is evidence that political choices impact national outcomes. After World War II, North and South shared a common culture, language, geography, and history, yet chose dramatically different political and economic systems.

>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

South Korea embraced free enterprise, international trade, and economic liberation. North Korea adopted central planning, state ownership, and authoritarian rule. One developed into one of the world’s most advanced economies with residents enjoying personal freedoms and prosperity, while the other remains impoverished and isolated.

This contrast is even visible from space. Satellite photographs show South Korea illuminated at night by extensive infrastructure and a vibrant city, while North Korea remains dark due to an undeveloped power grid, poor infrastructure, and political factors that prioritize military needs over civilian energy consumption.

Geography didn’t create that divergence—communist policies did.

Similarly, Venezuela was among the wealthiest nations in Latin America for much of the 20th century, driven by large oil reserves. If natural resources guaranteed prosperity, it would be among the richest countries today. Instead, Venezuela fell from one of the most prosperous South American countries to one of the least prosperous in the world, with the Fraser Institute’s Economic Freedom Index ranking Venezuela number 22nd globally in 1980 and number 165th in 2021.

In less than half a century, empty promises made by socialist policymakers and enacted big-government policies undermined Venezuela’s economic foundation. The Manhattan Institute finds three policies implemented by dictator Hugo Chavez responsible for the nation’s widespread economic and humanitarian crisis: “nationalization of private industry, currency and price controls, and the fiscally irresponsible expansion of welfare programs.”

Chavez first nationalized agriculture by taking wealth and property from landowners and giving it to workers—leading to mismanagement and destruction of those resources. He then implemented controls to keep prices artificially low, which pushed out remaining firms and led to nationalized central authority. Finally, he expanded welfare programs purported to address poverty, educational shortcomings, and healthcare; all financed through high taxation and currency printing to the point of hyperinflation.

Inflation spiked, shortages of food and medicine became commonplace, government dependence increased, investment collapsed, and millions emigrated out of the country in search of better opportunities.

>>> The Conservative Coalition We Need to Save the West

But remember, in 1998 Chavez was democratically elected president. He campaigned on providing relief to poor- and middle-class populations by redistributing oil wealth in the form of social services—awfully similar to the “tax the rich” slogans of American socialists today. What starts with government programs, free buses, and artificially lower grocery prices ends with centralized authority, overreach, and the very socialist regimes that have killed citizens and destroyed entire countries in practice.

The lesson is that prosperity depends on policy—and this fact is increasingly relevant in the United States.

Socialist ideology has already made its way to America’s blue cities, with the youth driving this ideological shift from capitalism to socialism. Their affordability grievances are real, yet history repeatedly demonstrates that concentrated power in the hands of the state risks liberty, innovation, and long-term prosperity.

America’s future is not guaranteed. It depends on whether future generations defend and renew the principles and economic systems that historically made America great. Individual freedoms, economic mobility, and national prosperity should not be considered expectations, but rather privileges of ordered policies and culture.

That’s why policymakers and citizens must constantly, intentionally agitate for limited and constitutional government, a strong rule of law, and free enterprise to secure America’s future—because as Reagan reminded us, economic destiny is not guaranteed. It’s fought for and won time and time again.

#7788. How To Win Back the Disillusioned American Dream

Conservatives often assume socialism is easy to defeat. After all, the failing historical record of central planning and the economic success of free markets are on their side. But that hasn’t stopped socialism from gaining ground, particularly among young Americans.

A Fox News poll finds that while 72% of Democrats under the age of 45 believe capitalism is not working well, 66% think moving to socialism would be a good idea. Those numbers should concern any American who values economic freedom.

Many older conservatives immediately respond by pointing to the Soviet Union, Venezuela, or Cuba as evidence of the horrors of socialism. They’re not wrong, but they’re not addressing the question young voters are actually asking.

Young people are choosing socialism not because they hate America, but because they believe the once reliable American Dream is out of reach. Homeownership is becoming unattainable. Student debt delays major life decisions. Family formation is becoming more expensive every year. Upward mobility seems impossible when wages barely outpace inflation.

Their frustration is real, and though the promises of socialism are empty, those of capitalism—or at least what they think is capitalism—have gone unfulfilled.

The median sales price of a new home was over $410,000 in 2025, nearly five times the median household income, a ratio almost twice as high as in 1980. Student loans cost the average new graduate hundreds of dollars per month. And despite inflation coming down from pandemic peaks, 3.4% CPI eats away at weekly paychecks.

>>> The Cost of Growing Up: Why Gen Z Feels Priced Out of the American Dream

Simply put, the cost of adulthood has become unaffordable for millions of young Americans.

Socialists have recognized this reality, and though their proposed solutions are economically unsustainable, at least they acknowledge the problem. And too often, conservatives are quick to condemn socialism without addressing the underlying reasons why Gen Z finds it attractive.

Socialists blame capitalism for modern economic hardship, but the affordability crisis should not be treated as evidence that competitive capitalism is failing America’s youth. In most sectors burdening young Americans, competition has been weakened by government intervention, political favoritism, and policies that distort prices and restrict supply.

Look at housing. For decades, local governments restricted development with zoning regulations, permitting delays, and other barriers to construction. Simultaneously, government-backed mortgage policies increased purchasing power without addressing supply shortages. Then, politicians responded to rising costs with rent control and rent freezes that further distorted the market and drove up homeownership costs.

It’s no surprise, then, that the average age of a first-time homebuyer is at an all-time high of 40.

Next, look to higher education. Government-backed student lending has enabled colleges to raise prices. The result is a system that saddles students with tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars of debt and politicians that propose student loan forgiveness or other subsidies as the solution—which neither adds value to the credential, lowers the cost of providing education, nor changes the broken mechanism behind why college tuition is so expensive.

The housing and college markets are not examples of a free market operating properly. They reflect government-created scarcity, regulatory dysfunction, and cronyism.

Therefore, cost-of-living concerns facing Gen Z should not be used as evidence that competitive capitalism is a failed model—especially when most economic problems stem from policies fundamentally opposed to the free market.

For policymakers, this means acknowledging Gen Z’s reasonable concerns and showing them how freedom, not government control, can improve life.

>>> The Surprising New Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left

When conservatives respond to rising socialist affiliation only by warning about unsuccessful experiments, they fail to address the affordability problems people experience every day, which are driving this ideological shift.

The average American is not watching lectures on the historical failures of central planning or reading through textbooks comparing the economic philosophies of Karl Marx and Adam Smith. Young Americans are instead trying to make monthly rent payments, budget to buy a house, pay back student loans, and afford groceries—all while entering adulthood, starting a career, and raising a family.

So, a successful conservative strategy must both demonstrate how free-market policies solve modern problems and expose the socioeconomic failures of socialism.

This means increasing housing supply, removing government distortions in housing and other markets, lowering barriers to entrepreneurship, promoting energy abundance, reducing regulatory burdens, and making family formation more affordable. Most importantly, Americans need evidence that economic freedom reliably produces upward mobility.

The greatest victories against socialism were never won through slogans, but through prosperity. When people can afford homes, start businesses, raise families, and build wealth, socialism loses its appeal. But when those opportunities disappear, socialism gains favor.

The future debate over socialism won’t be won by arguing endlessly about 20th-century failed experiments in foreign nations. It will be won by proving that economic freedom can still deliver opportunity and prosperity for all Americans in the 21st century.

#7787. May Court Order Parent to "Immediately Cease All Disparagement of" Other Parent "via Social Media"?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

An appellate court orders a trial court to consider whether such an order is consistent with the First Amendment.

From McWilliams v. Meghrian, decided Monday by Georgia Court of Appeals Judges Jeffrey Watkins, Christopher McFadden, and J. Wade Padgett:

This appeal arises from a child custody modification proceeding in which the trial court, [among other things,] … permanently enjoined … Mother … from making any "disparaging" statements about Father "via social media or other means" and modified child support. Mother appeals, and for the reasons below, we vacate the trial court's final order and remand for further proceedings. The parties are the parents of one child, born in 2008….

Mother argues that the final order and accompanying parenting plan included unconstitutional prior restraints on speech. The final order directed Mother to "immediately cease all disparagement of [Father] whether via social media or other means." The final order also adopted and incorporated the parenting plan proposed by Father, which provided that the parties "will not speak badly of each other or the members of the family of the other parent." …

During the final hearing, the trial court stated, "So, Ms. McWilliams, when we're dealing with, you know, parents—and I understand what you said. You're putting your truth out there and saying your truth. Disparagement doesn't care about the truth. It just means that you're putting down another parent." Mother responded, "Yeah." The court concluded:

And so publicly like that is something that you just—you can't do, and so we want to be careful about that. There's a reason that we're careful about that. Things on social media get back to kids. They just do. And I think that we're all—we're all cognizant of that in this day and age, but we have to be careful about what we put out there. And if we can't say anything nice, we just don't need to say anything at all, and that's the best rule to live by in terms of this. So that's—that's kind of what we need to—what we need to work on there….

As to Mother's failure to assert her constitutional challenge before the trial court, it is true that "[b]ecause this Court is a court for the correction of errors, we will not consider matters, even of constitutional magnitude, that were not raised and ruled upon in the trial court." However, the injunction, in its objectionable form, was not entered until the final order. And Mother raised the issue in her application for discretionary review, which was her first opportunity to do so.

Accordingly, on remand, the trial court is instructed to address the constitutional issue in the first instance. As we do not reach the constitutional issue, we need not decide whether, as Father argues, it is moot because the child has reached 18 years of age…. In sum, we vacate the grant of attorney fees, the injunction (both in the final order and in the incorporated parenting plan) restricting speech, and the order of child support….

Malone Williams Allen represents the mother.

Even these lower rates will double people’s property taxes. Furthermore, the lower rates are designed to be offset by new valuation methods being cooked up by the city Department of Finance to increase the assessed value of properties.

The rollout was messy from the start, when the city published a list of 900,000 high-value properties along with many of the owners’ full names. The city appeared to adopt a kind of guilty-until-proven-innocent tax liability, making residents argue they aren’t subject to the pied- à-terre tax. Owners were left with confusion and a loss of privacy.

Since Manhattan has roughly 16,700 condos and co-ops valued above the $1 million threshold, it will be hit hardest by this tax. Secondary residents will owe an average surcharge of $68,559 each year. Brooklyn also shows significant exposure, with the outer boroughs coming in at smaller counts.

New York projects the measure will raise about $500 million in annual revenue. But that assumes the owners stay. Revenue could easily fall by tens of millions of dollars if some owners leave and sell off their secondary residences, which is why wealth taxes elsewhere have repeatedly fallen short of projections. Each property owner who leaves the city shrinks the tax base.

Ultimately, this is a tax on investment in New York real estate with ramifications that will affect even middle-class New Yorkers. Picture a wealthy Californian considering a second residence on the East Coast. At Phase One’s top condo rates, a unit in Manhattan with a $5 million assessed value—the median Manhattan residence is more than $1 million—now has an extra $262,500 tax bill, simply because his primary residence is elsewhere.

>>> Mamdani’s City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying for Every Banana

Suddenly, Cape Cod and Miami look a lot more attractive, so the wealthy begin taking their spending elsewhere. Local businesses lose sales and need fewer employees. The Real Estate Board of New York argued before the State Legislature that the surcharge would discourage development, reduce construction jobs and drive high-end buyers to other cities.

Supporters argue the tax discourages luxury units from sitting vacant, hence the one-year-lease exemption. But that’s not where New York’s housing crisis is. Very few people can afford $5,000 a month for a one-bedroom apartment downtown. Filling a few luxury units won’t change that.

Legal fights are well underway, and while a Staten Island judge called the rollout “arbitrary and capricious,” the process was ordered to be redone, not canceled entirely. None of the legal challenges has succeeded in striking down the tax itself.

Part-time residents already pay taxes to fund city services, and these surcharges will incentivize those folks to leave, reducing revenue from the surcharge as well as existing taxes. As the more mobile wealthy flee for greener pastures in low-tax states, the burden of funding Mr. Mamdani’s socialist utopia will increasingly have to fall on the less mobile middle class.

#7784. California’s Potential Billionaire Tax Has Already Cost The State

California’s latest proposed tax increase has already led to so much wealth fleeing the state that tax revenue is set to fall, not rise. Golden State politicians announced the upcoming opening day of hunting season on billionaires and are about to find out they can’t fund welfare programs by taxing people who have already left.

At issue is California’s Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ net worth, which proponents claim will raise $100 billion for state-funded health care. Unfortunately for them, the wealthy were paying attention. At least seven high-profile billionaires left the state before Jan. 1 of this year, the residency date that determines who owes the tax.

They took with them roughly $539 billion of the state’s $1.9 trillion in billionaire wealth. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin alone shrank the expected haul by $25 billion.

The fact is, $100 billion was never a realistic revenue projection. That estimate ignored losses from departures and legal challenges and both are certain to keep coming. The retroactive residency date alone invites a raft of constitutional challenges.

Supreme Court precedent bars retroactively imposing a “wholly new tax.” Locking people into paying whether they stay or leave, before voters have even approved the tax, burdens the constitutional right to travel. And as the Tax Foundation notes, uncapped penalties on appraisers of hard-to-value assets raise Excessive Fines Clause concerns, since they’re grossly disproportionate to good-faith errors.

>>> California Risks Killing the Golden Goose With Proposition 40

Once departures and litigation are counted, Stanford economists Joshua Rauh and Benjamin Jaros estimate the tax would bring in closer to $30 billion. That’s less than one-third of what was promised, which is bad news for Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program.

But the bigger problem has already arrived. While a wealth tax is collected once, an income tax is collected every year. Rauh and Jaros estimate California’s billionaires pay between $3.3 billion and $5.8 billion in state income tax annually, and every billionaire who relocates takes his share with him permanently.

Weigh that lost income tax revenue against Prop 40’s one-time haul, and the net present value of the tax comes out to negative $38.9 billion.

In other words, the tax is a money-loser for the state. And this estimate isn’t a mere outlier from unlikely assumptions: economists ran 100,000 simulations with different revenue estimates and discount rates, and the state came out behind in 85% of them.

California already depends on a sliver of total earners for most of its tax receipts, with the top 1 percent of earners supplying roughly half of all personal income tax revenue. These are the people creating business, funding startups, and employing thousands of Californians. Losing even a handful of them does real damage to state and family finances alike.

>>> New York’s Property Tax Hike Chases Wealthy Wallets Away

Ironically, the billionaires who flee suffer less than the average Californian. As F. Scott Fitzgerald said, the rich are different from you and me; they can leave for Florida, Tennessee, Texas, or another low-tax state. It’s California’s public services, funded by their income, that will suffer.

Medi-Cal and the other programs counting on this money will still need funding. When $100 billion becomes $30 billion, followed by a permanent reduction to income tax revenue, politicians will clamor for more tax hikes.

But with a shrinking tax base of billionaires, the hikes will inevitably fall on the middle class. A tax sold as making billionaires “pay their fair share” will end up costing the residents not wealthy enough to leave.

Supporters will point to research showing high-earners rarely move because of taxes. But the best-known study examined ordinary income tax rates over many years. A levy on someone’s entire net worth is a different animal and will prompt more people to leave, as seven just did.

Before Californians vote on Prop 40, they should understand how much the tax will realistically raise—and who will get stuck with the actual bill in the long run.

#7783. How Trump's Undermining of the Constitution Helped Cause a "Blue Tsunami"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Trump's unconstitutional policies on tariffs, the Iran War, and immigration played a big role in his party's enormous "Blue Tsunami" election defeat.

On Tuesday, Trump and the Republican suffered a massive electoral defeat, losing control of both houses of Congress. Many have called it a "Blue Tsunami". The defeat was caused by multiple factors. But Trump's unconstitutional actions on tariffs, the War in Iran, and immigration played a major role. Violations of the Constitution don't always result in political setbacks for the perpetrators. But in this case they did "bigly." As Texas GOP Senator Ted Cruz put it, "Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long."

This connection is perhaps most obvious in the case of tariffs. Since returning to power in January 2025, Trump has engaged in a series of massive tariff power grabs, repeatedly attempting to usurp congressional authority in this field, and use it to impose the highest tariff schedule since the Great Depression. He started with the IEEPA tariffs. When the Supreme Court invalidated them, he tried again with Section 122 and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and the Section 338 tariffs against Canada. In each case, he illegally tried to transform relatively narrow delegations to the executive into a blank check to impose tariffs at will. The net effect of these actions has been to raise prices for consumers,  reduce economic growth, and impose some $700 billion in new taxes on Americans over a 10-year period (unless courts end up striking down the new tariffs, too). The tariffs also failed to produce the promised increase manufacturing employment.

Most relevant for present purposes, affordability and price increases were clearly a huge issue in the election. And most voters have come to realize that tariffs increase prices, and damage the economy. Exit polls reveal that 66% of voters believe Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy (compared to only 21% who believe they helped), and a similar percentage (64%) believe they hurt the economy in their area (only 14% believe they helped it). Numerous other polls show widespread opposition to the tariffs, as well (e.g. here and here). They became a major issue in the elections, linked to the broader issues of price increases and "affordability."

Polls, pundits, and even Donald Trump and Vice President J.D. Vance all agree the Iran War was a major factor in GOP losses. The military stalemate combined with resulting energy price increases have enraged voters. Exit polls showed that 74% of voters said the war was a "crucial" or "important" factor in their decisions, and the vast majority of them disapproved of Trump's conduct of it.

And, as I have argued from the beginning, that war is unconstitutional because it was never authorized by Congress.  As I warned at the start of the conflict, the failure to build up the public supported needed to secure congressional authorization greatly reduced the odds of success:

This [constitutional] limitation on presidential power is more than just a technical legal point. The requirement of congressional authorization for the initiation of war is there to ensure that no one person can take the country to war on his own, and that any major military actions have broad public support, which can be essential to ensuring that we have the will and commitment needed to achieve victory against difficult opponents. Trump's failure to seek and secure that kind of broad public support has ensured that only about 27 percent of Americans approve of this military action, compared to 43 percent who disapprove, according to a Reuters poll. Other surveys show similar results. This is a historically low level of public support at the start of a major military action and bodes ill for U.S. staying power if we suffer reverses or a prolonged conflict results.

I think that prediction has (so far at least) been vindicated by events.

The immigration situation is somewhat more complicated than that with tariffs and war. But, here too, various unconstitutional actions have damaged the GOP's political standing and hurt the party in the election. Trump's cruel mass deportation policies have made ICE by far the most the most unpopular federal agency (surpassing even the IRS) and alienated Hispanic voters in Texas and elsewhere;  this was a key factor in the Republicans' defeat in that state. GOP immigration policies  led many Hispanics who backed Trump and the GOP in 2024 to turn against them in 2026.

In part because of indefensible double standards in relevant Supreme Court precedent, courts permit a wide range of harsh and cruel conduct in immigration policy, that would be invalidated in any other context. But many of Trump's policies went beyond even these overly permissive bounds. As a result, the administration has lost many thousands of immigration detention and deportation cases, including many on constitutional grounds, and many before GOP-appointed judges. Trump's immigration crackdown has violated the Constitution in various other ways, as well, as in the case of his use of an absurdly broad definition of "invasion" in order to justify detaining and deporting even legal migrants without due process.

In all three of these cases, voter backlash arose primarily because of the awful - and highly visible - practical consequences, rather than because of the constitutional issues themselves. Most voters care far more about military failure, rising prices, and visible cruelty of these policies than about their legality. Nonetheless, it is still true that unconstitutional conduct played a major role in causing the tsunami that swept away many GOP officeholders.

We should not be overly optimistic about this chain of events.  It would be a mistake to assume that unconstitutional policies always lead to electoral punishment, or even usually do so. In many cases, voters are unaware of illegality or don't give it much weight if they do find out. Previous presidents have often avoided significant political backlash for violating the Constitution. Barack Obama, for example, also waged two unconstitutional wars (those against Libya and ISIS). But because the wars were (at least initially) militarily successful, led to few casualties, and had little visible negative economic impact, he largely avoided political damage. Later, Obama concluded that the Libya war was his worst mistake. But Democrats didn't pay much, if any, political price for it.

Trump's unconstitutional actions on these three issues turned out be politically costly because the negative effects were large and highly visible. Even many generally ignorant and inattentive voters noticed them.

Here, as always, I do not claim that public support for my position somehow proves I was right. As the author of Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, I recognize that majority public opinion is heavily influenced by ignorance and bias, and thus often a poor guide to goo policy. Moreover, while majority opinion agrees with me in condemning Trump's policies here, it would not go as far as I would in sweeping away nearly all tariffs and immigration restrictions.

Despite these caveats, I am glad that the public punished the GOP for these terrible unconstitutional policies. I hope this outcome might deter future presidents from imitating them. At the very least, they might hesitate to pursue them on the same massive scale as Trump did.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7782. Lindsay Clancy judge considers retrial at hearing to dismiss murder case

Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press)

The possible retrial date for Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, might be March 2027, according to a Massachusetts judge during a Monday hearing to determine whether the triple murder case should be dismissed.

Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan offered the tentative retrial date, and prosecutors in the case said they fully intend to retry Clancy, 36, who admitted to strangling to death her three children—5-year-old daughter Cora; 3-year-old son Dawson; and 8-month-old son Callan—during a postpartum psychosis episode. She later cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window, which paralyzed her from the waist down, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

The five-week trial resulted in a jury deadlock after one juror held out to convict Clancy. Eleven jurors were prepared to present a not guilty by reason of insanity verdict, which would have sent Clancy to a psychiatric facility instead of sentencing her to life in prison.

Michael Desronvil, the lone dissenter, wanted to convict and faced scrutiny after his name was leaked on the internet.

Jennifer Sprague, a Plymouth County, Massachusetts, assistant district attorney, defended Desronvil’s decision but did not comment on what charges that Clancy would face in a new trial.

#7781. Karin Slaughter on Mo Hayder, thrillers by women, and the legacy of “Gone”

I clearly remember the first time I read Mo Hayder. Birdman was published in 2000, a year before my own first novel was published, and I felt an intense sense of wonder with every finely crafted sentence. The plotting was fantastic. The characters were not just believable but brought out an array of emotions from lust to disappointment to love to abject fear. The tension knotted more tightly with every turn of the page. I had never read anything like it—and it made me feel more inspired, more challenged, in my own career.

At the time, the genre was a hard place for women. We are supposed to be sugar and spice, the docile victims of these sorts of stories, not the ones who gain control and agency by writing about them with an unblinking eye. That Mo was able to accomplish this, that she broke ground for the many who came behind her, will always be an enduring part of her legacy.

The women who were able to follow, from Gillian Flynn to Ivy Pochoda to Jennifer Hillier, owe a tremendous debt to Mo for helping carve out space in a genre that often celebrates women on the page, but seldom celebrates them the same way in life.

But that’s exactly who Mo Hayder was: a mold-breaker. She was an iconoclast who could not be put in a box, neither as a person nor as a writer. She was bold. Her wit razor sharp. Her humor quirky. She didn’t shy away from writing about very dark things, and that made her an outlier. Her voice on the page was always confident and assured but never bordered into authorial intrusions. She never wrote the same book or told stories the same way twice. Mo Hayder was an icon.

In Birdman, Jack Caffery is a young, driven, seemingly unshockable detective who is faced with the daunting task of hunting down a serial killer who’s leaving behind a trail of horrific crimes—but the story is much more than the plot. Caffery is a character who grabs you by your bones and shakes you into seeing all the darkness in the world. He has messy relationships. He screws up a lot.

But in the end, you’re rooting for him—not just because you want the crime solved but because you want something, anything, to finally go his way. Readers often take it for granted that they will care about a character, but making them care about a character who does unlikable things is the difference between a writer and a master storyteller. Mo certainly deserves that title.

Gone is the fifth book in the Jack Caffery series but it stands very well on its own. By this point, Caffery’s counterpoint, Police Diver & Sergeant Phoebe “Flea” Marley, has been introduced. Marley is a lot like Mo: determined, beautiful, incredibly capable, but not invincible.

Flea and Caffery should have a closer relationship. They would fit together like two puzzle pieces. Unfortunately, they both carry around an awful lot of baggage. While this is tough for them, it makes them come alive on the page. They are excellent counterparts as detectives, and by the end of this novel you’ll be rooting for them both, despite their very deep flaws.

It’s no surprise that Mo won the Edgar® Award for Gone. She takes what already worked so well in this series and pushes up the volume by a thousand. The villain is completely fresh and extremely frightening. The plot takes amazingly satisfying twists that you’ll never see coming. And the story will creep and crawl right under your skin where it will stay forever.

Mo Hayder’s novels are dark, visceral, bold, and brilliant, and she leaves behind a lasting legacy. When she passed away in 2021, the crime writing world was devastated—tributes poured in and readers found solace in her novels—the incredible, brave, important stories she left behind.

Mo was always a writer—and a person—who looked at life as a question to be answered, as shown by her varied career path—not one to simply sit down to write in a vacuum, she made sure she had a wealth of life experience under her belt (she worked as a barmaid, security guard, filmmaker, hostess in a Tokyo club, educational administrator, and a teacher of English as a foreign language, to name but a few). Mo also held an MA in film from The American University in Washington, DC, and an MA in Creative Writing from Bath Spa University.

Writing was her love and her craft, and she took it very seriously. The legacy she leaves behind is not only that of a thriller writer, but of a generous, smart, passionate author and champion of other authors. I remember her as someone who squeezed every ounce out of life and did us all the great kindness of pouring some of that energy into her novels.

Over her many years as a writer, Mo, whose real name is Clare Dunkel, and detective Jack Caffery earned a legion of loyal fans, with Mo’s compulsive stories becoming staples of every crime reader’s bookshelf up and down the country—and indeed, across the globe. The series went from strength to strength, and Mo’s unique writing style and her refusal to shy away from the darker side of life became more and more apparent, setting her apart from other thriller writers and making it impossible for anyone to replicate her.

I am to this day still in awe of her tremendous talent and am deeply saddened that she is gone. We are so lucky that her work lives on.

Karin Slaughter is one of the world’s most popular storytellers. She is the author of more than twenty instant New York Times bestselling novels, including the Edgar-nominated Cop Town and standalone novels The Good Daughter and Pretty Girls. An international bestseller, Slaughter is published in 120 countries with more than 40 million copies sold across the globe. #7780. How Alain Delon Got Caught Up in a Murder Investigation at the Height of His Fame

The actor lies still. Eyes closed. Waiting for the signal.

‘Silence sur le plateau . . .!’ shouts director Jacques Deray.

The crew falls quiet. A silence descends upon the Saint-Tropez villa. Just the clicking of the cicadas, drunk on the late-summer heat in the scrubland surrounding the azure pool. Thick cables everywhere. Lighting rigs. Flight cases.

‘. . . Moteur . . . Ça tourne . . .’ calls the assistant director.

The camera motors fire up, a soft clicking as the film turning on the reels gets up to speed. The entire crew poised, ready . . .

The camera pans slowly across the glimmering, phosphorescent surface of the swimming pool until, languidly, it finds him: bronzed, lean, 33. Reclined by the water. Dark hair resting on hot sandstone slabs. A glass of orange juice perched on his belly, rising and falling with his breath.

His other hand toys with the water’s surface. Delicately it is withdrawn. Glistening droplets run the length of his fingers and drip sensuously onto his face, revealing to the camera for the first time one of the most famous men in the world.

Not Narcissus, but something colder, l’homme fatal. Nonchalantly, from being mesmerized by the water’s surface and his own reflection, he turns his head towards the sky, raises the glass from his chest and pours the juice into his mouth, slow and sensual.

Dark glasses on. Eyes closed. Pinned to the tiles by the late-summer heat. The remnants of the orange juice drying on his tanned skin.

He is, for now, untouchable. At the height of his powers.

Once the initial observations are complete, the two forensic pathologists begin the next phase of the autopsy. They make a clean incision across the scalp and peel the skin down on either side, revealing the smashed cranium beneath. The top of the skull is sawn off, the brain removed. Next, they open the torso, slicing through the abdomen to extract the vital organs. No major anomalies, except the liver. Enlarged, discoloured. Consistent with long-term alcohol abuse.

Once the examination is complete, the organs, including the brain, are placed back in the body cavity. The skull is reassembled; the skin pulled back into place and stitched at the crown. Fingerprints are taken and sent to the central police archives in Paris. The man still has no name.

Based on decomposition, the doctors estimate the time of death to be a week earlier, most likely during the night of 22 to 23 September. In their report, they write plainly: the skull had ‘completely collapsed in’. Cause of death: blunt force trauma to the head with a heavy object. The theory holds – for now – that it was a fight, something that got out of hand.

They sign the paperwork. The report is dispatched to the investigating judge.

Patard reads the autopsy report and gives the photographs a cursory glance. He can’t place it, but something feels off.

It’s the hands that catch his eye. Everyone insists the victim is a vagabond. But how many vagabonds have manicured nails?

The next day, a fingerprint match comes through. The deceased is one Stevan Markovic. Thirty-one years old. Born in Belgrade, 1937. The same prints first appear on records in 1958, when this man applied for political asylum in Paris. Then again:

Prison in Chambéry, 1962 La Santé, Paris, 1965 Namur, Belgium, 1964 Annecy, 1967

His last registered address? 22 Avenue de Messine, in the prestigious 8th arrondissement on the Rive Droite. A stone’s throw and the quartier of the Elysée Palace.

Then another twist. When cross-referenced, it would appear that 22 Avenue de Messine is also home to a famous actor: Alain Delon.

A file arrives from the Brigade Mondaine – the Paris vice squad. Technically tasked with investigating moral crimes, the Mondaine is unofficially tasked with monitoring the rich.

Patard flicks through their dossier on Delon, it’s only a few pages long; a couple of minor run-ins with the law. But then there are the photos: Delon with known gangsters, Corsicans, men who once fought for the Resistance and now run rackets out of Pigalle or control the ports in Marseille.

Who exactly is this Delon? Patard wonders. He calls in two detectives. ‘Go to Avenue de Messine,’ he says. ‘Interview Delon. Find out who this man was to him.’

The detectives stand there, open-mouthed.

‘Right,’ Patard says. ‘Let me know what you find.’

Patard glances at the paperwork again. The residency permit lists the dead man as a political refugee. Occupation: doublure – a stand-in. A stand-in, it would seem, for Alain Delon.

Unlike the two detectives, Patard isn’t impressed. He’s never seen a Delon film. Doesn’t plan to. But something tells him – this case is about to get complicated.

Edward Chisholm, author of A Waiter in Paris, was born in England and moved to Paris after graduating from the School of Oriental and African Studies in London. His work has appeared in The New York Times, The Guardian, and The Financial Times magazine. He lives in England.

#7779. Declaratory Judgment + $275K in Attorney Fees in Settlement of N.H. "XX" Wristbands Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The Institute for Free Speech, which litigated the case, reports on the settlement agreement:

Take off the wristbands or leave. That was the message Bow school officials gave parents and a grandfather who were silently protesting in support of female-only sports by wearing pink "XX" wristbands at a girls' high school soccer game in 2024…. After more than two years of litigation …, the Bow School District has agreed to a judgment declaring that it violated the plaintiffs' rights by barring them from wearing the wristbands at the game. U.S…. The settlement also provides $275,000 in attorneys' fees and costs.

The judgment declares that the plaintiffs "have a First Amendment right to silently wear pink wristbands bearing the XX symbol on the sidelines, in the spectator's area, or in the parking lot of any Bow District sporting event." It binds the district and its Board of Education, and it remains in effect even if the district amends its policies….

The plaintiffs wore the wristbands, whose "XX" symbols reference female chromosome structure, to protest a policy permitting a biological male to compete on the opposing girls' team. School officials, accompanied by a police officer, confronted them. The referee halted play until one spectator removed his wristband, and school officials later issued trespass orders barring Fellers and Andy Foote from school grounds, preventing them from attending their children's games and other school activities for a time….

After the district court denied a preliminary injunction in April 2025, the plaintiffs appealed. In August 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit ruled in the plaintiffs' favor, finding that they "have established a likelihood of success as to their viewpoint discrimination claim." The court concluded that the protest "fell short of harassment and disruption," and that school officials "cannot favor one side of a debate involving parental speech on an issue of prominent public concern." …

Here's my August post excerpting the First Circuit's opinion, written by First Circuit Judge Sandra Lynch, joined by Judge Jeffrey Howard:

On September 17, 2024, [plaintiffs] were instructed by Bow High School officials to remove pink "XX" wristbands they wore in protest while watching their daughters (in [one plaintiff's] case, granddaughter) play in a girls' soccer game against a team with one transgender athlete. Further sanctions followed…. [W]e conclude that appellants have established a likelihood of success as to their viewpoint discrimination claim arising from the sanctions imposed on them for their passive speech in wearing these wristbands….

The district court analyzed the school playing fields and adjacent parking lot, as appellants requested, under the mode of First Amendment law applicable to limited public fora as to impermissible viewpoint discrimination…. [The] appellee school district argues that this case must be analyzed more in the mode of Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969) … [and other cases that] recognize the particular interests inherent in the public elementary and high school settings, and the necessary discretion given to public school administrators in the difficult job of running public schools….

Neither of those two different classic modes of First Amendment analysis, urged on by these opposing parties, is a perfect fit for this public high school speech case, and we note that the Supreme Court has not addressed this precise question. We need not and do not reach the complex question of which (or whether) either of these alternate modes is the appropriate First Amendment type of analytical model for the facts of record here. We conclude that on these facts the differences in analysis would not affect the outcome here….

The school's legitimate interest in regulating certain kinds of speech on the playing field sidelines … is not demonstrated by the evidence in this record. There is no evidence that appellants' protest caused a material disruption [which would be relevant under Tinker]. There was no disruption until school officials chose to intervene, after which the referee suspended the game for approximately fifteen minutes and the school officials chose to impose restrictions on appellants' speech and impose sanctions. The appellants did not stage any pregame demonstrations; did not march, shout, chant, or otherwise disrupt the game; and did not confront Tirrell or any other player. Instead, they waited until halftime before donning the "XX" wristbands in a passive, silent gesture of protest. There is also no evidence of harassment, given there is no evidence in the record that any player actually saw the wristbands.

The lack of any evidence demonstrating harassment also defeats the school district's argument that it had an affirmative duty under Title IX to protect students from the speech in which appellants engaged…. While it is true that appellants chose to protest at the September 17 game because of Tirrell being a player, the record does not contain evidence of appellants engaging in harassment before or during the game. To the contrary, appellants did not shout, chant, make threats, or aggressively gesture at Tirrell to communicate their views against her participation. Nor is there evidence that Tirrell or any other player even saw the wristbands or "subjectively perceived the environment to be hostile or abusive."

Principal Fisk did note the challenges that transgender students face generally. But Fisk did not ever explain how appellants' display of the "XX" symbol constituted sufficiently severe or pervasive conduct to qualify as harassment under Title IX. And to the extent the district court concluded that the silent wearing of "XX" wristbands on the sidelines of a school soccer field, without more, always amounts to harassing speech, we disagree.

The school district responds that it may make "predictive judgment[s]" to proactively prohibit conduct that it believes will eventually lead to an actionable Title IX claim….. We agree with the general proposition. But the argument fails on the facts of this record…. We need not decide in this appeal whether and under what circumstances passive speech, on other facts, consisting of displaying the "XX" symbol on school property during school events could be reasonably thought to be harassing. But appellants' silent display of the "XX" symbol at the September 17 game fell short of harassment and disruption, and we conclude that the district court erred in holding that the school's interest in prevention of harassment justified the prohibition.

While it is a closer issue, we conclude that the school district likely was not justified in sanctioning the appellants for their passive speech based on its concerns derived from the earlier exchanges with the appellants and other parents. None of appellants' reported discussions, including their possible different methods of protest reported to Bow High School officials by other parents, led to any attempt to "heckle and intimidate" Tirrell. And that was evident both before and throughout the game.

It is true that Fellers initially attempted to convince his daughter to get the Bow High School players to wear the wristbands, but his daughter informed him that "she could not get full support from the team and was afraid that it would divide them." Fellers's Facebook post made the night before the game encouraged spectators "to protect the integrity and safety of female athletics" and "come out to support our XX Lady Falcons and show your solidarity with our girls' team." But the record shows only that the appellants and perhaps others of similar views engaged in a passive protest and only started the protest at halftime. While the school district may make predictive judgments about whether disruption may occur and "need not be certain of its forecast," it cannot use those projections to immediately suppress a passive, silent protest, that did not impair any of the legitimate school administration interests recognized by the Supreme Court.

This brings us to the school officials' other stated reasons for sanctioning appellants. Superintendent Kelley stated that the "XX" symbol conveyed an "exclusionary" message about gender. Principal Fisk, who ordered appellants to remove the wristbands, described the symbol both as "hateful" and as "anti-trans." As to these justifications for the sanctions imposed, the record evidence demonstrates the likelihood that the school district imposed sanctions on the appellants' wearing of the wristbands because it disagreed with the protest message conveyed….

Although the leading Supreme Court case on viewpoint discrimination in academic limited public fora, involved colleges and not high schools, and involved a limited public forum, both significant differences, Rosenberger's anguage about viewpoint discrimination is pertinent. "The government must abstain from regulating speech when the specific motivating ideology or the opinion or perspective of the speaker is the rationale for the restriction."

The characteristics of the school as a place of learning reinforce that administrators cannot favor one side of a debate involving parental speech on an issue of prominent public concern, and which, in those parents' views, concerned the safety of their children. As the Supreme Court stated in a case involving a high school football game, "learning how to tolerate diverse expressive activities has always been 'part of learning how to live in a pluralistic society.'"

Judge Julie Rikelman concurred in the judgment, reasoning that Tinker might not prohibit viewpoint-discriminatory speech restrictions, but that in this case the school district had accepted the viewpoint neutrality requirement:

The school district accepted that the limited public forum framework applied to the facts here and conceded repeatedly, both in its brief and at oral argument, that it could restrict speech at the September 17 soccer game only for viewpoint neutral reasons…. Although it did urge us to conduct our First Amendment analysis with the principles of Tinker in mind, it did so only in arguing that its actions were reasonable and thus satisfied the [reasonableness] prong of the limited public forum test….

With the school district's concession in mind, I agree that the record lacks evidence of actionable harassment or material disruption from the plaintiffs' speech at the September 17 soccer game. The record also demonstrates that school officials likely restricted the XX symbol because they viewed it as "exclusionary" and demeaning to transgender students. That amounts to viewpoint discrimination under relevant precedent.

Del Kolde, Brett Nolan, and Nathan Ristuccia (Institute for Free Speech) and Richard Lehmann (Lehmann Major List, PLLC) represent plaintiffs. were on brief, for appellants.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. #7777. Bobcats, “Twin Peaks,” deer: What influenced Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes’ new novel

I love and often teach the memoir People Who Led to My Plays by Adrienne Kennedy. In the book, Kennedy lists all the diverse people, objects, works of art, images, songs, and events that shaped her as an artist. The result is a portrait of a singular artist, a time period, and a manual for becoming an artist.

I have borrowed her form here to explore some of my influences.

Many years ago, my parents sent me a video of a female bobcat being released in the woods outside their home in Northern Wisconsin. It was deep winter, the snow several feet high. An acquaintance of theirs had trapped the bobcat to stop it from terrorizing his neighbor’s chickens and he felt my parents’ woods was a safe place to release her. This news alone would have been interesting enough, but the specifics of the video fascinated me.

The bobcat snarled in the cage, her fluffy winter coat standing on edge, looking both surprisingly small and terrifyingly dangerous. Her captor placed a frozen duck carcass on the snow outside the cage, opened the door, and quickly backed away. But the bobcat didn’t move. She stayed in the cage. The door was open, yet she stayed.

That image captivated me and I started building a story and characters around it.

In my twenties, everyone in my friend group loved Twin Peaks. But I hated it. It frightened me, on many levels, and I hated the way Laura Palmer’s dead and aestheticized body was used to create a story around, a story she had no say in. I wanted to examine this trope of the “beautiful dead girl”: to see if I could write about the real danger women and girls face without making them a spectacle, to see if there was a way to give them agency in a culture that took so much from them.

“—But I love/ life/ I get to be/ in it/ From somewhere else/ in the world/ I am living….”

I consumed all seven episodes ravenously and in quick succession, in the days when I could stay up all night watching TV, letting the images soak into my mind in the thin, vulnerable hours of early morning. I loved the misty forests and the character of the deep, dark lake, the isolation and strangeness. Though the story takes place in New Zealand, the setting felt very similar to places I’d known in Wisconsin. And the missing girl takes action, shapes the story, has a life after the crime that incites the series.

I’d heard and read this folktale, of a mysterious woman completely covered in hair who haunts the jungles of the Caribbean. Her backwards feet confuse those who’d try to track her and her name means “so beautiful” despite or in spite of her sometimes-vengeful nature and her unabashed wildness.

When I saw paintings of her by Firelei Baez—her hair intricately painted fur, her body melding with palms and fauna, her backward feet sprouting kitten heels—the ciguapa began haunting me, stalking in and around my novel.

My family, like countless others, has been irrevocably shaped by the opioid crisis. I carried, and still carry, rage against the Sackler family and others whose criminal and greedy actions caused so much pain and suffering. I wanted to punish them. I wanted to indict them. But I write novels and I didn’t want to write a novel about them. Instead, Clear Water was a way of transforming that rage, of telling the stories of the victims and survivors of this crisis.

In Wisconsin, deer are everywhere. They are full of contradictions: both sustenance and a nuisance—carrying disease, eating flowers and vegetables, totaling cars. They can be both prey and cause destruction. They can seem almost tame, yet are dangerous to approach. They are common and graceful. These contradictions became an intricate part of my book—deer acting as both symbols and forces of their own in the narrative.

Stephen Graham Jones has written many fabulous books since Ledfeather in 2008, but I read this novel at a pivotal moment in the writing of Clear Water. The way Jones interweaves different timelines, the way history shapes the present, and the relationships between humans and animals served as a North Star for my own writing.

I listened to her early albums on repeat while writing Clear Water. Her songs look without faltering at the pain of poverty, violence, and loss yet remain so tender, so full of love and hope.

The forests and lakes of Wisconsin are both the setting of Clear Water and forces that shape the story and the characters. Oaks drop acorns that messages could be carved on. Pines are the only green visible for months in the winter. Birch roots hold the land together. Leaves and pinecones and acorns drop into the lakes, dyeing the water a deep brown tinged with orange.

Even shallow water is opaque. Many beings seek refuge there. Anything could hide there.

Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes is the author of The Sleeping World, Clear Water, and Are We Ever Our Own. She has received fellowships from Hedgebrook, Willapa Bay Artists in Residency, Yaddo, the Millay Colony, Lighthouse Works, and the Blue Mountain Center. She holds a BA from Brown University, an MFA from the University of Colorado, Boulder, and a PhD from the University of Georgia. She is an associate professor at the University of Maryland. She lives in Maryland with her family.

#7776. Wole Talabi on the intersection of first contact stories and mysteries

In 1985, just a few weeks after a bloodless coup during which Major-General Ibrahim Babangida overthrew the military government of Major General Muhammadu Buhari in Nigeria, American astronomer Carl Sagan published Contact. A novel in which humanity first encounters advanced extraterrestrial intelligence when a team of scientists at SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) detects a radio signal from the star system Vega, located twenty-six light years away containing a sequence of prime numbers.

As they investigate, they uncover an embedded video and instructions in binary for building a mysterious interstellar Machine. Nations unite to fund and construct the device and a small international crew travel through the machine to meet the alien intelligence near the center of the galaxy where the aliens reveal their grand cosmic plans. It’s a great story.

First Contact narratives like Contact are some of my favorite stories in all of science fiction. As a species, we’ve long wondered about our place in the universe: if we were alone in it and if not, what would it be like to encounter alien intelligence.

Ever since I was a boy growing up under military dictatorship in Nigeria, discussing current affairs, history and astronomy with my dad on the weekends, I have found it endlessly fascinating to imagine all the different ways that a first encounter between humans and extraterrestrial sapient life could go. So of course, I enjoyed reading Contact when I found it in my school library and especially loved watching the 1997 screen adaptation starring Jodie Foster.

Readers often think of First Contact stories like Contact, and the many others that came before and after, as being focused on scientific or philosophical discovery, but undergirding all the talk of orbital mechanics, biology, astronomy, communications protocols and alien artifacts are much simpler things: questions.

First Contact stories are about answering questions. That, I think, is exactly what makes most First Contact stories at their core, mystery stories. After all, what makes a mystery story? I would argue that the defining feature of a mystery story is a central puzzle (usually a crime, hence the typical bundling together in bookstores as “mystery/crime”) where the truth is hidden until the end. Mysteries rely on an investigator of some kind as a key protagonist, as well as misdirects, suspicions, clues, all of which let the reader follow along with the protagonist until a final reveal.

Given that, it’s easy to see how Contact, and many other First Contact novels like Rendezvous With Rama, The Three-Body Problem, Semiosis, Solaris, The Mountain In The Sea, and even my own new novel The Fist Of Memory, function on a significant level, as mystery stories. The puzzle may have shifted from a murder in a locked room to an alien signal/presence, but the narrative engine is the same: evidence appears, theories emerge, assumptions are challenged, and the truth slowly reveals itself.

That last bit is important. Both First contact stories and mystery fiction depend on information asymmetry and management to be effective. In both cases, truth emerges in fragments, until a final big reveal which should be both surprising and make complete sense in hindsight.

A mystery where the investigator reveals the solution too soon or without sufficient buildup can be unsatisfying. First Contact narratives are pretty much the same. They derive their emotional and philosophical power from a series of carefully managed revelations.

A perfect example is the movie Arrival (another one of my favorites) based on the novella “Story of Your Life” by Ted Chiang, in which a linguistics professor Dr. Louise Banks, is recruited by the military to try to communicate with twelve massive alien spacecraft that have landed across Earth to learn why before panicked world governments ignite a global war.

After several false starts and apparent failures, the film’s climax arrives (ha!) in a powerful revelatory moment when she finally comprehends the alien language and her perception of time shifts, as does the audience’s understanding of the film’s events. It’s so brilliantly done; I get chills just thinking about it.

When I started writing my own First Contact SF thriller, The Fist Of Memory, I brought with me that imbibed spirit of mystery as an essential element and I wanted to give readers those familiar feelings. I open the book with a classic first-contact mystery premise, riffing on Rendezvous With Rama (yet another favorite of mine): an enormous alien spacecraft appears in the sky, approaching Earth. It’s uncommunicative and unresponsive to our signals.

My main character Tope is an assassin caught in the very Nigerian brand of political turmoil the alien craft’s arrival precipitates (inspired by my experience growing up under political instability). But once I had that opening as my setup, I knew I also needed a scientist as one of my protagonists. Because in First Contact, the scientists and explorers perform the same role that detectives perform in mystery and crime fiction: discover something previously unknown, gather evidence, analyze clues, formulate hypotheses, eliminate suspicions, search for patterns, solve the puzzle.

So, I created Itumeleng Sefako, an astronomer struggling to balance his scientific beliefs and his cultural traditions and connections. It’s through him that the mystery of aliens as well as their connection between humanity is investigated, analyzed and eventually revealed. Tope and Itumeleng become co-protagonists, performing a literary pas de deux, but without Itumeleng working through the core mystery, the book wouldn’t work.

That said, I think there is one thing that First Contact stories can do which traditional mysteries and detective fiction cannot (at least not without risking the ire of readers) and that’s this: leave the mystery unsolved (as is the case in Rendezvous With Rama). First Contact stories can do this because a truly alien intelligence may lie beyond our capacity for understanding. Or their worldview may be so radically different from ours that it’s essentially incomprehensible.

Think of all the meetings of separate human cultures/civilizations that were previously unaware of each other and just how many misunderstandings there were. Now increase that several orders of magnitude. Can we ever understand the motivations of, say, boron-based sentient crystals? Could we comprehend the morality of an inorganic mind that evolved in the magnetic poles of a neutron star? Sometimes, in First Contact, the closer we approach a solution, the more we discover the limits of our own perception.

Luckily, like in Contact, I chose not to lean into this too much in The Fist Of Memory. The mystery is resolved. At the end of the novel, there is an explanation of who/what the aliens are and a reveal that leaves all of humanity with a choice and a potential for change.

I felt this was important because in the end, while First Contact stories are ostensibly about humans meeting the other, they aren’t really about that. Not really. They’re about us. They’re a storytelling device through which we examine ourselves, attempting to think through the mystery of who we are and what our place in the universe might be.

Ultimately, First Contact stories are really mystery stories because they are driven by our own endless search for meaning and that, I think, is what makes them so appealing.

Wole Talabi is an engineer, writer, and editor from Nigeria. He is the author of the critically acclaimed Shigidi And The Brass Head Of Obalufon, which was named one of the best books of 2023 by The Washington Post, as well as The Fist of Memory. He has hopped around the planet quite a bit but right now lives in Australia. He has been a finalist for the Hugo, Nebula and Locus awards, the Caine Prize, and has won the Sidewise award for alternate history. Talabi's work has also been translated into 7 languages. His fiction has appeared in Asimov's, F&SF, Clarkesworld, and is collected in the books Incomplete Solutions (2019, Luna Press) and Convergence Problems (2024, DAW Books).

#7775. New York State Bar Association tells lawyers not to bill for time saved by AI

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use them. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use them.

Law360 reported Monday that the state bar association’s Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies issued a report classifying the cost of buying and maintaining such software as an overhead expense that can be passed along as a disbursement only when tied to a specific client matter and when the basis for the charge has been disclosed.

According to Law360, the report added that lawyers generally don’t have to tell clients about AI use for administrative tasks—such as word processing, spelling and grammar checks, calendaring or timekeeping—provided that the use doesn’t affect fees.

“Generative AI is indelibly changing the practice of law. As part of our mission to be the leading voice for the legal profession, we are providing clear guidelines on the use of AI tools as a resource, so attorneys can use AI responsibly and ethically in their practices,” said Taa Grays, the president of the New York State Bar Association, in a statement. “The guidelines can help attorneys avoid possible perils of using AI, including inadvertently practicing law in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use.”

The committee also flagged familiar hazards, such as biased training data that may deepen existing inequities. Confidentiality is another concern: If an AI tool learns from one client’s information in a way that makes it available in another client’s matter, lawyers must turn to the New York Rules of Professional Conduct.

The report cautioned against building tools that deliver automated legal services in ways that could amount to unauthorized practice or using AI to pass as a human with prospective clients.

Supervising lawyers were reminded that they remain responsible for their subordinates’ compliance and should not assume that a law firm-approved tool or policy removes the need to review work on each matter.

According to Law360, the state bar association’s governing body adopted the report Saturday.

The fate of billable hours is in the hands of artificial intelligence

#7774. Crime and the city: Harbin, China

Harbin, capital of China’s Heilongjiang Province—what used to be known as Manchuria—China’s “Wild East.” It’s long been China’s most northerly and Russified city—train lines into Russia and for many decades run by the Russians to the warm-water port of Dalian and connecting to the Trans-Siberian Railway. And then, after 1917, a new Russian influx fleeing the Bolsheviks.

Even today, sitting up towards the border at the Amur River between China and Russia’s vast Far Eastern provinces, the city has onion dome Orthodox churches and synagogues with streets that would not look out of place Khabarovsk or Tomsk. But this is certainly Chinese territory now and so crime writing is, as we’ve seen in Crime and the City columns on Shanghai, Beijing and Chengdu subject to certain censorship and restrictions.

Yangsze Choo’s The Fox Wife (2024) is set up in Manchuria in 1908 where young woman is found frozen in the snow. Her death is clouded by rumors of fox spirits, believed to lure people into peril by transforming into beautiful women and men. Bao, a detective with a reputation for sniffing out the truth, is hired to uncover the dead woman’s identity. Since childhood, Bao has been intrigued by the fox gods, yet they’ve remained tantalizingly out of reach. Until, perhaps, now.

American Sinologist Scott Seligman’s true crime Murder in Manchuria (2023) is a brilliant evocation of the Soviet spies and fascists, adventurers and chancers who gathered in interwar Harbin, a city at once highly modern—trains, art deco hotels, American cars—yet with old world animosities that boil over into kidnapping, murder and espionage.

Semyon Kaspé, a young Jewish musician, is kidnapped, tortured, and ultimately murdered by disaffected, antisemitic White Russians, secretly acting on the orders of Japanese military overlords who covet his father’s wealth. When local authorities deliberately slow-walk the search for the kidnappers, a young French diplomat takes over and launches his own investigation. Amazing…. And it’s all true!

Novelist Mark Oulton fictionalizes this same period in Red Spy in Harbin 1: In the Making (2025). It’s 1935 Harbin, a city of spies, racketeers, and would-be revolutionaries. Chinese agent Chen Minghe is ordered to infiltrate the Russian émigré Fascist Party—led by Konstantin Rodzaevsky, a real-life White émigré whose vanity and erratic leadership belie his dangerous ambitions. 1937 dawns and full-scale war with Japan begins, Chen’s mission starts to unravel. Rodzaevsky’s affair with a planted mistress comes to light. The resulting scandal begins to unravel the operation.

Chen’s adventures in espionage continue in Red Spy in Harbin: Book 2: The Price of Survival (2026) but in this tale move to World War Two Japanese occupied Taiwan.

Another series with Harbin at its centre and in the same “nest of spies” interwar period is Tom Stickel’s Special District: Harbin: Drawing the Tiger’s Bones (2022). It’s 1929 A patrolman, Borya Melnikov, sits at the bottom ranks of Harbin’s Special District police force. A dismembered body. A raging Red Terror campaign. A brewing war with the Soviet Union….Borya is assigned to investigate the dismembered body of one the city’s foreign businessmen uncovered in the nearby Japanese zone.

Special District: Harbin: Book 2: The Tigers of East Mountain (2023) starts with the discovery of body of a local Jewish businessman in a Harbin back alley threatens to tip the city into mob violence… It’s 1932 and Borya Melnikov returns to police ranks after the Japanese take over Harbin and end Soviet control, only this time with the Judicial Police of the new state of Manchukuo (Japanese- occupied Manchuria).

And finally, Special District: Harbin: Book 3: Visiting the Tiger’s Den (2024). It’s 1935, and Borya Melnikov has risen to the rank of Senior Inspector on Harbin’s Judicial Police unit in Manchuria. But his position is becoming untenable as Manchukuo’s Japanese masters are increasingly intolerant of his independent style…and now this anonymous threat lands on his desk. It’s not in his nature to back down to threats, but it is only weeks before his wife returns to Harbin. He must quickly solve all four of his open investigations before she arrives or risk putting her into danger also.

Brian Klingborg’s City of Ice (2021) is more contemporary and has Harbin partially as a backdrop. In a remote Chinese town – where the theft of a few chickens counts as a major crime—a young woman is found brutally murdered…with her heart, lungs and liver removed.

Inspector Lu Fei, a weary cop who fled the city, suddenly finds himself under the intense scrutiny of the ruling party in Beijing. Determined to find her killer, Lu Fei must navigate a society where politics can be deadly, corruption is rife, and the powerful are untouchable. As evidence connects the case to a string of unsolved murders, Lu must decide what he will risk in search of justice….

There are more Lu Fei novels, mostly set in northern China, including Thief of Souls (2021), The Magistrate (2023) and Wild Prey (2022), which takes Lu Fei to Myanmar.

Caroline Petit has written several historical fictions set in China, usually southern China—Hong Kong and Macao. The Fat Man’s Daughter (2006) ranges too from Hong Kong up to Manchuria. In Hong Kong in 1937 orphan 19-year-old Leah Kolbe is approached by a Mr. Chang, who claims to have known her father and offers her a commission to go to Manchukuo to smuggle out Chinese Imperial treasures. She consents and, accompanied by her faithful amah and a Russian émigré woman in Chang’s pay, takes the train north.

And finally, a writer I’ve been trying to squeeze into Crime and the City for a long time, Japanese author Haruki Murakami. Not naturally a crime writer admittedly but his novel The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle (1994) counts I reckon. Toru Okada, an unemployed man living a quiet suburban life in Tokyo, watches his life unravel after his cat disappears, his wife Kumiko grows increasingly distant, and he starts receiving strange phone calls.

From there the story explores deep psychological trauma, historical violence (particularly Japan’s actions in World War Two in Manchuria), personal alienation, and the hidden depths of human memory. The Manchurian sections of the novel are extremely atmospheric and often harrowing, a stark, visceral departure from his usual dreamlike, whimsical magical realism.

It is a book partly about Japan’s war crimes in China, brutality and multi-generational trauma. A trauma, by the way, that still lingers over Heilongjiang Province and the city of Harbin.

Paul French is a British author of books about modern Chinese history and contemporary Chinese society including Midnight in Peking and the 2018 release City of Devils.
