#7752. The November argument session begins on Monday

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It was a relatively quiet week at the court, as the justices – and the SCOTUSblog team – prepared for the November argument session to begin next week. On the interim docket, the court decided one immigration-related dispute and moved closer to being able to decide another.

On Thursday, an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church urged the Supreme Court to deny the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. For more on their filing, see the On Site section below.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court denied a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that prevents enforcement of a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to pause certain deportation proceedings. There were no noted dissents.

The court’s November argument session will begin next week. On Monday, the justices will hear argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

Congress may be “the battleground in the 2026 midterm elections,” but the Supreme Court is playing a role in many races, according to USA Today. Republican and Democratic candidates alike are highlighting “disputes about the high court’s membership, its size and its ethics” and calling on voters to keep these battles in mind when they head to the polls next week. In particular, candidates are raising the possibility of a Supreme Court vacancy during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office and emphasizing that the party that controls the Senate will be able to determine whether another Trump nominee is confirmed to the court.

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong has “barred immigration agents in Southern California from stopping people based on racial stereotypes,” citing what she described as “a mountain of evidence” showing that agents are “targeting people who appear Latino,” according to the Los Angeles Times. “The injunction … requires agents to establish individualized reasonable suspicion before detaining someone for immigration enforcement.” The Times noted that the evidence cited by Frimpong in her new order “had not yet been turned over by the government when the Supreme Court last year stayed the judge’s earlier order barring stops based solely on race or ethnicity, language, location or employment, either alone or in combination.” Frimpong acknowledged the Supreme Court's decision in her new order, but emphasized that the court “had not explained its reasons for granting the stay.” “This Court cannot be faulted for failing to follow guidance that was never given,” the judge wrote. The Trump administration has indicated that it will appeal Frimpong’s order to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

On Wednesday, Utah “filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity,” according to the Associated Press. “The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.” The AP noted that “[t]he felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the U.S. Supreme Court.”

Last week, the University of North Carolina School of Law “tested whether AI could replicate the reasoning of US Supreme Court justices” by staging “a simulated Supreme Court argument based on an actual case the high court heard in 2025,” according to Reuters. Participants found that although the three AI justices used in the test drew the same conclusions as the real-life justices, “deciding the case the same way the actual court did,” the bots did not excel at mimicking their behaviors during oral argument. “The AI justices asked questions and hypotheticals of the law students who argued the case, but their interactions felt robotic and they didn’t interrupt or interject the way the real justices do.” “There’s still this huge gap in it actually feeling human,” said Nicole Downing, the law school’s assistant dean for AI, to Reuters.

In his newsletter for The New York Times, Adam Liptak explored the Trump administration’s battle against what it describes as “rogue activist judges,” a category that has come to include judges who expressed frustration with government lawyers or criticized the administration’s actions in media interviews. Liptak noted that the Supreme Court held, in a 1994 opinion from Justice Antonin Scalia, that “[e]xpressions of impatience, dissatisfaction, annoyance and even anger” are “within the bounds of what imperfect men and women, even after having been confirmed as federal judges, sometimes display” and do not necessarily establish “bias or partiality.”

The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction.

The court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools. The schools argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because the state will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

(SCOTUSblog Plus) Earlier this month, the concept of cruel and unusual punishment briefly captured the country’s attention after the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30 tried and failed to execute Christa Pike. The botched execution drew attention to a range of past rulings on the death penalty, while also highlighting a number of unresolved issues in this fraught area.

In his Controlling Opinions column on Wednesday, Richard Re reflected on Justice Samuel Alito’s effort in his new book to discourage judicial “insecurity” – that is, “a judge’s self-conscious worry that he might be advancing his own policy preferences under the guise of impartial adjudication.” According to Re, “what Alito labels insecurity is better understood as a form of humility and self-awareness,” impulses that are laudable, not problematic.

As it currently stands, the 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor. But that could soon change, because by mid-January the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review from the Trump administration or Trump himself.

In his Justice, Democracy, and Law column on Tuesday, Edward Foley explored a growing battle over the division of authority between states and the federal government when it comes to “determining who can vote in congressional elections and regulating how the voting process occurs.” One such case involves the issue of alleged noncitizen voting in California, which may soon arrive at the Supreme Court.

In her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1926’s Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty, in which the Supreme Court, after rehearing the case and “a dramatic reversal in several justices’ positions,” paved the way for modern zoning. Boden noted that “[t]hree justices dissented, though they never said why.”

Sarah Isgur and David French zoom in on the cases prosecutors have brought against political enemies of the Trump administration. Then, they review the latest news from the battle over a Washington, D.C., golf course before tackling the administration’s sue-and-settle case in Texas.

The election is upon us, and worries about possible anti-democratic actions have many on alert. Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka peer ahead to see what to watch out for and review the relevant constitutional law and history.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice John McKinley, who served on the court from 1838 to 1852.

With the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act of 1837, Congress added two more seats to the court. The first went to Justice John Catron, and the second went to Justice John McKinley, whose confirmation created a nine-justice court. While the seat itself was an honor, its duties were less so, as McKinley would discover.

McKinley was born in May 1780 in Culpeper County, Virginia. His family soon moved to Kentucky, where he taught himself law, passed the bar in 1800, and practiced in both Frankfort and Louisville. After moving to Alabama around 1818, McKinley grew wealthy from land speculation, partnered with Andrew Jackson in the Cypress Land Company, and helped found the city of Florence, Alabama. Jackson himself called McKinley “the most prominent man” in the state.

McKinley entered the Alabama Legislature in 1820, and, after backing Jackson for the presidency (he had previously supported Henry Clay), won a U.S. Senate seat in 1826. In the Senate, McKinley advocated for bankruptcy policies “favorable to small farmers.” However, his vote to override Jackson’s Maysville Road veto (the Maysville Road Bill essentially proposed federal stock purchases for internal improvements, like state roads) raised doubts about his loyalty, and he was not reelected in 1830. After one term in the U.S. House and another in the state legislature, he won a second Senate term in 1836, only to leave the seat within two months due to his Supreme Court appointment.

In 1837, the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act expanded the court to nine justices, and Jackson’s advisers pushed McKinley for one of the new seats, but Jackson preferred his friend William Smith instead. When Smith declined, the pick then fell to the newly inaugurated President Martin Van Buren, who went with McKinley. Van Buren gave McKinley a recess appointment in April 1837, and the Senate confirmed him by voice vote that September.

After his nomination, McKinley wrote to then-House speaker James Polk that he had “accepted the appointment, although it is certainly the most onerous and laborious of any in the United States.” The new 9th Circuit included Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, and eastern Louisiana and required eight circuit terms a year. McKinley told Polk he would travel more than 5,000 miles annually, although McKinley later reported a figure closer to 10,000. The duties also likely ate into his finances (the justices were required to personally pay for their own circuit court duties) and took a toll on his health (he later had a paralyzing stroke on his way to Jackson, Mississippi).

Even before his first term started, McKinley asked Van Buren in person about changing the new 9th Circuit, but the president left the issue out of his next annual State of the Union, upsetting McKinley. Following McKinley’s first full term, the justices disbanded in March 1838 to “confront some 6,000 cases on their cumulative circuit dockets,” according to Steven Brown, who wrote McKinley’s first full-length biography. McKinley’s share from the 9th Circuit alone made up 4,700 of those.

Brown detailed one of the more interesting stories from McKinley’s extensive circuit duties in a 2011 Journal of Supreme Court History article. In April 1839 while holding circuit court in Jackson, a fight spilled into the courtroom and an officer of the court (who had been called “a stupid jackass” by McKinley for not bringing in the court marshal) pulled McKinley’s nose. Newspapers reported that the justice swore never to return to Jackson, and McKinley referenced the “gross personal indignity” in a letter to Van Buren.

In his 1839 State of the Union address, Van Buren told Congress that the circuit’s schedule and distances made it “impossible” for its judge to keep up. McKinley missed much of his circuit duties, along with the entire 1840 term, due to illness. Combined with his failure to hold court in Arkansas for almost five years, states in his circuit felt “neglected,” and the Mississippi Legislature called for McKinley’s impeachment. Congress eventually reorganized the circuits in August 1842, relieving McKinley of Mississippi and Arkansas; beginning in 1843 he rode the reconstituted 5th Circuit, which covered Alabama and Louisiana.

As for McKinley’s actual approach to cases, he was strongly for states’ rights, supporting them “over the authority of the federal government.” During his time on the court, McKinley wrote 19 majority opinions, four dissents, and two concurrences by one count, 22 opinions by another, and 23 by a third, the lowest per-term rate of his era. One of his opinions for the court was in 1845’s Pollard’s Lessee v. Hagan, where he held that new states enter the union on equal footing with the original 13, including ownership of the lands beneath navigable waters. Four years later in the 1849 Passenger Cases, McKinley argued in his concurrence that the federal government, not the states, controlled immigrants arriving from overseas until they became permanent residents of the states.

Increasingly ill after a stroke in 1842, McKinley died in Louisville in July 1852 at age 72, after 14 relatively difficult years on the court. He was replaced by Justice John Archibald Campbell, also from Alabama.

#7751. Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Hate Crimes in Deadly Attack on Boulder, Colorado, Gathering

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled.

The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference of the United States, has been developing rules for AI use for several years, but efforts have encountered setbacks and resistance, slowing down the possibility of any new policy.

Attorneys, scholars and judges have criticized proposed evidentiary rules, such as one involving how to handle AI deepfakes, according to a story by Law360.

“Bottom line: I’m not hopeful at this point,” Maura R. Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo in Canada whose research has shaped the AI proposals, told Law360.

#7748. Semaphore: Senior Product Engineer

Semaphore is a remote-first software company building continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) products for engineering teams. Our customers rely on Semaphore Cloud and our self-hosted enterprise products to build, test, and deliver software securely and reliably.

We have spent years building developer infrastructure at scale. We are now using that foundation to create new products and capabilities for a world in which software is increasingly built by people working with AI coding agents.

We are looking for a senior product engineer who can take an important idea from an early, ambiguous problem to a useful product running in production.

You will work across product and engineering boundaries: understanding the user, shaping the solution, making technical decisions, building the system, and improving it based on real use. Some work will extend mature Semaphore products. Some will start as a small experiment or a new product. In either case, you will be responsible for getting to a strong outcome, not completing a predefined list of tickets.

AI coding agents are part of our daily engineering workflow. We expect you to use them fluently to explore, build, test, and ship faster. You remain accountable for the work: choosing the right problem, setting direction, making trade-offs, reviewing what is produced, and ensuring that the result is coherent, reliable, and maintainable.

This role is for someone with strong ownership, initiative, taste, and judgment. You should be comfortable moving between product questions, system design, code, infrastructure, and user experience as the work requires.

We care more about the quality and ownership of what you have built than a specific number of years, previous title, or exact match with our stack.

This is a senior individual-contributor role with broad ownership. You will work closely with engineering, product, infrastructure, and company leadership. Teams are small, communication is direct, and the person closest to the work is expected to exercise judgment.

You will have room to shape both the product and its implementation. In return, we expect you to take responsibility for the whole outcome: what gets built, why it matters, how well it works, and what happens after it ships.

#7747. Five November criminal law arguments, and one last look at the 2025-26 term

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

While all eyes are on what seem like inevitable Supreme Court election law “emergency” petitions, it may be comforting to realize that the regular business of the Supreme Court still goes on. Argument calendars released months ago show five criminal law and related cases set for argument in November. Below are some quick summaries of them. But first, an announcement and one more quick look at last term.

My ABA “Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term: Criminal Cases”

For some 30 years I have written and the American Bar Association has published an “Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term: Criminal Cases” for the prior term. This is a booklet of manageable size for persons interested in a complete picture of the hundreds of pages the justices write every year on topics and cases related to criminal law. That’s also what this regular SCOTUSblog column aims to do – but the review provides a lot more detail. This effort – and believe me, it takes hours to compile – is a fun and (I hope) useful part of my pro bono work.

This year’s booklet will be published here on the ABA Criminal Justice Section‘s website next week. It is downloadable, and while I hold the copyright, anyone can use and distribute it. Summaries of 45 merits decisions and 26 separate writings by justices on the orders docket last term are included, as well as 14 criminal law and related cases granted for argument (so far) this term can be found in it as well. If you enjoy the booklet or have suggestions or criticisms, please let me know.

Before getting to the November sitting, here’s one interesting question from last term (more can be found in the booklet) that only recently occurred to me regarding two pairs of very different cases: Olivier v. City of Brandon versus Fernandez v. United States, and Hunter v. United States versus Clark v. Sweeney. At a high level of generality, is one case in each pair inconsistent with the other?

In brief, the court ruled in Fernandez that doubts about a prior conviction must be pursued in habeas, not the federal compassionate relief statute. Two months earlier in Olivier, however, the court ruled that a prospective challenge to a statute under which a person was previously convicted need not be pursued under habeas but instead can be filed under §1983 – even though that challenge might well “imply the invalidity of Olivier’s conviction.” Justice Elena Kagan wrote Olivier for a unanimous court, while Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote Fernandez in an 8 to 1 result.

Similarly, in Clark v. Sweeney the court summarily reversed the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit for granting habeas relief on grounds not argued by the parties. But then, seven months later in the term in Hunter, the court ruled that a court of appeals can ignore a waiver of appeal if a “miscarriage of justice” is perceived – presumably even if that miscarriage has not been raised by the parties. The court emphasized that the independence, discretion, and “integrity” of the judiciary is at stake. Again, the votes were not close: Hunter (Kagan again) was 8-1, and Clark was an apparently unanimous summary reversal.

I wrote separately about both Clark and Hunter in columns last term, and now, the broad overview of all the decisions together occasioned by compiling my booklet led me to comparisons not apparent at the time. The pairings I have identified are not directly inconsistent, and cases can always be distinguished from each other on a granular level. But at some general level I think there are clear tensions between the animating philosophies in each pair. Those tensions reflect deep differences among the justices on fundamental liberty and fairness questions reflected in their approach to criminal law. More of which we turn to now.

As indicated in my September column about upcoming criminal cases, December will be a “big” month, with AR-15 rifle possession and “forfeiture for a six-pack of beer” set for argument on Dec. 1 and 2. One criminal case, Beaird v. United States, has already been argued, presenting a relatively abstract question about how much deference to give to federal Sentencing Guidelines commentary notes. But November will be action-packed with five cases related to criminal law.

To be fair, none of the five cases raises what I would call a “pure” criminal law issue. Instead, there’s a variety of topics related to criminal law: habeas corpus rules (two cases), immigration, private causes of action for constitutional violations, and a purely civil procedure case arising from the firing of a supervisory assistant district attorney. But all present interesting legal issues for Supreme Court nerds like me (us?). Here are brief thumbnail sketches, in order of my own level of interest, not their respective argument dates.

For pure fireworks among the justices, the oral argument a week from Monday may be quite a show. But the result seems pretty much preordained: the court will either overrule an old civil rights precedent or once again limit it to its exact facts.

In 1970, the liberal Warren court ruled in Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents that individuals may sue federal officials directly under the constitution for damages caused if they have violated the Constitution, despite there being no statute that provides for such a “cause of action.” The vote was 5+1 to 3 and the decision has been controversial ever since. Multiple justices have said or suggested that without a congressional statute approving such claims, Bivens violates the constitutional separation of powers. Over time, and with changing personnel and views on the court, Bivens has thus repeatedly been limited, with the court declining to extend it to other circumstances over a dozen times.

In the instant case, Kekai Watanabe was attacked in a federal prison gang riot, and he alleges that he was denied medical care (with prison paramedic Francis Nielsen allegedly saying “stop being a cry baby”) and instead placed in solitary confinement for months. Only then was a serious spinal column injury identified and addressed. In 1980, the Supreme Court had extended Bivens (which had been based on the Fourth Amendment) to Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference claims. But that was the last time the court has ever looked favorably on Bivens. Nielsen now asks that Bivens be overruled, while the solicitor general suggests more mildly that the court might wait for a Fourth Amendment case to do the same.

At oral argument, I have no doubt that the three liberal justices will speak vigorously for Bivens and about the injustice of not allowing remedies for wrongs that violate the Bill of Rights. Chief Justice John Marshall’s famous invocation of the maxim “every right ... must have a remedy,” in Marbury v, Madison, will almost certainly be brought up. But just as vigorously, other justices will invoke the constitutional separation of powers and say that it is Congress, and not an unelected judiciary, that must write legislative protections for legal wrongs. The rhetorical and emotional heroics in this argument may rival those heard in voting, abortion, and birthright citizenship cases. Yet an anti-Bivens result seems virtually pre-ordained.

When a federal prisoner is nearing the end of their term of imprisonment, they often can be transferred to a “halfway house,” which is just what it sounds like: the prisoner is confined to a group home setting at night, but free to leave during the day (with conditions) to look for employment, attend rehabilitation programs, and the like. The prisoner is still within the government’s control and supervision. But is a halfway house “custody” so that legal aspects of it – or in this case, alleged entitlement to it – can be challenged in a habeas corpus proceeding?

Richard Cooke has published on SCOTUSblog a nice account of the issues and briefed arguments. William Maxwell, a mafia-affiliated fraudster who was sentenced in 2015 to 20 years in federal prison, filed a habeas petition claiming that he is entitled to “accelerated release” to a halfway house. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed dismissal, ruling that habeas does not encompass a mere transfer between prison settings. As Cooke writes, the issue is “tricky” because prior cases have used various words to describe the reach of the federal habeas statute, including one (back in 1973) that habeas corpus can extend to a claim for “good conduct” time credits. The federal habeas statute explicitly also addresses prisoners “in custody,” but then lists specifics that don’t quite capture the claim here. And yet, a halfway house is certainly a “level of custody,” even if less restrictive than prison. Moreover, if Maxwell can’t use habeas, he does not appear to have any other judicial remedy available, because 42 U.S.C. §1983 (which authorizes people to sue state officials for violating a constitutional right) can’t be applied to federal officials (as noted in my description of Watanabe).

Neither the solicitor general nor Maxwell liked the 5th Circuit’s description of the proper habeas analysis. So a former law clerk of Justice Samuel Alito has been appointed to argue for affirmance here. Folks who love the intricacies of habeas law – imagine tax law mavens but in criminal law – will find the Maxwell arguments fascinating. But I imagine that the overall numbers of listeners who tune in for Monday’s live argument – has anyone ever filed a FOIA request to get those numbers? – won’t be very high.

This is another case involving the intricacies of habeas law. And it is founded on a complicated procedural history, which is often the case in state criminal cases that finally make their way to the Supreme Court after multiple rounds of lower court litigation. Statutes that regulate habeas petitions filed by both federal and state prisoners permit successive habeas petitions to go forward, even if a prior habeas petition has been filed and denied, if the new petition raises a “new rule of constitutional law ... that was previously unavailable.” The question presented here seems relatively simple (after the procedural thicket is penetrated): is a rule “previously unavailable” when it was “practically unavailable” because the federal courts with jurisdiction over the prisoner would have automatically denied it?

Dexter Johnson is on death row in Texas and says he is intellectually disabled. In 2002, the Supreme Court ruled in Atkins v. Virginia that intellectually disabled persons are protected from execution under the Eighth Amendment’s cruel and unusual punishment ban. In 2015, the 5th Circuit denied a habeas petition Johnson had filed, but then in 2017 the Supreme Court issued a decision that Texas’ definition of intellectual disability was wrong. That is, a new psychiatric Diagnostic Manual allowed a person like Johnson to be declared intellectually disabled. Johnson then filed a successive habeas petition arguing that the change in Texas law created a “new rule” allowing an Atkins claim in his jurisdiction, which had been “previously unavailable” because circuit precedent had declared it meritless. In other words, Johnson says the 2002 Atkins rule was “unavailable” to him until 2017, because it would have been a waste of time, even frivolous, for him to file it prior to the change in the legal standard for Atkins protection. The 5th Circuit appears to have accepted that idea in the litigation leading to this case.

At oral argument next Wednesday, plain language textualists may have a field day. The Atkins ruling was clearly available prior to 2017, and Texas argues, quite simply, that its new constitutional rule was thus not “unavailable” when Johnson filed his first habeas petition. However, as Johnson contends, “available” is variously defined as “capable of being employed with advantage” or “usable.” He therefore argues that the Atkins rule was simply not usable – it was “previously unavailable” to him – until the legal standard for Atkins was made clear in 2017.

It thus turns out that the statutory phrase at issue here is not “plain,” but rather subject to different textual interpretations. Which means, I think, that the oral argument is likely to fall back (as is often the case in habeas cases) on the ideological orientations of various justices. It will be the kind of semantic battling and linguistic nitpicking that, although obviously important, can make the average American simply sick of lawyers.

Although this important immigration case will be argued on the first day of what insiders call “the December calendar,” it actually occurs on the last day of November, when some of us may still be eating Thanksgiving leftovers. Like Guerrero, the case involves the practical application of a simple phrase that literally might mean something else.

There are two noncitizen cases consolidated in one petition here, but discussing the lead respondent is enough for today. Tamer Wassily is a noncitizen who was granted asylum in the United States in 2000, and the applicable statute says that “any alien granted asylum” is eligible for adjustment to permanent resident status. The twist is that Wassily’s asylum status was terminated in 2004 following his conviction of a crime. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit ruled that “granted asylum” must mean “presently be granted asylum” and so it does not encompass applicants whose asylum status is later terminated. The solicitor general agrees, contending that a “common-sense understanding” of the statute must mean that a person who was once granted asylum status which was later terminated cannot take advantage of that prior status. In opposition, Wassily takes the textual position that the unqualified statutory phrase “any alien granted asylum” describes him, and the statute says nothing about a later revocation.

One might cynically guess how this case will come out, but that is not what interests me most. Instead, note how the textualist arguments flip between Guerrero and Wassily. The government seeks a simple plain meaning result for “previously unavailable” in Guerrero but wants a non-textual “common-sense” interpretation in Wassily. There’s nothing wrong with using different arguments in different cases – that’s what law and lawyers are for (smiling emoji). But I sure wish these two cases were being argued on the same day: the combined debate between textualist and commonsense-driven justices and their ideologies likely switching in mere hours might make our heads spin.

Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia (Nov. 2)

Finally, if you feel like Maxwell (described above) might be a bit of a snoozer, wait until the next argument the same day. I wouldn't include Jasmine Younge here at all if she weren't a fired supervisory prosecutor suing her former district attorney office. According to Younge, she was fired about two weeks after telling her boss that she was pregnant. She sued on the basis of pregnancy discrimination, and only months later did the DA’s office invoke a statutory exemption to pregnancy discrimination statutes, something the office had not asserted in its answer to Younge’s complaint or earlier discovery maneuvers. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit affirmed judgment for the DA’s office on that exception, saying there had been no prejudice to Younge from the DA’s delay in bringing up this affirmative defense. Other circuits have ruled that an affirmative defense simply cannot be raised that late – so we are off to the races.

Rodger Citron writes for this blog that the case “will quicken the pulse of civil procedure afficionados.” I’ll be calmer, listening with only one ear to hear how the DA’s attorney explains how they missed the statutory exemption, as well as wondering whether the number of listeners has gone up or down from the Maxwell argument immediately prior.

Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

James Thomas Ashbacher, 37, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, a former U.S. government contractor, was arrested by the FBI on Tuesday for allegedly leaking national defense information by posting the information on a popular social media site, unlawfully retaining other national defense information at his residence, and stealing night vision goggles from the U.S. Army’s Special Operations Command.

According to the indictment, beginning in or about 2021, the defendant worked as an employee of a private company that provided security and emergency management services at the U.S. Army Special Operations Command facility in Fort Bragg, North Carolina. To perform the required functions of his employment, Ashbacher held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

The classified materials were later re-posted by other users to a second social media site. The FBI Charlotte Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the U.S. Department of the Army’s Criminal Investigative Division.

#7743. Justices to debate when an established rule is “previously unavailable” in habeas case

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Nov. 4 in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

But let’s back up a bit: If inmates want to challenge the grounds for their detention, they must typically bring a habeas claim. The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, seeking to curb the number of such petitions, made it significantly more difficult to bring successive applications. Specifically, under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2) of AEDPA, a new claim in a second federal habeas petition is barred unless it falls under one of two exceptions. The first is when such a claim “relies on a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The second exception covers claims based on “the facts underlying the [initial] claim,” but only if those facts would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable factfinder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

Texas inmate Dexter Johnson brought his claim under the first exception, contending that he cannot be put to death based on the court’s 2002 ruling in Atkins v. Virginia, which held that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment. Johnson did not present the Atkins claim in his initial petitions but, after qualifying as intellectually disabled under revised diagnostic standards, raised this in a subsequent petition. The question before the justices is whether Johnson’s Atkins claim was “previously unavailable” to him.

In 2007, Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death in Texas for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. At trial, a defense expert testified that Johnson’s IQ was between 74 and 88 and he “did not have obvious deficits” with regard to “personal independence and social responsibility when compared to other people of similar age and sociocultural background.” Under the diagnostic standards in place at that time, the expert concluded that Johnson was not intellectually disabled. (Johnson did not raise an Atkins claim in his initial habeas petitions but invoked Atkins in those petitions to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.)

In May 2013, while Johnson’s federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the fifth edition of its diagnostic manual, known as the DSM-5, which Texas’ highest criminal court adopted in 2018. The new edition de-emphasized IQ cutoffs and recognized that someone whose score is above 70 may still be intellectually disabled. In April 2019, an expert gave Johnson an IQ test on which he scored 70, and a second expert agreed that Johnson met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability.

Johnson filed a successive habeas application in the district court, in which he claimed that he could not be executed under Atkins. After an evidentiary hearing, the trial court determined that Johnson’s Atkins claim was previously unavailable and consequently stayed his execution. The state appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, which in July 2025 affirmed the district court’s decision. The full 5th Circuit then declined to rehear the case by a vote of 9-7. In February, the state asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, which the Supreme Court agreed in June to do.

In its brief, the Office of the Texas Attorney General maintains that “Johnson’s Atkins claim does not rely on a change in the law.” Instead, it emphasizes, Atkins was decided well before Johnson filed his initial habeas application, and “before Johnson even committed the capital murder for which he was sentenced to death.” Nor, according to the Texas AG’s office, would permitting Johnson to bring such a claim serve the purpose of enabling successive petitions, which is to allow for new evidence as to whether a person is “guilty of the underlying offense.”

The state further presses the point that no “rule” was previously unavailable here. “An object—or a rule—can be available even when it is not needed or useful. A carpenter, for example, likely has a hammer ‘available,’ even when working on a task for which a hammer would not be necessary or useful,” the state writes. The publication of the DSM-5 may have allowed Johnson to discover a new factual predicate, according to the state, but it does not change the availability of any rule. Instead, the 5th Circuit’s approach “erases the line Congress drew between new law and new facts and effectively writes § 2244(b)(2)(B)’s limitations out of the statute.”

Johnson’s attorneys counter that something is “available” only if it is “capable of being used by a person, for a purpose”; prior to the publication of the DSM-5, no such usage was possible. “No one would say the hammer was available to the carpenter if it were locked in a toolbox he couldn’t open,” Johnson’s team writes. “Mr. Johnson did not change; his intellectual and adaptive characteristics are the same as always. What changed was the framework that made Atkins capable of protecting him. Atkins was not available to him before; now it is.” Nor, contrary to the AG’s claim otherwise, Johnson’s lawyers argue, would this open the “floodgates” to many other such challenges. Because very few rules are retroactive, such issues rarely arise.

Perhaps unsurprisingly given its stance on capital punishment, the Trump administration filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting Texas. Echoing several of the state’s arguments, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asserts that “[s]tandards promulgated by a board of psychiatrists cannot transform a decision of this Court that predates a prior habeas application into a ‘new’ and ‘previously unavailable’ rule of constitutional law.” Louisiana and 21 other states, also supporting Texas, call the 5th Circuit’s rule “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality,” pointing out that a professional association also moved the age by which intellectual disability must appear from 18 to 22 in 2021 – raising the possibility that such age-based claims could also be brought and questioning the possibility that the habeas floodgates would remain closed were the court to agree with Johnson.

On Johnson’s side, the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers compares Johnson’s claim to second petitions based on new science about “microscopic hair comparison analysis, arson science, and shaken baby syndrome.” According to the NACDL, “claims of constitutional error grounded in faulty science in a second or successive petition” must be allowed to go forward because “flawed analytical methods may not be debunked until” it is too late.

One final thing worth mentioning: Last term, after hearing argument in Hamm v. Smith, a dispute over how courts should weigh multiple IQ scores in Atkins cases, the justices dismissed the case as improvidently granted (known as a “DIG”) – that is, they decided that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and did not resolve it. At the end of his brief, Johnson asks the court to do the same in his case on the ground that the state has continually changed its arguments. Whatever the merits of Johnson’s position on that front, it seems unlikely the court will DIG two Atkins cases in successive terms.

The decision in Guerrero v. Johnson is expected by late June or early July.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7740. Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”

“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”

“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”

According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”

According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

The FBI Washington Field Office investigated the case, with assistance from the U.S. Department of State's Diplomatic Security Service.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

#7738. Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award.

Reuters reported Monday that the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that ​they actually expended unreasonable,” wrote 10th Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh for a unanimous three-judge panel.

The appeals court also upheld the ​dismissal of the lawsuit.

In her opinion, McHugh acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient. But she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves.

According to Reuters, the case began in 2024, when industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker Flux Drive filed a suit against a Chinese manufacturer, alleging that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to them. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants’ legal fees. On appeal, the company argued that the defense billed for “ministerial tasks,” and that AI use should have lowered the bill.

The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research, and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Brownstein Hyatt partner Christopher Ottele, who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace.

“This ​decision confirms that the use of AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still ​must exercise in every filing with the court,” Ottele told Reuters.

Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

#7734. A surge in cases on religion and schools

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Welcome to a new month and a new argument session. The justices will hear argument in seven cases over the next nine days.

Today, the justices will hear argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

On Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

#7728. Justice Kagan: firing point blank in Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In the 1983 movie A Christmas Story, Ralphie’s teacher, Miss Shields, assigns her students the task of writing “a theme.” The fourth-grade class at Warren G. Harding Elementary school erupts in groans; after all, writing is hard work.

But Ralphie sees it as an opportunity to make his case for a Red Ryder BB gun, “the Holy Grail of Christmas gifts.” And as the words “pour[] forth from [his] penny pencil with feverish fluidity,” he gets right to the point: “What I want for Christmas is a Red Ryder BB gun with a compass in the stock and this thing that tells time.”

Doubtless, Miss Shields had admonished her students – like our teachers admonished us – that each paragraph of a theme must begin with a thesis (or topic) sentence. But is that always right? Pay attention to skilled writers, and you’ll discover that – like many things – it depends.

Skilled writers do locate a paragraph’s issue (topic) and its point (thesis) where readers expect to encounter them. But readers have different expectations about where that should be. Sometimes readers expect the issue and the point in the first sentence, but sometimes they expect them to be separated. Readers change their expectations depending on what type of paragraph they are reading. And sometimes a paragraph has no point at all.

Justice Elena Kagan shows how this works. She never makes a reader hunt for her point, even though she might locate that point in different places for different types of paragraphs.

Take Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos as one of many potential examples. In Smith & Wesson, the court held that Mexico had failed to plead its way around a federal statute barring claims against gun manufacturers. Starting with meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, Kagan does exactly what Miss Shields might insist upon. She locates both the issue and the point of the paragraph right at the beginning, then uses the rest of the paragraph to prove her point.

In Section I.A. of the opinion, for example, Kagan sets out the requirements of the statute being interpreted, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act. Taking only the first sentence of each paragraph, readers learn exactly how the statute works with zero effort. We read:

“[The PLCAA] bars cer­tain lawsuits against manufacturers and sellers of fire­arms.”

“But PLCAA’s general bar on those suits has an exception, usually called the predicate exception, relevant here.”

“Notably here, the predicate violation PLCAA demands may come from aiding and abetting someone else’s firearms offense.”

After each thesis, Kagan deploys the PLCAA’s language to prove that she’s right. For example, to prove that the PLCAA “bars certain lawsuits,” she quotes language providing that a “qualified civil liability action . . . may not be brought in any Federal or State court.” But again, before she shoves the reader’s nose into the language, she first tells us the point of it all.

In adopting this structure, Kagan is giving English readers what they expect. In his book “The Sense of Structure,” George Gopen calls these meat-and-potatoes paragraphs “medial paragraphs.” Here, in the middle of an exposition, “readers tend to appreciate being given the point up front.” Fail to put the point up front and one risks “having the reader disappear before the point actually arrives.” You run an especially grave risk if you are writing for busy legal readers – an audience that’s typically looking for a reason to stop reading.

But in other types of paragraphs, Kagan does not front-load a traditional thesis sentence, and she’s right there too. Consider the way Kagan writes introductions and narrative paragraphs.

In her Smith & Wesson introduction, Kagan reveals the issue or the topic in the first sentence, but she only gives the point or thesis in the last sentence. In the first sentence, we read that Mexico has sued American gun manufacturers – what the case is about. But before we can understand the court’s holding – the point – we need to learn some context. We need a sketch of what the law requires. So Kagan next sets out the statutory requirement: Mexico must plead that the gun manufacturers aided and abetted unlawful sales to the cartels. Only now, at the end of the paragraph, do we know enough to understand the point: Mexico did not plausibly plead aiding and abetting.

Again, according to Gopen, Kagan is satisfying her readers’ “remarkably fixed expectation that the point of an opening paragraph will arrive at the end.” We readers don’t want to be punched in the face with an answer before we know enough to understand it. Writers should make us “comfortable with the surroundings before we have to go to work.”

Narrative paragraphs involve yet another difference: readers don’t expect a traditional thesis in a passage that feels like “once upon a time.” Gopen notes, “Not all paragraphs were born to make a point.” Sometimes writers write “just to tell a story, to put some facts on the table.”

In her narrative paragraphs, Kagan sometimes just tells the story, and sometimes she fires a thesis point blank:

In the end, your old English teacher was mostly right. Ordinary, meat-and-potatoes paragraphs ought to have a sentence in which the issue and the point are together at the beginning of the paragraph. But specialized paragraphs might be different. So, before you start line-editing the sentences of a draft, employ a process to evaluate the strength of your paragraphs.

For your meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, prefer paragraphs that state the point and then prove it. Be on the lookout for paragraphs that write to a conclusion rather than stating it up front. To diagnose these paragraphs, try to create a reverse outline by copying the first sentence (sometimes two) into a different document. Ask yourself whether the argument makes sense with only those sentences. It will if the issue and point are stated up front.

In your statement of facts, mark which paragraphs have a thesis and which don’t. Know that you have a choice about when to include one, and make that choice.

Finally, give special attention to paragraphs that begin a text or a new section. Take the reader from the issue, through the necessary context, and then conclude with the point.

Why so much care? Because hitting the wrong target can be dangerous; you’ll shoot your eye out. A legal reader won’t just stand by trying to guess where the next round is being aimed.

Correction (Nov. 2 at 5:00 p.m.): A prior version of this article gave the case name as Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos de Mexico.

Professor Gray teaches legal writing courses for first-year and advanced students at Duke Law.

#7726. Trial opens for suspect whose multiple email threats include ‘skinning’ federal judge

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.” (Image from Shutterstock)

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.”

David Brooks Pokorny, 45, of El Cerrito, California, allegedly sent 11 email threats in a span of 44 minutes to assault, kidnap and murder Breyer, a senior judge for the Northern District of California, according to U.S. Assistant Attorney Kent Stejskal in opening statements Tuesday.

“Words within those 11 emails constitute what are called true threats,” said Stejskal, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

He allowed the 14-person jury to view snippets of the emails during the trial. Pokorny is charged with making felony threats against a judicial officer and faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

According to Pokorny’s public defender John Reichmuth, his client’s words were “truly shocking, truly offensive, truly ugly, but not true threats.”

Reichmuth said the emails were free speech, and the prosecution would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Pokorny, who has a history of sending threats to public officials and media outlets, meant to perform the actions described in his emails.

Presiding U.S. District Judge Jon Tigar of the Northern District of California noted that the prosecution does not have to prove that Pokorny intended to carry out the threat for it to supersede the protections of First Amendment free speech rights.

#7724. Is Montgomery affirmative action’s final chapter?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted cert in a case called Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. I am surprised it hasn’t received more press coverage because it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.

Perhaps you think the Supreme Court already hammered in that nail in Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President & Fellows of Harvard College, but you’d be wrong. In that case, the court found racial preferences at Harvard and the University of North Carolina to be illegal. Nevertheless, many scholars are now urging schools to turn to what I call “race neutral affirmative action.” These are programs that seek to increase the number of some racial groups relative to others not by selecting for race itself, but by selecting for characteristics correlated with race. For example, instead of using race preferences in admissions, a university uses preferences for applicants who live in zip codes that are nearly all black, applicants who grew up on Indian reservations, or applicants for whom English is a second language. These are real-life examples of what some universities have done when they were forbidden from using race. Many affirmative action supporters think these sorts of things are perfectly legal.

But I have long argued that race proxies are just as illegal as using race itself. My arguments became moot points after the Supreme Court allowed universities to use race itself in admissions in the 2003 case of Grutter v. Bollinger. But now that SFFA has taken that off the table, the question I teed up is back in the limelight: is it constitutional to use racial proxies instead?

That’s what Montgomery County allegedly did to pick the students for its magnet middle schools. Its efforts predated SFFA because, even before the Supreme Court told universities not to use race, they had told school districts not to. In a nutshell, the alleged facts are these: Asian children make up only 15% of the school system’s population – it is majority black and Hispanic – but were taking up half the spots in the magnet middle schools. This didn’t go over well with many parents, so the school board sought to even things out. The board tried several plans but ultimately used a lottery among the applicants who scored above the 85th percentile in their neighborhood on standardized tests. Because the pool was based on how well applicants did compared only to others in their own neighborhood, the plan spread magnet school spots across the county – and, because many neighborhoods don’t have much racial diversity, it spread the spots across the races, too. The number of black and Latino students went up and the number of Asian students went down.

According to Supreme Court precedent, this is unconstitutional. We have a long history of attempts to discriminate indirectly when we couldn’t discriminate directly – and we have an equally long history of the Supreme Court telling us it’s illegal. For example, when we couldn’t deny the ability to vote on the basis of race, we tried using literacy tests and grandfather clauses and felon disenfranchisement instead. The court said those things are illegal. When we couldn’t segregate schools, we tried drawing school district boundaries around mostly black neighborhoods and mostly white neighborhoods instead. The court said we can’t do that, either.

The doctrine is this: if your “purpose” is to discriminate on the basis of race and your “effect” is to discriminate on the basis of race, then you are engaged in discrimination on the basis of race – even if you aren’t using a racial classification. It’s something like the old adage: if something walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it’s a duck.

Most scholars supported these precedents when people were discriminating against blacks. But now not so much. Thus, I expect a bevy of amicus briefs from academics contorting their way through them. But the contortions I have seen thus far are very weak. For example, the leading theory on why these precedents don’t doom Montgomery County is the old distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination: the purpose to help is different than the purpose to hurt. The precedents involved the purpose to hurt blacks, whereas Montgomery County was trying to help blacks (and Latinos); hurting Asians was just a byproduct, not the purpose.

If you thought the Supreme Court had already rejected – over and over again – the distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination, you’d be right. After all, that’s how we got SFFA. As the court explained there, life is often zero-sum: if you help one race by giving them more spots, you necessarily hurt other races by giving them fewer spots. What is “benign” for one is “invidious” for the others. It’s a distinction without a difference.

The scholars say the cases rejecting the benign-invidious distinction don’t count because they involved racial classifications, not racial proxies. But the court in SFFA anticipated this move and cut it off: “[U]niversities may not simply establish through . . . other means the regime we hold unlawful today. … [W]hat cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. … The Constitution deals with substance, not shadows.” Yes, that’s dicta, but isn’t it very, very probative of what the very same justices will think about the very same question next year?

Moreover, the dicta didn’t come from nowhere: in fact, the Supreme Court has already struck down “benign” racial proxies – a bunch of them. When governments engage in racial gerrymandering of voting districts, they don’t use racial classifications: voters are assigned to one district or another based on where they live, not their skin color. Yet, even when these gerrymanders have been designed to help black and Latino voters, the Supreme Court has struck them down all the same, including just this past term in Louisiana v. Callais. Is not Montgomery County engaged in gerrymandering no less than Louisiana? It’s just school districts, not voting districts.

It is true that the court has required discriminators to try “race-neutral alternatives” before they can use race itself. But the court requires race-neutral alternatives only when discriminators otherwise have a compelling interest to justify their discrimination. All this means is that the court prefers racial proxies to racial classifications when forced to choose; it doesn’t mean racial proxies are insulated from constitutional scrutiny.

Still, the court may not need to get into all this because the question presented in the Montgomery County case merely asks what counts as a discriminatory “effect.” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit held that the Asian students had to show a “disparate impact” – a term borrowed from Title VII law that means the challenged practice impacts one race more than another – and they couldn’t do so because, even after the gerrymandering, they still comprised a greater portion of the magnet school spots than they did of magnet school applicants.

Although it is true that disparate impact is one way to show a racial effect under the Supreme Court’s purpose-and-effect precedents, as I previously explained, it is not the only way. For example, when the Supreme Court said that school districts couldn’t evade its desegregation decrees by drawing district lines around mostly white neighborhoods and mostly black neighborhoods, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., schools of different quality); it was enough that one school was overwhelmingly white and the other was overwhelmingly black. When the Supreme Court has said that legislatures couldn’t gerrymander voting districts, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., differential vote dilution); it was enough that the racial composition of the districts had been affected.

It is true that what exactly the racial effect is in the voting cases is undertheorized. There is no obvious baseline to compare to the gerrymandered district lines in order to measure the “effect.” For this reason, some scholars think the court has all but read out the effect requirement from the purpose-and-effect test. Maybe so. The effect requirement comes from an old case called Palmer v. Thompson: there, Jackson, Mississippi, closed all their public swimming pools rather than desegregate them; the court held that this wasn’t unconstitutional racial discrimination because all the races had been affected equally. The ruling is unpopular among scholars on the left; law professor Randall Kennedy at Harvard has compared it to Korematsu. Thus, I doubt many will mourn its demise; plaintiffs would still have to show an injury to establish standing in federal court. But overruling it will only help the plaintiffs in the Montgomery County case.

Still, a lingering question that hasn’t been asked enough is whether the purpose-and-effect doctrine – or even a purpose-only doctrine if Palmer goes away – is consistent with the original understanding of the Constitution. It is hard for me to see how it couldn’t be: it is very easy to evade any rule by proxy; surely, they knew that even back in 1868. But I haven’t seen any historical analyses yet. I hope there are some in the briefing.

I appreciate that for many scholars it is inconceivable that we could end up in a world where it is illegal to do anything about racial disparities. Many of them endorse so-called “antiracism” and believe that all racial disparities must be the product of racism – and, indeed, that we, too, are racists if we don’t do something about them. This means we can sometimes have “too many” Asians. Maybe they’re right about that, maybe they’re wrong. But the 14th Amendment does not enact Mr. Ibram X. Kendi’s “How to Be an Antiracist.”

Brian Fitzpatrick was a law clerk to Antonin Scalia and is currently the Milton R. Underwood Chair in Free Enterprise and Professor of Law at Vanderbilt Law School.

#7722. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”
