#7692. What businesses should know about consent rules when calling consumers

Rules around obtaining consumer consent before calling or texting are in a state of legal and regulatory uncertainty – and companies should remain cautious.

Senosiain is an associate and Rollins is a shareholder at Gunster. Views are the authors’ own.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act governs calls and text messages sent by businesses to consumers. One such rule is that businesses must obtain express written consent prior to sending text messages to consumers, if they are using an automated telephone dialing system or making calls using an artificial or pre-recorded voice, including the use of AI bots.

The TCPA also provides that businesses may not call or text consumers on the federal Do Not Call List unless prior express consent is given. Even basic telemarketing calls and text messages require prior express consent. Violation of the statute can trigger liability for up to $1,500 per call or text message sent.

Additionally, many states have their own version of the TCPA, deemed “mini-TCPAs,” that require compliance for all businesses who make calls to consumer-residents in that state, regardless of where the business is domiciled.

Many companies use lead generators which gather consumer consents for multiple businesses and then provide the companies with consent and contact information for those potential consumers. Lead generators who obtain proper written consent can be a very useful tool for companies. This was generally permissible under the TCPA.

However, in 2023, the Federal Communications Commission updated its TCPA rules requiring “one-to-one consent” which was to become effective Jan. 27, 2025.

The one-to-one consent rule provides that if a business uses an ATDS, artificial or prerecorded voice, the business must obtain prior express consent, one seller at a time.

Thus, it prevents lead generators from using a single consumer’s consent for multiple businesses. Additionally, the one-to-one consent rule provides that the consent must be clear and conspicuous, and the calls and texts initiated pursuant to the consent must be logically and topically associated with the interaction that prompted the consent. This rule applies to both text messages and phone calls.

On Jan. 24, 2025, the FCC postponed the 2023 order by a year, until Jan. 26, 2026. Later that same day the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the 2023 Order, thus eliminating the one-to-one consent rule.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held “that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority under the TCPA because the 2023 Order’s new consent restrictions impermissibly conflict[ed] with the ordinary statutory meaning of prior express consent.”

Notably, the court ruled that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority at the outset, when it created the one-to-one consent rule. The court held that the 2023 Order’s one-to-one prior express consent restriction impermissibly conflicted with the ordinary statutory meaning of “prior express consent.” Thus, the Court vacated application of the 2023 Order, and remanded for further proceedings.

As a result, it is very likely that we will see other cases challenging TCPA regulations, especially as to the consent required before making a telemarketing call or text message using an ATDS.

It is unclear whether the FCC will revise its 2023 Order to comply with the Eleventh Circuit’s decision. In order to be prepared for this rule to come into effect, and in an abundance of caution, businesses who use lead generators to source potential consumers’ consent should ascertain that the lead generators are obtaining individual, one-to-one consent.

Businesses should also only contact consumers who provide this consent for telemarketing that is logically and topically associated with that which the consent was provided. Further, in addition to storing consumer contact information, businesses must retain the consent forms, information as to when consent was given, and through whom. Even businesses that do not use lead generators to obtain consent should continue to review their consent practices to ensure strict compliance with the TCPA and mini-TCPAs.

The TCPA requires prior express consent, and in many cases, prior express written consent, for calls and text messages made to prospective consumers. Regardless of any changes to the TCPA, the FTSA still requires that businesses obtain prior express written consent when making unsolicited telephone calls (including sending text messages) using an automated system. And lastly, to further protect your business, the consent form should have robust terms of service, including a class action waiver.

We continue to recommend that businesses ensure compliance with the TCPA, FTSA, and any other state regulations by always obtaining express written consent prior to contacting potential consumers via calls or text messages.

#7691. Virginia lawmakers assess misuse of automated license plate readers

Automated license plate readers have drawn backlash after reports of police abuse of the surveillance tech.

RICHMOND, Va. (CN) â Members of the Virginia General Assembly met Thursday to review a report on misuse of automated license plate readers by law enforcement agencies and the need for stronger guardrails.

âThe report, commissioned by the Virginia State Crime Commission, surveyed 191 local law enforcement agencies that reported using the controversial surveillance technology as of August. Of those, 10% self-reported unauthorized use of the technology, which uses a network of cameras to track vehicle movement.

âThe commission, comprised of legislators, commonwealth’s attorneys and appointed citizens, discussed the need for more guardrails.

â"It seems to me that we need probably stronger consequences for law enforcement agencies that are not following the laws that we pass," State Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, a Democrat, said at the meeting.

âRepublican Delegate Wren Williams discussed limiting access to the database to certified law enforcement employees. Hampton Commonwealth’s Attorney Anton Bell questioned whether those in his role should have discretion to bring charges against police for misuse. The criminal penalty for law enforcement is a class 1 misdemeanor, but prosecutors have charged only seven officers despite the report outlining numerous instances of misuse and noncompliance with state law.

Virginia-based state and federal courts have upheld the technology’s use in Fourth Amendment challenges. But criminal justice advocates and concerned Virginia residents used the public comment period to push for a complete ban.

â"There is no policing the police," Rob Poggenklass, representing the ACLU of Virginia, said. “While technology can be helpful to law enforcement, we cannot continue to hand over sensitive personal information such as location data to the highest bidder, and that’s exactly what’s happening with these surveillance technologies.”

âMitchell Smith, representing the Institute for Justice, echoed the sentiment and said his organization is pushing police to obtain warrants before using the database.

â"We do not surrender our constitutional rights when we leave our houses and go out in public," Smith said. “The best way to stop abuse is to prevent it from happening in the first place.”

âOf the 191 agencies that used ALPR technology at the time of the August survey, six reported not having an ALPR policy as state law requires. Of the 178 agencies that have policies, 33% do not publicly post their policy as required by law. Seven agencies reported data retention periods longer than the 21-day maximum allowed. In addition, 27 agencies acknowledged they did not engage in public awareness before implementing the technology in their communities.

âThe report also cited a May scientific article in Urban Science that outlined the higher concentration of Virginia’s ALPRs in areas with more of people of color. According to the commission, 42% of investigatory detentions resulting from ALPR-related stops between Jan. 1 and Sept. 30 involved Black people, despite only comprising 20% of the state’s population.

âTwenty-two agencies also reported their systems sometimes, or very often, produced false-positive hits. The report found agencies train officers to use the ALPR database in widely varying ways.

âVirginia enacted sweeping regulations in 2025 that limited permissible uses, mandated a 21-day maximum retention period, restricted data sharing and required monthly audits. Virginia’s regulations rank fourth on the NYU School of Law’s Policing Project’s license plate reader policy scorecard, losing points only for lacking a formal data-sharing process to ensure ALPR data sharing is lawful, authorized and documented.

âThe survey found 86% of agencies contracted with Flock Safety for their ALPR needs. Of the 191 responding agencies, 52 reported acts of vandalism ranging from people spray-painting the cameras, cutting power cables and purposefully hitting the cameras with vehicles. Vandals also set them on fire and shot the cameras, according to the report.

âDozens of Virginia localities have suspended, ended or decided not to renew their contracts with Flock Safety and other ALPR companies since responding to the August survey, including Alexandria, Arlington, Richmond and Lynchburg.

#7689. New Mexico Supreme Court permanently disbars prosecutor after disciplinary findings

The New Mexico Supreme Court, after hearing from a disciplinary board, has permanently disbarred a prosecutor who was found to have pattern of misconduct that denied defendants fair trials. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New Mexico Supreme Court, after hearing from a disciplinary board, has permanently disbarred a prosecutor who was found to have pattern of misconduct that denied defendants fair trials.

Cosme Ripol, a prosecutor from the district attorney’s office for the Eighth Judicial District in Taos, New Mexico, was disbarred Monday, effective immediately.

All five justices on the state supreme court agreed on the disciplinary board’s recommendation. The proceedings focused on three criminal cases that Ripol prosecuted between 2022 and 2024.

According to coverage by the Santa Fe New Mexican, a pivotal case in the investigation was State v. Desiree Lensegrav, where the defendant was convicted in 2022 of first-degree murder, kidnapping, conspiracy and tampering with evidence.

The New Mexico Supreme Court vacated Lensegrav’s convictions after it learned that Ripol, who had been licensed to practice law in the state since 1986, used inadmissible evidence and made derogatory statements about the defendant during the trial.

“As the supreme court noted, prosecutors are held to a higher standard because of their unique responsibility to seek justice,” said Marcus Montoya, the district attorney for the Eighth Judicial District, in a statement Monday. “When improper tactics are employed in the courtroom, even by an attorney with more than 30 years of criminal law experience, that standard is not met.”

#7688. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7687. Minnesota high court urged to shield negative Google reviews from defamation suits

Though the underlying suit was tossed, the court will decide if such reviews qualify for increased free speech protections that speed up litigation and force losing plaintiffs to pay legal fees.

MINNEAPOLIS (CN) â Minnesota Supreme Court justices grappled Thursday with whether negative online business reviews should be awarded heightened free-speech protection against defamation suits.

While the reviewer, Robinet Productions LLC, paints the case as an attack on a small business owner attempting to warn others, the contractor, Paragon Restorations LLC, insists it is a simple dispute over unpaid, defective work that was weaponized to damage its reputation.

The feud stems from a failed commercial contract between the two parties. After Paragon refused to pay for promotional video work, Robinetâs owner posted a one-star Google review, claiming it was denied payment and urging others to avoid working with Paragon.

Paragon then sued Robinet, claiming defamation and arguing the review was false as the production company did not fulfill its contract obligations.

Robinet moved to dismiss the claim under Minnesotaâs Uniform Public Expression Protection Act â an anti-SLAPP statute designed to protect critics from âstrategic lawsuits against public participation,â which are âbaselessâ claims intended to silence speech through litigation.

âParagon never expected to win a monetary judgment,â Robinetâs attorney, Vince Reuter, said. âIt instead sought to punish Mr. Robinet for refusing to take down his business review, or through litigation, to force him to decide how much money he wanted to spend to protect his own free speech.â

Anti-SLAPP laws grant defendants fast-tracked judicial timelines, and granted motions force plaintiffs to pay attorneys fees and litigation expenses. Crucially, the act does not apply to purely private disputes, but rather âmatters of public concern.â

While the lower court notably dismissed Paragonâs defamation claim â finding the core statement that Robinet was denied payment technically true â it did so without applying the act, blocking the company from receiving attorneys fees.

The Minnesota Court of Appeals later agreed Robinetâs review was not a public concern â but rather a personal grievance based on a private transaction.

Robinet argues that reading cripples small business owners who lack the time and money required for litigation â noting the owner chose to forgo legal action in favor of an online review warning others against doing business with Paragon.

âThis Google review is an express warning to others,â Reuter said. âMr. Robinet used his experience to tell others about Paragonâs unprofessionalism and ultimate refusal to pay him anything for the hours of work that he provided.â

The Minnesota Supreme Court has an established constitutional test evaluating the content, form and context of a statement to determine whether it addresses a matter of public concern for First Amendment defamation purposes â which the lower courts use as a strict gatekeeper to evaluate anti-SLAPP protection.

Reuter argued this framework forces everyday consumer reviews through a system designed for high-stakes defamation, counter to the legislatureâs intent to protect public commentary.

âThe purpose of this law is to expand and broaden free speech,â he said.

Paragonâs attorney, Samuel Johnson, cautioned the court that opening the door to qualify business reviews as matters of public concern would bypass context and broaden the act’s intended reach.

âIf the legislature did what appellants say it would do, by making all ratings and reviews of businesses occupy that highest rung of First Amendment protection, that would invade the role of this court to decide what constitutional protections exist,â Johnson said, arguing the only purpose of the review was to express anger over unpaid services.

Justice Anne McKeig pushed back on Johnsonâs stance.

âIt seems the secondary purpose was to actually warn others,â she said, though Johnson argued there was no evidence anyone responded to Robinetâs review, meaning the speech had little to no social or political impact.

The bench was highly skeptical of this âcommunity connectionâ argument, questioning whether thatâs a fair way to measure impact or public concern.

âShould we be a little bit worried that weâre creating or adopting a test that sort of privileges popular statements and disadvantages unpopular statements?â Justice Karl Procaccini asked.

If the court sides with Robinet, negative online business reviews, consumer complaints and other warnings about bad business practices will have a clearer path for anti-SLAPP protection, which Robinet argued is essential.

âThe issue is, they get the advantage of these five-star reviews, but if somebody has the audacity to give them a one-star review on true facts and an honest and personal opinion, that person is dragged through the mud in a defamation claim,â Reuter said.

Justice Paul Thissen countered that a lot of people are harmed by defamation suits, but that may not necessitate heightened protection.

âIt could be that itâs really just, we want to protect those very highest levels of constitutional speech, and so the fact that maybe only 2% of business reviews are subject to the anti-SLAPP act may be exactly what the legislature intended,â he said.

#7685. Mootness, maps, and motor vehicles

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

After two weeks without a conference, the justices return Friday to a relist lineup with a distinctly Southern accent. Four newly relisted cases come from Alabama. Three concern the same congressional district map and its seemingly inexhaustible capacity to generate Supreme Court litigation. The fourth asks whether using a car makes an otherwise local kidnapping a federal crime – even when the car never crosses a state line.

The Supreme Court’s long-running dispute over Alabama’s congressional districts is back for yet another round. Three related relists – Allen v. Milligan, Allen v. Singleton, and Allen v. Caster – ask the justices to revisit a congressional district map they have already considered several times. Readers may recall that in 2023, the court upheld a preliminary injunction against Alabama’s 2021 congressional map because the challengers were likely to succeed on their claim that it unlawfully diluted Black voting strength under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Alabama responded by drawing a new map that, like its predecessor, contained just one district in which Black voters had an opportunity to elect their preferred candidates.

After an 11-day trial, a three-judge district court found in 2025 that the replacement map violated both Section 2 and the 14th Amendment’s prohibition against intentional racial discrimination. But this spring, the Supreme Court changed the standards for Section 2 liability in Louisiana v. Callais and vacated the district court’s judgment for reconsideration. In the wake of that decision, the district court revisited the record and reached substantially the same conclusions that it had previously, issuing another preliminary injunction against the 2023 map. On June 2, the Supreme Court stayed that injunction, concluding that Alabama had shown a likelihood of success on the merits. That cleared the way for Alabama to use its preferred map in this week’s congressional elections.

Redistricting cases are among the rare types of cases over which the Supreme Court still has mandatory appellate jurisdiction. Alabama now seeks to appeal in Milligan and Singleton, and certiorari before judgment in Caster, the appeal of which is pending in the 11th Circuit. Alabama argues that the district court failed to follow Callais by disregarding the state’s legitimate redistricting priorities, particularly keeping Mobile and Baldwin Counties together as a Gulf Coast community of interest and protecting incumbents. It also contends that the district court wrongly attributed voting patterns to race rather than politics and failed to respect the presumption of legislative good faith. Alabama asks the justices to summarily reverse or, alternatively, take the cases for full review.

The challengers see things differently. They lead with mootness. In their motion to dismiss or affirm in Milligan, their motion to dismiss in Singleton, and their response in Caster, they argue that the injunction covers only the 2026 elections, which are underway using the 2023 plan, so that no live controversy remains. The Singleton plaintiffs note that the district court has scheduled trial for early 2027. Alabama responds that the injunction could continue to have legal effects, that election administration extends beyond Election Day, and that the requirement to use the court-drawn map may remain in force until Alabama adopts a new plan.

In Milligan and Caster, the challengers argue that the district court properly found the state’s asserted priorities were rationalizations for intentional discrimination. They point to legislators’ use of racial data, the removal of the city of Selma from Congressional District 2 “to ensure that Black voters there were ‘utterly unable to elect a representative of their choice,’” and unusual last-minute legislative findings “inserted into the bill on the morning of passage.” They maintain that Callais did not overrule the Supreme Court’s earlier Milligan decision and does not undermine the district court’s findings of intentional discrimination.

The justices’ June stay suggests that Alabama may have a receptive audience for its merits arguments. Whether the justices will reach those arguments – or conclude that no live controversy remains over the preliminary injunction – is less certain. Whatever happens, it seems unlikely that we’ve seen the last of Alabama’s congressional maps.

How can a car trip that never leaves Alabama become a matter of interstate commerce? That’s the question in Brown v. United States, which asks whether every automobile is automatically an “instrumentality of interstate commerce,” regardless of how it is used. The answer determines whether the federal government can prosecute a kidnapping committed entirely within one state based solely on the kidnapper’s use of a car.

In 2019, Derick Brown and her boyfriend abducted a three-year-old girl, driving her in Brown’s Toyota Sequoia from Birmingham to nearby Center Point, Alabama. The child was subsequently found dead. A federal jury convicted Brown of kidnapping (resulting in death) and conspiracy to kidnap, and she received a life sentence. The federal kidnapping statute, as amended in 2006, reaches kidnappings committed using “any means, facility, or instrumentality of interstate or foreign commerce.” Brown argued that using a car for a kidnapping committed entirely within Alabama, however, did not supply the interstate-commerce connection necessary for a federal prosecution. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit rejected Brown’s statutory and constitutional arguments, relying on its recent decision in United States v. Bryan holding that automobiles are per se instrumentalities of interstate commerce, even when used entirely within a single state.

Brown argues that the 11th Circuit’s rule would give Congress virtually unlimited authority over activities involving automobiles – potentially including everything from kidnapping to parking violations. More importantly for certiorari purposes, she identifies a circuit split. In United States v. Chavarria, she argues that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the proposition that motor vehicles are automatically instrumentalities of interstate commerce with regard to the federal kidnapping statute. Judge Victoria Calvert dissented in Bryan, warning that the majority had placed the 11th Circuit on the “wrong side of a developing split.” Georgetown law professor Randy Barnett and the Cato Institute filed amicus briefs supporting Brown, emphasizing the original limits of Congress’ commerce power.

The U.S. solicitor general responds that automobiles are instrumentalities of interstate commerce because they use highways, which are channels of interstate commerce, much as airplanes use airspace and railroad cars use railroads. Congress therefore may regulate their use even when the particular trip is entirely intrastate. The government also disputes the existence of a circuit split. It maintains that Chavarria held only that the broader category of “motor vehicles” – which can include lawnmowers, elevators, and motorized wheelchairs – is not invariably an instrumentality of interstate commerce. Brown calls that distinction “mere wordplay,” pointing out that the vehicle in Chavarria was a Jeep Cherokee, not a lawnmower.

We’ll be back next week to see whether the justices are ready to act – or whether these cases need another trip around the conference table.

Issue: Whether an automobile is per se an instrumentality of interstate commerce, which would make a federal offense of every kidnapping involving an automobile under 18 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1).

#7684. Texas asks Fifth Circuit to unblock law targeting companies that boycott fossil fuels

The state is seeking to lift an injunction issued by a federal judge who found the law violates the First Amendment by punishing companies for anti-oil and gas rhetoric.

(CN) â A Fifth Circuit panel Thursday wrestled with the constitutionality of a Texas law prohibiting the state from investing in or contracting with companies boycotting fossil fuels.

Senate Bill 13, passed in 2021, was the first major state law penalizing corporate climate initiatives. The law prohibits Texas’ retirement and school funds from investing in financial firms that boycott fossil fuel companies, and it also bans state contracts worth $100,000 or more with companies that boycott fossil fuels.

Texas is asking the Fifth Circuit to reverse a federal judge’s ruling that the law violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Alan Albright, a Donald Trump appointee in the Western District of Texas, issued an injunction blocking the law in February, but a separate Fifth Circuit panel put that judgment on hold pending appeal.

On Thursday, the panel judges â all also Trump appointees â grappled with whether the law allows the state to punish companies for anti-oil and gas rhetoric.

The dispute comes down to a phrase in the statute saying a company is boycotting fossil fuels if it takes “any action that is intended to penalize” fossil fuel companies. Plaintiff American Sustainable Business Council, a coalition of businesses that advocate for sustainable practices, argues this includes anti-fossil fuel speech.

U.S. Circuit Judge Cory Wilson asked Beth Klusmann, a lawyer with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, about the plaintiff’s argument that the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts has used the law to blacklist companies like major investment firm Blackrock for speech critical of fossil fuels, even though Blackrock still invests in fossil fuel companies.

Blackrock was initially added to Texas’ blacklist in 2022, but it was later removed after it withdrew from environmental initiatives like Climate Action 100+ that aim to reduce corporate greenhouse gas emissions.

Klusmann told the panel a company can be boycotting fossil fuels under the law’s definition while still investing in fossil fuel companies if it’s holding such companies to different standards.

“Think about it this way: In the context of, for example, a discrimination case under Title VII, you can hire women and still discriminate against them by holding them to higher standards, by paying them less, things of that nature,” she said. “You can still invest in fossil fuel companies but hold them to higher standards or require certain things of them that you don’t require from other investments. That would be considered penalizing under the statute, but it still falls within boycott, and it’s not focused on speech.”

The law exempts actions taken for “an ordinary business purpose.” Wilson questioned whether that phrase is unconstitutionally vague, as firms have been blacklisted despite providing commercial reasons for not investing in fossil fuels.

Klusmann responded that refusing to invest in a fossil fuel company because of environmental harm, rather than based on the financial viability of the company, would not be an “ordinary business purpose.” She returned to the comparison to Title VII.

“You can discriminate on the basis of sex if it is a bona fide occupational qualification, such as, for example, a sex-segregated locker room attendant,” she said. “Now, I couldn’t therefore say, well, I think women miss work more often because they stay home with their kids when they’re sick, and therefore that’s my bona fide occupational qualification. We can look through that and see, no, you’re just discriminating against women at that point. And so that’s what the comptroller is essentially trying to do here.”

The American Sustainable Business Council’s attorney, Rachel Nguemaha, argued excluding ordinary business purposes from the law’s definition of boycott is problematic because it “takes out commercial actions from the core of the definition, so you’re left with essentially a null set unless you include expressive activity.”

“Well, of course, there would be a problem if you didn’t put that in, right? Because then there could be any number of business decisions that would be eminently reasonable because you looked at P/E ratios or whatever, and you decided you weren’t going to invest in a particular asset class or a different particular group of securities, right?” U.S. Circuit Judge Andrew Oldham responded. “I mean, this is literally what business managers do all day, every day, is make decisions. We’re going to be long in this, short in that. We’re going to exclude this other thing. I mean, that’s the essence of being an investment advisor.”

The judges also pressed Nguemaha on Texas’ authority to regulate state investments.

“Why does the state have to join your boycott?” Wilson asked. “You’re saying that no matter what we do, that we have a right to compete for these funds and have state funds invested in our funds, regardless of whether we hurt the state.”

“It’s not no matter what we do,” Nguemaha responded. “It’s that the state cannot penalize companies on account of their protected expression.”

U.S. Circuit Judge Don Willett joined Wilson and Oldham on the panel. The judges took the case under submission and did not indicate when they would rule.

#7683. Investors say Carvana lied about title and registration compliance

The United Association National Pension Fund says it has met all requirements to certify a class of investors injured by Carvana, which is accused of artificially inflating stock prices.

PHOENIX (CN) â Attorneys for disgruntled Carvana investors rehashed arguments Thursday that the used car retailer caused massive drops of stock value through misleading statements regarding compliance with titling and inspection standards.

In a Phoenix courtroom, United Association National Pension Fund attorney Rachel Cocalis said the group has met all qualifications to certify the class of investors who lost money after Carvanaâs dramatic market plummets, and argued the retailer has not severed the link between price impacts and the specific misrepresentations it’s accused of.

Carvana instead blames its stock drops on national economic trends.

Amid high inflation and rising interest rates coming out of the Covid-19 pandemic, âsurprisingly car sales went down,â Carvana attorney Peter Hammel told the court.

The parties did not disagree that the pension fund meets the standards necessary to represent a class: that the class is numerous, that there is a common question of law or fact, that the claims of the representative plaintiffs are typical of the class as a whole and that the representative plaintiffs will adequately protect the interests of the class.

But Hammel argued that no class period can be established because no more than one statistically significant stock price fluctuation occurred in the proposed period of May 2020 to October 2022.

âTheyâre trying to start a class period on a day that nobody was misled,â Hammel said. âItâs impossible for an investor to have been injured by an accurate statement.â

Because Carvanaâs experts found only one statistically significant price fluctuation, there is no range of misdeeds to establish the beginning and end of a class period, he argued.

Representing the plaintiffs, Rachel Cocalis said a lack of statistical significance is not a death sentence for this type of claim if the defendants cannot prove a lack of causation.

United Pension Fund attorneys point to 10 public statements made by Carvana between 2020 and 2022 that artificially inflated stock prices by falsely ensuring compliance with title and inspection standards.

From 2020 on, Carvanaâs rapid sales growth outpaced its ability to obtain legal titles for those cars and register them in the states they were sold. The plaintiffs say Carvana lied in SEC filings and shareholder communications when it insisted that its reliance on temporary out-of-state plates complied with all licensing regulations and titling laws. The plaintiffs also accuse Carvana of lying about vehicle inspection standards and exaggerating its profit margins.

Relying on these assurances, investors bought Carvana stocks at artificially high prices, only to lose money when the truth finally came out, according to a 2022 lawsuit.

Plaintiff’s attorney Rachel Cocalis, of the San Diego firm Robins Geller, connected Carvanaâs tumultuous stock turns to specific Carvana statements followed by revelations of misdeeds.

Carvana touted retail sales growth in August 2021, raising stocks by 9%, only for news to later break that North Carolina suspended Carvanaâs dealer license in Wake County for title and registration violations. Stocks similarly fell six months prior after Michigan put Carvana on probation for violating inspection standards.

All the while, Carvana assured investors it was in compliance.

âBut Carvana continues its innocent until proven guilty approach despite knowing it would lead to DMV fines and loss of dealership access,â Cocalis said.

Defending Carvana, Hammel said the plaintiffs cannot prove that stock price changes had anything to do with statements made by Carvana.

âAfter four years, thereâs no statistical evidence that carvana stock went up on any specific day,â Hammel said.

Statisticians brought on as experts reported no statistical significance in the stock fluctuations occurring around specific events referenced by the plaintiffs, save for one.

The exception was Feb. 24, 2022, when stock price rose by 17%.

âThat is evidence of price impact,â Cocalis said.

On that day, though, Carvana announced a $2.2 billion cash acquisition of ADESA U.S., the nation’s second-largest wholesale vehicle physical auction business.

Because U.S. District Judge Michael T. Liburdi already dismissed the specific statement the plaintiffs linked to that fluctuation. Hammel argued nothing else could legally be used to explain it.

âThere was an obvious reason why the stock price did move,â he said.

In general, Hammel blamed the eventual drops not on any revelation of wrongdoing, but on external market factors that both Carvana and its direct competitors faced alike. Many of those competitors went out of business.

âThere were dramatic macroeconomic factors affecting the stock price at this time,â he said, referring to a global pandemic and economic recession.

Hammel maintained that none of Carvanaâs challenged statements were actually misleading, but Cocalis argued they donât need to be, as long as they omitted the truth about Carvanaâs title and registration violations.

âIf they didnât engage in that conduct, those sales numbers would be lower,â she said.

Liburdi, a Donald Trump appointee, said he would try to rule in the next month.

#7681. Law firms are susceptible to insider theft but can take steps to protect themselves

The Georgia-based Dozier Law Firm was a victim of ongoing internal theft that went undetected for years.

Investigators in July uncovered evidence of forgery and theft at the firm, and police later charged employee Nadine Brooks with more than 100 felonies and misdemeanors. She is suspected of stealing $190,000 from the firm’s Macon, Georgia, location through fraudulent credit card payments over a five-year period.

In Louisiana, Sarah Steiner, an employee of the Trey Morris Law Firm, pleaded guilty to one count of felony theft of $25,000 or more and was ordered to pay $147,000 in restitution to the firm. She was sentenced to 10 years in prison last month.

And three years ago in Texas, Christiane Kathleen Irwin, a law firm controller, admitted to embezzling $1.48 million by inflating her payroll check over three years. She was sentenced to 50 months in prison and ordered to pay the embezzled amount in restitution.

The amount of money law firms lose to occupational fraud is unknown, but experts believe the figure is significant. Because firms are busy trying to protect themselves from wire fraud, phishing scams and ransomware attacks, they often neglect to arm themselves against inside threats. Fraud frequently occurs through a firm’s routine operations: managing trust accounts, payroll, credit card and expense reports, billings and collections.

Insider thefts cost U.S. businesses between $20 billion and $50 billion per year, according to some estimates. In May, the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners published Occupational Fraud 2026: A Report to the Nations which examined 2,402 cases that took place around the world and reports organizations lose an estimated 5% of revenue to fraud each year. The study’s Fraud Tree lists three main classifications: asset misappropriation, corruption (conflicts of interest, bribery, illegal gratuities, economic extortion) and financial statement fraud.

Attorneys are accountable when a nonlawyer employee steals from a client. For example, if a firm’s receptionist stole money from a client’s prepayments, the lawyer is still liable and legally responsible for the money, according to Emil J. Ali, an attorney who specializes in ethics and discipline matters. He recommends steps such as regularly reviewing a firm’s check log and examining records overseen by the receptionist.

Attorneys often prioritize working with clients and leave other professionals to handle administrative tasks. “However, even a 20-year veteran in accounting needs supervision, whether for intentional or unintentional acts. The buck stops with the lawyer,” says Ali, a partner at McCabe Ali in Los Angeles and president-elect of the Association of Professional Responsibility Lawyers.

Philadelphia-based ethics attorney Ellen Brotman, who formerly practiced criminal defense, now represents lawyers and judges who need help with defending their licenses, reinstatements and bar admissions. Brotman, a member of the Pennsylvania Bar Association Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee and the Philadelphia Bar Association Professional Guidance Committee, also advises judges and lawyers about conflicts rules, termination, handling money and defending disciplinary prosecutions.

“We get a lot of calls about money,” Brotman says. “It’s shocking to me how good lawyers don’t understand the rules about money.”

Lawyers should pay attention to keeping trust accounts separate from general accounts. “Your trust account is always other people’s money. Your operating account is always your money,” says Brotman, noting that attorneys may not oversee some processes. For example, if a bookkeeper is a long-term trusted employee or close relative, the theft may go unnoticed by the attorney. “It’s your obligation to keep that money safe.”

Employees who steal from law firms aren’t always easy to spot, but there may be signs, such as beginning to live extravagant lifestyles disproportionate to their incomes. Dedicated employees who insist on working alone, stay late and come into the office at odd times also might be trying to conceal theft.

International Fraud Awareness Week, a public campaign beginning Nov. 15, encourages companies to learn about occupational fraud and share tips. It is sponsored by the ACFE, which published the Occupational Fraud 2026 study.

“There are things that organizations can do to limit the occurrence and impact of occupational fraud,” says Mason Wilder, research director for the ACFE study.

Wilder says the organization has seen losses decrease over the last decade. “We hope that some of that is because of some of the awareness we’ve raised with this report and the resources that we provide not only our members but the general public to help better detect, prevent and respond to fraud.”

For instance, lawyers can learn to better understand financial statements and look for questionable expenses and revenues, along with fake receipts or personal purchases disguised as business expenses, Wilder says.

#7680. Airlines accused of sharing pricing data to inflate fares

Two airline passengers say seven major carriers used a shared database to monitor pricing and suppress fare competition.

(CN) â Seven major airlines used a shared database to monitor each other’s prices, curbing competition and driving up the cost of domestic air travel, two airline passengers claim in a proposed class action.

Ashley Ward and Gregory Morris sued the airlines, Airline Tariff Publishing Company and its subsidiary 3Victors on Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The plaintiffs claim the companies conspired to exchange confidential pricing information in violation of federal antitrust law.

The airline defendants include American, Delta, United, Southwest, Alaska, Hawaiian and JetBlue. Ward says she bought tickets from Southwest while Morris purchased flights from United, and both claim they paid artificially inflated fares.

At the center of the lawsuit are two products operated by 3Victors: Iris, an airline shopping and pricing data aggregator, and PriceEye, an analytics tool that lets airlines monitor competitorsâ fares and pricing changes.

The plaintiffs say airlines contribute shopping data and dynamically generated prices to Iris in exchange for access to PriceEye. The dashboard provides pricing alerts, competitive benchmarks and tools to detect unusual changes, allowing airlines to track rivalsâ pricing in near real time.

The arrangement operates on a âgive-to-getâ model. âParticipation in Iris is based on a simple principle: the more you contribute, the more you receive,â the plaintiffs say.

Ward and Morris say the system undermines the secrecy that dynamic pricing was supposed to bring to airline ticket sales. Airlines can use individualized offers to compete for customers, but sharing that information with competitors makes it easier to monitor and respond to price cuts.

3Victors advertises that PriceEye lets airlines âconfidently monitor the competitive landscape and adjust pricing strategies as markets shift â hour by hour, not day by day,â the plaintiffs say in the complaint.

They trace the arrangement to a working group called Airline Tariff Publishing Company, or ATPCO, formed in 2016 to study dynamic pricing. A study presented at an industry conference the following year illustrated how airlines unable to monitor one anotherâs private offers could engage in price wars, driving fares down.

ATPCO subsequently developed a system to standardize dynamic pricing data and began collecting airlinesâ shopping information. The company announced a program in 2023 that allowed airlines to analyze collective shopping data, and it acquired 3Victors later that year.

By 2025 and 2026, the plaintiffs say, ATPCO had integrated the technology into Iris and PriceEye, creating a system that allowed participating airlines to exchange and analyze sensitive pricing information.

The plaintiffs, represented by Steve W. Berman of Hagens Berman, seek to represent classes of domestic airline ticket purchasers. They want the court to block the information-sharing arrangement and award damages.

At the LBJ School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin, Hinojosa unveiled the leaders of her transition team and sought to set the tone for what Texans can expect from her administration, telling reporters, âNow the fun part starts.â

âWe will have a bipartisan transition, and we will have a bipartisan administration and government in Texas,â Hinojosa said.

âI think it’s important that as elected leaders we respect what the people of Texas have said,â Hinojosa explained. âThey want change, and I would hope that elected leaders from both parties don’t get in the way of the progress we can make together to deliver for working people.â

As of Thursday afternoon, Hinojosa leads Abbott by seven points, a bruising defeat for the longtime governor who was seeking a fourth term in office.

Political pundits, lawmakers and Texans are still in a state of reeling after Tuesdayâs historic election. The Lone Star State, previously seen as the Republicansâ crown jewel, flipped entirely, with all statewide offices breaking for Democrats. âTexas is blue,â Cruz wrote. âThat is a hard sentence to utter. But Texas, today at least, is blue. As we sit here today, I am the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas. Thatâs not something I ever thought I would say.â

The argument next week in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. should give the justices a break from the back-and-forth sniping in high-profile stay applications of the last several weeks as they consider a lower-stakes problem of statutory interpretation under the Natural Gas Act.

A major topic under the Natural Gas Act is the construction of interstate natural-gas pipelines. Among other things, the statute delegates to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission authority to approve construction of such pipelines, which grants a federal “certificate of public convenience and necessity” for the project. If the holder of the certificate is unable to purchase the land needed for the pipeline by agreement, the statute grants the holder the right to exercise the federal power of eminent domain to acquire a “necessary right-of-way.”

Not surprisingly, a common problem in such projects is that parties holding the relevant land do not readily agree to allow the pipeline to be built through their property (which usually requires an easement of some sort). In turn, federal courts traditionally require in eminent domain cases that the condemning party pay the “just compensation” that the Fifth Amendment requires when property is “taken for public use.” State courts are obligated to provide at least as much compensation, but often, for one reason or another, provide more than the Constitution requires. In this case, for example, it is at least plausible that the law of North Dakota (where the Hoffmanns and their family own land through which WBI Energy Transmission seeks to build a pipeline) requires the condemnor to pay not only the value of the land but also the reasonable attorney’s fees of the landholder.

The question is whether just compensation here should be determined by referring to state law.

For the Hoffmanns, the key to the case is the absence of any statement in the Natural Gas Act as to what law courts should apply in assessing appropriate compensation. Acknowledging that federal standards should apply when the United States takes property in its own name, the Hoffmanns argue that state law typically applies when the condemnation power has been delegated to a private party like WBI. In their view, the baseline in disputes between private parties (the pipeline company and the landowner), as supported by cases such as United States v. Kimbell Foods, should be the law of the state where the land is located.

For WBI, by contrast, the key to the case is the source of the condemnation power in federal law. Because it is clear that the federal government operating under that statute would pay “just compensation” and nothing else, WBI argues that Congress could not have intended to subject pipeline operators to local laws that require payments beyond just compensation. The federal government, appearing in support of WBI, argues emphatically that a contrary rule would permit states to discriminate against types of construction that the federal government, as opposed to the state, would support.

WBI and the federal government point to two key pieces of evidence, close in time to the adoption of the Natural Gas Act. The first is a statute (the General Bridge Act of 1946) that explicitly called for compensation to be “ascertained and paid according to the laws of [the] State.” For the government and WBI, the absence of similar language from the contemporaneous Natural Gas Act is powerful evidence that federal standards always apply under that statute. The second is a case, United States v. Miller, decided just a few years before adoption of the Natural Gas Act, in which the Supreme Court held that in a condemnation under an earlier statute with similar wording federal rather than state compensation standards applied. Hoffmann responds that the case is irrelevant because it involves a condemnation by the United States rather than a private party.

One last twist that I expect will come up at oral argument: Because the particular dispute here involves attorney’s fees, it surely is relevant that the court has adopted something of a clear statement rule that courts will not award attorney’s fees under a federal statute absent an explicit statement from Congress. Whatever the justices might think about federal and state standards on other topics, my guess is then that some of them will shrink from mandating an award of attorney’s fees under a statute that is silent on the topic.

I would not expect a heated argument in Hoffmann, as the issues seem far removed from the hot button topics that have been dividing the justices so much recently. But, of course, you never can tell.

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

#7676. Judge orders Albertsons to pay Washington $900 million over role in opioid crisis

The pharmacy chain put profits over the safety of patients, the state court determined.

SEATTLE (CN) â A Washington judge on Thursday ordered Albertsons to pay a whopping $900 million judgment after finding the grocery pharmacy chain neglected to guard against the misuse and diversion of addictive medications.

âThe state of Washington is in the throes of an opioid epidemic that is so wide-reaching and damaging that it has impacted Washingtonians throughout the state,â wrote King County Superior Court Judge Janet Helson in a 219-page opinion. âBased on the evidence presented at trial, the court finds that defendants Albertsons Companies, Inc. and Safeway, Inc. substantially contributed to the creation and maintenance of this public nuisance, and that the same yearslong unfair acts or practices that contributed to the nuisance also violated Washingtonâs Consumer Protection Act.â

The judgment follows a nine-week bench trial in which the state presented evidence of Albertsons failing to investigate or report shipments of significant quantities of suspicious orders of opioids into their own pharmacies.

The evidence also showed Albertsons had improper safeguards that led to diversion â transfer of prescription opioids to the black market â and failed to conduct due diligence when dispensing staggering quantities of opioid prescriptions that raised red flags of diversion.

âThe opioid crisis has been an equal opportunity monster, bringing its destruction not only to urban areas, but to many small towns and rural areas throughout our state,â Helson wrote. âThis ongoing crisis has affected, and interfered with, public health, public safety, public spaces, and the day-to-day life of Washington residents to the point that any efforts to remedy it will necessarily be massive in size, scope, and time.â

Albertsons acts as both a distributor and dispenser of prescription opioids and is required by the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Controlled Substances Act to provide effective controls against diversion. Helson found the national pharmacy chain failed to do so.

âThe preponderance of evidence demonstrates that Albertsons never implemented and enforced policies or procedures that were effective at preventing the shipping of suspicious orders of prescription opioids to their stores, or the dispensing of âred flagâ prescriptions from those stores, without the required due diligence,â Helson wrote. âMoreover, Albertsons possessed, but routinely disregarded or ignored, information and tools that could have helped prevent diversion, choosing sales and profits over patient safety.â

The state presented evidence showing instances where tens of thousands of opioid pills were either diverted or inappropriately dispensed. Helson found the disregard for the health and safety of Washingtonians substantially contributed to the ongoing opioid crisis in the state.

Albertsons owns and operates more than 200 pharmacies in the state.

The court also found Albertsons repeatedly violated the Controlled Substances Act by dispensing and distributing addictive painkillers to increase its profits. The state presented evidence showing the pharmacy filled red-flagged prescriptions more than 6.5 million times without documenting its efforts to make sure the prescriptions were legitimate.

In a footnote, Helson acknowledged that many factors have contributed to the opioid epidemic â manufacturers misleading the public and medical community, well-intentioned state policies and medical community guidance regarding the need to treat pain, incompetent prescribers â but wrote that the existence of other factors, even substantial factors, does not excuse Albertsonsâ conduct.

Helson found Albertsons didnât properly staff its pharmacies, nor properly train the pharmacists on dispensing controlled substances. Nor did the pharmacy establish an adequate compliance department, putting company profit over patient safety, Helson determined.

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown celebrated the courtâs ruling.

âThis is a victory for the people of Washington. When giant corporations put profits above safety, they will be held accountable,â Brown said in a statement. âThis verdict canât undo the devastating harms of the opioid crisis, but it will provide desperately needed resources to support treatment and prevent future crises.â

An expert witness testified that more than 19,000 state residents died from opioid-related overdoses between 1999 and 2023. During that time, the death rate nearly quadrupled from 3.5 to 36.2 per 100,000.

Over the last three years, 7,400 Washingtonians have died from opioid overdoses.

The stateâs evidence illustrated how Washingtonâs opioid crisis has decreased public safety, increased criminal justice costs and strained local government and law enforcement, Helson wrote. It also showed how the crisis has impacted public spaces, with a rise in homelessness, public drug use and litter of used needles and drug paraphernalia.

The state said the $900 million will help expand treatment and prevention resources.

Albertsons did not respond to a request for comment before press time.

#7674. Court to hear argument on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for violations of the Constitution

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Monday, Nov. 9, in a lawsuit brought by a Hawaii man, Kekai Watanabe, who contends that a prison paramedic violated his constitutional rights when he failed to provide medical treatment after Watanabe was injured during a fight while in federal custody. Both the paramedic, Francis Nielsen, and the Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting Nielsen, urge the justices to shut down Watanabe’s case; Nielsen also suggests that the court should go even further and foreclose efforts to recover from federal officials for violations of the Constitution.

More than 50 years ago, in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, the Supreme Court ruled that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages.

In the years that followed, the justices have extended their decision in Bivens only twice. In Davis v. Passman, in 1979, the court held that a former congressional staffer could sue a member of Congress for alleged sex discrimination in violation of the Fifth Amendment. And in Carlson v. Green, the court held that the estate of an inmate, who died after having an asthma attack, could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

But since then the court has resisted efforts to rely on Bivens. Four years ago, in Egbert v. Boule, it observed that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.” Moreover, Justice Clarence Thomas noted for the majority “that if we were called to decide Bivens today, we would decline to discover any implied causes of action in the Constitution. But,” Thomas wrote, “to decide the case before us, we need not reconsider Bivens itself.”

In the present case, Watanabe was badly injured during a gang-related fight while at a federal detention center in Hawaii. He contends that he told Nielsen, who treated him, that his pain was a 10 on a scale of 1 to 10, but Nielsen gave him only over-the-counter pain medication. Watanabe alleges that he was kept in solitary confinement for more than two months, during which he did not see a specialist or go to a hospital. When Watanabe eventually obtained an x-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

In February 2022, Watanabe went to federal court in Honolulu. Relying on Bivens and Carlson, he alleged that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment because Nielsen was deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs.

The district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim arose in a new context – that is, it was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case for his claim to go forward.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to new contexts,” but in its view “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

Nielsen appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

In his brief on the merits, Nielsen contends that Watanabe’s case fails both prongs of the “demanding two-part test” that the Supreme Court has established for Bivens claims. That test, he adds, boils down to “whether there is any reason to think Congress might be better equipped to create a damages remedy.”

The first question is whether the claim arises in a new context from the three cases in which it has recognized Bivens claims. “Even ‘small’ differences from the original Bivens trio” of cases “will present a new context,” Nielsen writes: “‘a modest extension is still an extension.’” Watanabe’s claim, Nielsen argues, is not modest but is instead “meaningfully—profoundly—different” from Carlson. As an initial matter, he says, the facts are markedly dissimilar, because the inmate in Carlson died just hours after the attack, so that monetary compensation for his estate was the only possible remedy. By contrast, Nielsen asserts, Watanabe’s “injury was neither fatal nor life-threatening,” and instead of monetary damages he could have sought more treatment or a move to a hospital through either internal prison appeals or by filing a lawsuit in court.

If the context is new, Nielsen continues, the next question is whether “there are ‘special factors’ indicating that” courts are “at least arguably less equipped than Congress to ‘weigh the costs and benefits of allowing a damages action to proceed.’ ‘If there is even a single “reason to pause before applying Bivens in a new context,” a court may not recognize a Bivens remedy.’” Nielsen points to at least two “special factors” at play in this case that “‘suggest[] that Congress did [not] want’” prisoners to be able to recover monetary compensation from federal officials. First, he said, the Administrative Remedy Program – a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979 – “provides an alternative remedial structure for federal prisoners.” Second, he added, the Prison Litigation Reform Act, enacted in 1996, requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

Nielsen further tells the justices that they should throw out not only Watanabe’s claim but Bivens along with it. Bivens, Davis, and Carlson, he says, “are relics of the bygone days when federal courts thought it appropriate to create causes of action congress had not authorized.”

The federal government sides with Nielsen to the extent that he argues that Watanabe’s claim should be thrown out. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the court that “Carlson has become entirely obsolete” in light of new laws like the PLRA and the creation of the ARP. “And given courts’ lack of authority and expertise in setting prison policy,” Sauer said, “courts will always have a reason to pause before extending Carlson to that new context. That means that no more Carlson claims will be viable.” But, Sauer continues, the court should decline Nielsen’s suggestion to “consider overruling Bivens in this case. If the Court wishes to consider that question,” Sauer writes, “it should do so in the context of a Fourth Amendment case that more closely resembles Bivens itself.”

In his brief, Watanabe insists that his case “arises in th[e] prototypical Carlson context.” “It is,” he writes, “a damages action against a federal prison officer who was deliberately indifferent to a federal prisoner’s serious medical needs in violation of the Eighth Amendment.” Moreover, he continues, both his claim and the claim in Carlson involved “the same kind of defendant in the same kind of federal institution under the same legal framework.” The fact that he suffered from a different medical problem than Carlson, or that the inmate in Carlson died while Watanabe survived does not make his case a “new context,” he argues. Instead, he contends, such differences “are case-specific, factual variations to which” Carlson’s “settled rule applies.”

Watanabe pushes back against Nielsen’s contention that, because he is still alive, he (unlike the inmate in Carlson) also has other remedies available to him. Only money, he says, can compensate him for “his past pain and suffering.”

Watanabe tells the justices that, contrary to Nielsen’s suggestion, Congress has indicated that claims like his and the one in Carlson should be allowed to go forward, albeit with some restrictions. He points first to the Westfall Act, a 1988 law that stripped prisoners of their ability to sue federal officers under state law for their injuries, but specifically carved out an exception for “federal constitutional claims like those in Carlson.” And although the Prison Litigation Reform Act requires prisoners to pursue all of their internal appeals “before pursuing a Carlson claim,” it nonetheless shows, Watanabe argues, that Congress intended for Carlson claims to be available.

Watanabe urges the justices to leave Carlson in place even if the court might reach a different decision today. Among other things, he argues, that decision “was not egregiously wrong” and Congress has relied on it in fashioning remedies for inmates – two factors that courts consider when deciding whether to overturn their prior cases. And more broadly, he contends, if the Supreme Court were to overrule Carlson, it “would create a novel situation, never contemplated by Congress, in which federal prisoners who are subjected to needless suffering in violation of the Eighth Amendment have no recourse against the responsible officers.”

A decision in the case is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7673. The midterms and SCOTUS

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In the aftermath of Election Day, Republicans and Democrats alike are grappling with what the blue wave means for the Supreme Court. Keep reading to learn how the Senate shake-up, in particular, could affect when a justice next leaves the court and how the confirmation process might unfold.

Plus, one year ago today, the justices heard argument in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, a challenge to President Donald Trump’s tariff regime. Just over three months later, the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs, holding that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not give the president the authority to impose tariffs.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

Tomorrow, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

#7672. Court to consider the reach of Article III courts in immigration contract dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem sure to get their focused attention: does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers.

Here, the Department of Labor, employing administrative law judges, for several decades has adjudicated disputes under the H-2A visa program, which allows employers to hire temporary foreign agricultural workers. The Department of Labor argues that Sun Valley Orchards failed in several ways to compensate such workers as it promised the government it would to qualify for the H-2A program. As is typical in such cases, administrative employees of the DOL (in its wage and hour division) charged Sun Valley with failing to live up to its obligations, and the DOL for the most part persuaded an ALJ that it was correct. On appeal, a different group of the DOL’s employees (its administrative review board) accepted the ALJ’s findings. At that point, for the first time, Sun Valley had a chance to take the dispute before Article III judges, but under the applicable statute the federal district court owes great deference to the DOL’s adjudication.

The case comes to the justices because the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit reasoned that the administrative adjudication of the department’s charges cannot be reconciled with Article III of the Constitution.

At a high level of generality, the doctrinal framework here is quite clear. All agree that Congress constitutionally can authorize adjudication by executive branch officials rather than judges, and all agree that its power to do so is limited to cases that involve “public rights,” a notoriously vague category designed to distinguish traditionally executive actions (like granting a visa) from disputes traditionally resolved in court (like tort and contract litigation). When those adjudications go beyond public rights, though, they infringe on the judiciary’s exclusive authority under Article III. The difficulty is that when you get down to details – defining the boundaries of “public rights” – the rulings have neither been stable nor persuasive. The point was made best by Chief Justice William Rehnquist (channeling Matthew Arnold), who famously characterized the decisions as “landmarks on a judicial ‘darkling plain’ where ignorant armies have clashed by night.”

For this particular dispute, the government contends that the case plainly involves public rights because it involves immigration or because it involves the assessment of remedies for transgression of privileges granted by the executive. By contrast, the employer characterizes the subject of the adjudication as a contract dispute. Granting the government’s free ability to decide (and adjudicate if it wishes to do so) the entitlement of any particular immigrants or group of immigrants to a visa or other immigration status, the dispute here involves whether the employer has complied with its employment contract. Because that is a prototypically private dispute – the kind of thing that could have been brought before a court at Westminster in Old England in the days of the drafting of Article III – the employer contends that it is not the kind of public right that Congress can have adjudicated by the executive.

It would be naïve to expect the justices will feel themselves constrained by the existing precedents on this topic. The case directly implicates the prerogatives of the judicial branch and the justices will see it that way. Moreover, decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a bench with a great appetite for reining in the administrative state even when precedents are settled and directly on point. And there is another problem for the government here – many of the cases they rely on predate the days of FDR and the rise of the administrative state. Furthermore, none of them crisply validates an administrative adjudication that takes money from one private party and gives it to another.

I would expect Justice Neil Gorsuch to be a major figure at the argument, as he has been pressing this particular point for several years, albeit in the context of the securities laws. For him, the government’s contention that the lower court decision would disrupt a large swath of long-accepted administrative arrangements will be a feature, not a bug. Chief Justice John Roberts also can be expected to be an important player, as he has written several of the modern opinions in the area. So this seemingly narrow dispute may herald something larger: yet another blow against the administrative state.

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.
